I.e. in 44, there are four quarter note beats, and in 68, there are six eighth note beats. (02-24-2019, 07:19 AM) sulkycellist Wrote: There's a lot of misunderstanding about the relationship between time signatures and beats. The top number in the time signature indicates how many beats there are in the measure, and the bottom indicates what note length gets the beat. I.e. in 44, there are four quarter note beats, and in 68, there are six eighth note beats. That makes sense. And the time signature does not change the tempo, it only changes the length of the notes. There's also a lot of confusion about that. The time signature (or meter) is independent of tempo, so yes, the time signature does change the length of the notes, but the tempo can also change the length of the notes. The time signature determines how many beats there are per measure, and the tempo determines how long a beat is. Georgian architecture followed the English Baroque style of renowned figures such as Sir Christopher Wren, Sir John Vanbrugh, Thomas Archer, William Talman, and Nicholas Hawksmoor, persisting until at least the 1720s when it began to overlap with a less extravardant Georgian style. James Gibbs played an essential role during this transitionary phase; although his initial designs reflected his experiences in Rome during the early 18th century, he later shifted towards a simpler style post-1720. Several notable architects contributed significantly to this stylistic evolution away from Baroque, including Colen Campbell, Richard Boyle (the 3rd Earl of Burlington) along with his protégé William Kent, Isaac Ware, Henry Flitcroft, and Giacomo Leoni, an Italian architect who mostly worked in England. Additional key figures of this era comprise James Paine, Robert Taylor, and John Wood, the Elder. During this time, the popularity of the European Grand Tour among affluent individuals led to the enduring impact of Italian design. Nevertheless, certain locations like Hanover Square in Westminster, established in 1713 and inhabited primarily by supporters of the new ruling house, seemed intentional in integrating Germanic motifs as tribute, particularly evident through features like continuous vertical lines between window panes.

We can predict earthquakes, just not with any certainty at all. Earthquakes aren't just the motion of the plates, they have friction between them, and the forces build over time. One of the problems is that the mechanisms for measuring the forces are not entirely clear yet. There's a pretty good chance that the next earthquake in California will be a magnitude 5, or possibly larger. The risk of a magnitude 6 or 7 in the next year is on the order of 10. Online debate forums and comparable digital platforms serve as crucial data sources for computational argumentation studies and practical implementations. These datasets are abundant with arguments but also contain extraneous or counterproductive material. This study introduces an approach focused on identifying irrelevant content through semi-automated methods using initial example seeds. The methodology involves learning elementary word patterns indicating relevance or irrelevance and progressively expanding them based on sentence matches. Applied to the argu.me dataset comprising 400,000 argumentative pieces, it identified nearly 87,000 nonessential sentences with a high accuracy rate of 0.97 via human assessment. Furthermore, this technique requires minimal adjustments when applied to different online argument databases, offering a universal solution for enhancing data quality.

She was very, very sick. Sick enough that she managed to turn her eyes away from what was happening. What he was doing. She was very, very sick, but he promised he'd make her all better. He promised he'd save her, day after day. It meant killing more than a handful of people, yes. And it is true, she remembered, that she said "No!" And she also said "No way, I'm not letting you do this." At first. But death has a way of tricking and shadowing the mind. It has a way of making men and women do things they thought they would never. Death has a way of bringing the worst in people; men and women, muggle and wizard alike. And, in the end, she agreed. She agreed, and he started killing. And he brought the bodies back to her, one by one, and day after day, they'd perform the spell. Transferring faded lives into him. Give him one more year to live. And then, then he would give her another day. Then they would dump the body in the attic, with the others. A life for a day, she would think, tears in her eyes, watching as he brought home body after body. She knew it was killing him, too. She knew. More than once she caught him crying, in the dead of the night, hating himself in secret for what he was doing. She knew it was killing him to become a killer. Death has a way of bringing out the worst in people. Yet she dared not say anything. Not at first. She was too scared. Scared he might give up. Scared he might stop it all, and that she would die. Scared of the void and the blackness and the unknown. "Together, you and me, we are gon na live forever," he would say, holding on to her hand for dear life, as he sat by her side on the bed. "We are gon na live forever." And, for a while, she believed him. She conceived an endless empire of eternal life, filled with dead innocent eyes and rising from under a pile of motionless, rotten bodies. She conceived a dream of infinity, just the two of them, surrounded forever by death and sin and love. And she wallowed in it, for a while. For a while, she even cherished it. But, in time, she saw into the madness, and came across sanity again. In time, getting up from the bed and dragging herself into the attic, she stared at the bodies, piles and piles of memories and human lives: friends, fathers, mothers, accountants. Lawyers. Aurors. Real people, giving their lives away so she could live one more day. Always, just one more day. Death. It has a way of bringing out the worst in people. It had to end, she decided. He wouldn't accept it, not at first. She sat him down and explained to him, between his tears, that it was time; she had accepted her death. It had to stop, all that massacre. "No, no, no," he uttered, between sniffs and snorts of despair. "I won't let you go." "You have to," she replied. "You have to, my love." "What of me? What am I to do once you're gone?" He asked, falling from the chair to his knees. "I won't let you do this, I won't!" "I will not perform my part of the spell anymore. You can not stop me." She lowered herself to the floor by him, holding his pale face between her hands. "It's over. I have to do this." "No. No!" His face contorted in an ugly grimace. His bitterness half anger, half sadness. "We will conquer this! We will conquer death!" "There is no more to conquer," she whispered, and, already, she could feel life fading away inside of her. Almost midnight. It was about the time of the spell. Without it, she would die. She dropped down to the floor, too weak now to even sit up. "Let me do it. Once again. Just one more day" He begged, leaning over her lay down body. "No, it ends now." Her voice was fading. She looked over at the wall, where the clock was seconds away from striking midnight. "It ends now." "I can not let you go. I can not. I hate this. I hate this. I love you." Raising her arm, she brushed her hand softly across his face, wiping the tears from his cheekbones. "I love you too. My beautiful Tom. My beautiful, beloved Tom Riddle." Death. It has a way of bringing out the worst in people, she thought, watching as the anger part of bitterness took over his pale face, just as she felt life finally giving away inside her chest. And then, the soft bell of the wall clock announced midnight, and her eyes closed forever.

"Right this way, ma'am." The butler said, turning down a hallway. He was tall, with an immaculate tuxedo and white mustache so straight that it appeared as if it had been cut with a laser. Typical. "Your quarters are right down this hallway, last door on the left." He said, gesturing to an open wooden doorframe. "I shall do you the favor of not intruding on your hall - and I expect you to extend the same courtesy to me. That is the first rule of this household, I am afraid: Irregulars shall not mix with others. That includes staff, so don't go getting any ideas." "Alright. I get it." I sighed, blowing a strand of unkempt brown hair out of my face. It wasn't the first time I had been quarantined, and somehow I felt it wouldn't be the last. "What about my things? Are they being sent up?" "Your..... things..... have been burned." The butler replied. "But I I started, outraged, but the butler cut me off with a gloved hand "Ah! Not a word!" He said. "They were in terrible condition, even the ones that weren't contaminated with filth. You should be grateful - the Master has seen to it that they have all been replaced. Not that you deserve it, in my opinion. Now, will that be all?" "Yes..." I grumbled. "Perfect. I expect you down by seven, washed and dressed in..... something clean." He rubbed his hands together, as if to remove dirt from his spotless gloves. "That brings me to rule number two of our household: Punctuality makes perfect. So don't be late." The door shut, and I heard a key turning in the lock. I sighed again. "The Master take a liking to you, too?" I jumped, almost colliding with the door as I whirled around. One of the doors lining the hall was open just a crack, letting a head covered in shiny blond hair poke through at just about waste level. "H-hello there." I said. "How old are you?" "I'm the one asking questions here, bitch. No need to crack jokes." The door opened wider, and I gasped as a woman walked through. Her face looked young, beautiful even, - but at her full height, she only came up to my waste. "I-I'm sorry!" I said, feeling my cheeks turn red. "I didn't realize..." The woman erupted into a loud cackle, cutting me off. "I know, dear, I know. Just having a bit of fun. You don't get to look like this without having a sense of humor - at least, not if you want to enjoy life a bit. So, you going to answer my question or not?" "Oh, ummm..." I replied, somewhat taken aback, but the woman just laughed even louder. "Is your problem that you don't have a tongue? Come on woman, spit it out!" "No it's not that..... it's..." I floundered for words, before finally settling on raising my left hand. The woman whistled. "Ooo..... that is a rare one. You don't see to many people with fused fingers these days. No wonder he liked you. How'd you get past the system this long?" "I..... was a natural birth." I said, the words spilling out before I could stop them. "My parents, they said I was perfect..... but with my hand..." "Oh, honey, it's ok!" The woman pulled me into an odd embrace. "Mine said the same thing. Of course, even they couldn't pass up on the price Master Jackson coughed up." She laughed somewhat bitterly. " 'S that what happened to you?" I shook my head. "No..... they. They aren't around any more." I blinked, realizing what I had just said. "It's ok though! I manage just fine on my own!" I amended, somewhat belatedly. "Of course you do, honey." The woman patted my waist affectionately. "Listen, I'd love to stay and chat, but that old bastard Ronnie's gon na be back here any minute to collect us for dinner. You don't want to get on the wrong side of that one." "R-right." I stammered. "Don't worry about that for now, honey. Just do what he says and everything will be just fine. And if anyone gives you any trouble, just tell them that ol' Kathrine will come bite their nads off unless they leave you alone! You got that, girl?" I nodded, brushing away tears. "Got it, Kathrine. Thanks." "Not a problem, honey." Her door snapped shut, and once again I found myself utterly alone.

When referring to 'assholes,' I am talking about individuals you personally find objectionable, rather than my personal opinion – it's yours. Observers often express disdain towards indulgent parents whose children exhibit entitled behavior, and resentment arises when an unpleasant coworker receives a promotion. There appears to be a logical aversion to witnessing immoral individuals fulfill their desires. No one roots for the antagonist to succeed; moreover, those who assist or fail to oppose such individuals are seen as complicit in the issue. As Edmund Burke famously stated, "The only thing necessary for the triumph of evil is for good men to do nothing." This raises the question: shouldn't we extend this concept to choosing our sexual partners? Ideally, sex should bring pleasure to both participants, requiring mutual enablement. Furthermore, since the notion of sex as a transactional experience exists (as evidenced by the prevalence of prostitution), one cannot assume someone doesn't subscribe to it, especially during moments of success. Consequently, it isn't far-fetched to suggest that engaging in sexual activities may lead individuals to feel rewarded, due to positive emotions and receiving something deemed valuable. This paper presents the link availability probability. We evaluate and compare the link availability probability for routing protocols; Ad hoc On-demand Distance vector (AODV), Dynamic Source Routing (DSR) and Fisheye Optimized Cost Estimation (FOCE). All three implementations have nearly identical performance when compared to each other, but they differ in their affect on network topology or security. DSR has a limited range of applications as it is an ad hoc protocol that cannot exchange information with fully-routed networks due to its inherent limitations, while AODV offers uncertain source location without any guarantee towards more efficient links, thus making it suitable for some applications such as peer-to-peer communication where privacy is essential. FOCE requires specialized hardware to implement which makes it unsuitable for most use cases. In this case we show how well our proposed systems perform under various conditions, including pre-existing path reliability and randomness of traffic sources and destinations at both ends. In summary, from experience, we noticed that there are no clearly defined solutions available even after years of networking research (especially in wireless environments); hence, what works great today might not be applicable tomorrow. Therefore, before deploying new routing technologies we should thoroughly analyze the existing options, especially through performance tests on real life scenarios. And just like a pilot airplane needs checklists before flying, so too does a router need similar checks before taking off into space!

Gibbs sampling is a Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling technique that iteratively samples variables from their conditional distributions. There are two common scan orders for the variables: random scan and ordered scan. Random scan randomly chooses variables to sample from their conditional distributions, while ordered scan cycles through the variables in a predefined order. Gibbs sampling is used to approximate a joint distribution by combining the conditional distributions of the individual variables in the model. It can be used for Bayesian inference, maximum likelihood estimation (MLE), and other types of estimation.

Motor Neuron Disease eventually takes away its victim's ability to speak, but a new AI-based tool developed by Rolls-Royce may help patients speak again. Rolls Royce worked with the Motor Neurone Disease Association and the University of Bath to develop the tool. It uses AI and machine learning to analyze the patient's brain activity and respond to their speech patterns. The goal is to help patients with MND speak without the use of a keyboard or an eye-gaze system, which can be challenging for those with limited hand and eye movement. The speech therapy tool is still in the development stage, but the Rolls-Royce team hopes to have it available in the coming years. Researchers looked at three areas of England, 20 years apart, and found new rates of dementia were lower than past trends would suggest. They say improvements in men's health is the most likely explanation. But charities warn against complacency, with more than 200,000 dementia cases diagnosed each year in the UK. Researchers, funded by the Medical Research Council and dementia charities, interviewed about 7,500 people aged 65 and over living in Cambridgeshire, Nottingham and Newcastle in the early 1990s. The whole process, which included detailed questionnaires about cognition and lifestyle, was repeated in the same way two decades later. They found rates of new cases of dementia had been fairly steady in women over this time, but had fallen in men. Extrapolating their findings to apply to the rest of the UK, they say there would be 40,000 fewer cases of the disease than estimates put forward two decades ago would suggest. Scientists admit they are unsure exactly what lies behind this trend but say it could be that men have become better at looking after themselves. For example, better heart and brain health - with fewer men smoking, less salt used in food, and a greater emphasis on exercise and blood pressure medication may have helped, they say. They acknowledge it is hard to decipher why the same trends are not apparent in women, but speculate men may be catching up on health gains that women already experience. Despite this, they warn that other factors - such as rising levels of obesity and diabetes - may reverse this trend in years to come. Prof Carol Brayne, at the University of Cambridge, and part of the research team, said: "I'm pretty optimistic that it's stabilising, but if we don't further improve health, then we would expect the numbers to go up with further ageing of the population, so it's a sort of cautious optimism." Scientists say the most important finding is that a rise in dementia is not inevitable and can be fought. And they call for a better balance of funds so more money is put into prevention in mid-life. Meanwhile, Dr James Pickett, head of research at the charity Alzheimer's Society, said the research was encouraging. But he added: "People are living for longer, and with other risk factors such as diabetes and obesity on the rise, there will still be over 200,000 new cases of dementia each year. "That's still an enormous number of people who require better information and health and social care support." Other experts point out the way dementia is diagnosed has changed over time and initiatives focusing on spotting the signs of dementia earlier may offset any reductions seen.

These bold creations represent some of the most substantial works in the annals of Cubism. In Leger's The Wedding, which was featured at the Salon des Independants in 1912, the concept of simultaneity materialized through the portrayal of diverse images coexisting within one chronological moment, merging reactions from both past and present into a powerful ensemble. The combination of this thematic content with simultaneity associates Salon Cubism with the nascent Futurist artworks created by Umberto Boccioni, Gino Severini, and Carlo Carra, who were all influenced by the initial phase of Cubism.

In a multiway relay channel (MWRC), pairwise transmission strategy can be used to reduce the computational complexity at the relay and the users without sacrificing the data rate, significantly. The secret sharing technique can be used to increase the data rate and provide secrecy at the same time in an MWRC. This paper considers the secret sharing based pairwise transmission strategy in the MWRC. Closed-form expressions for the secrecy outage probability (SOP) and the capacity are derived. We also analyze the achievable data rate and the corresponding SOP for the MWRC with the genie-aided relay and the noisy CSI at the relay. Finally, we investigate the asymptotic behavior of the SOP and the capacity when the number of users grows infinitely large.

To get away from the earth you always need to reach escape velocity (correspondingly to go into orbit you need to end below it). The thing is just that the farther you get away from the earth the lower that escape velocity gets (i.e. a "slow" rocket that left would still eventually cross escape velocity when it dropped low enough to be under its speed, if it doesn't then it can't leave and will eventually either fall back down again or go into orbit). As for why we tend not to do that, there are a few reasons. One of the big ones is that every bit of fuel you carry with you requires more fuel to lift it to that point. So burning as much as you can early reduces the weight that you'd need to carry higher before burning it. That said a lot of our rockets do actually accelerate "slowly" at first to reduce the amount of drag until they reach a low earth orbit; it's just that their "slow" is much, much faster than anything you would experience in daily life so it seems really fast.','From a physics standpoint there's nothing preventing you from escaping Earth slowly. Escape velocity depends on altitude, so as you get higher and higher you can escape with a lower and lower speed. Escape velocity is the velocity where you'll coast out of Earth's gravity, even with no more effort. If you imagine a ball thrown straight up from the moon (for the sake of ignoring drag) it experiences less and less gravity as it gets higher and higher, but it also slows down. If you throw it hard enough then gravity reduces faster than speed and it will never come back down. Due to some cool physics and complicated math it doesn't actually matter the direction you throw the ball, provided it isn't into the ground. If you throw it faster than that speed the it's never coming back down. If you threw it from a high tower then the speed you'd need to throw it at is much lower. Note that this is speaking of escape velocity. Something going to the edge of space (which most people put at 62 mi or 100 km, not 60 km) does not need to escape gravity. Astronauts on the ISS may give the appearance of zero gravity, but that's because they are being accelerated by gravity the same as the space station around them. They're still subjected to about 90-95 the same gravity as on the surface. We can also look at the question in terms of engineering. If physics allows for a spacecraft (e.g. a Mars Probe) to escape Earth's gravity slowly, why don't we? On or near the surface of Earth we can move slowly easily. Walking, driving, swimming, even ballooning all allow for slow transportation. The common feature of these modes of transportation is that they have a means of supporting weight. In space there's no ground, air, or water to support your weight, but there's still gravity. That means you have three options: support your weight with thrust, achieve orbit, or travel in a ballistic trajectory. Supporting your weight with rockets works, but it gets difficult fast. Rocket fuel is heavy and the more fuel you carry the more fuel you have to carry to lift that fuel, and so on. Spacecraft are designed to use the minimum amount of fuel necessary since fuel is such a big part of the weight of a spacecraft. Going slow means more time supporting your weight with rockets. Achieving orbit means that your weight is enough to pull your trajectory into a circular (or, usually, elliptical) orbit around Earth. In a sense you're "falling," but never getting closer to the ground because you're going sideways so fast. This isn't done slowly because the physics of orbit require a high horizontal speed. Finally, ballistic trajectories are sometimes useful (e.g. ballistic missiles) and allow for somewhat slower speeds as they don't need to achieve orbit. The Scaled Composites Spaceship One spacecraft touched space by making a brief ballistic flight out of the atmosphere. This is the closest you'll find to practical applications of going to space slowly.', "It doesn't. You could theoretically build a ladder (at least, out of super strong material) and climb it to get to space. You could even achieve escape velocity this way, if your ladder was tall enough, as it would drop as you climb, until you eventually exceeded it. Rockets go fast for two reasons, 1) to achieve orbit, as you have to move sideways very quickly to stay in orbit. This is because orbit is falling'around' the planet, and continuing to miss it. If you move sideways too slowly, then the spot you are trying to fall through won't be empty space, but instead Earth. This is bad for your flight plan. If you send a rocket straight up, it won't stay in space, gravity doesn't'run out' 60km up or anything. Once you turned the rocket off, it would plummet into the ground. 2) practicality. Fuel is heavy. If you are going slow, you need more fuel, which weighs more, which means you need more fuel to carry that fuel, and so on. This results in diminishing returns where some flight paths simply require a rocket too heavy to fly.," "It can. But going slowly with a rocket is an extremely inefficient way to get to space. Suppose you have a rocket that produces just enough thrust to support its own weight and nothing else. That rocket would burn through its entire fuel supply and never get off the pad. If instead you have a rocket that produces just enough thrust to lift off, you're going to be burning through astronomical amounts of fuel during your leisurely climb to space. And that means you need more thrust to support all that fuel, which means you need to carry even more fuel. Why does it have to exceed escape velocity? It only has to exceed escape velocity to put it on an escape trajectory. This is where the rocket has so much velocity that it will travel away from Earth forever, rather than falling back down or orbiting in an elliptical path. Escape velocity decreases with height, so a rocket could still, in principle, ascend slowly at a constant speed, and it would eventually end up on an escape trajectory. But as noted, this is an astronomically inefficient way to do things - so much so that it simply would not be possible with current technology.," "Getting to space does you no good, in and of itself. You'd just fall right back to earth. The trick is to get going sideways enough that you achieve orbit. Your velocity is exactly as fast as required for gravity to exactly bend your trajectory around the earth in a circle. Too slow and you fall back to earth. Too fast, and you go off out into space. The sideways speed is the problem, but obviously you can't just start accelerating sideways straight off the launch pad.

We evaluate chemical patent word embeddings against known biomedical embeddings and show that they outperform the latter extrinsically and intrinsically. We also show that using contextualized embeddings can induce predictive power to chemical patents, in terms of their assigned categories. We deploy a set of experiments to evaluate the effectiveness of chemical patent word embeddings. First, we compare them with known biomedical embeddings. We find that our chemical patent embeddings outperform the biomedical embeddings extrinsically (on downstream tasks) and intrinsically (in semantic similarity tasks). Next, we explore how contextualized embeddings can improve the prediction of patent categories. We show that using contextualized embeddings can increase the predictive accuracy of patent categories by up to 8. This suggests that context-aware embeddings can be used to better understand the content of chemical patents. Finally, we analyze the interpretability of the contextualized embeddings and find that they capture meaningful aspects of the chemical patent documents. Our results suggest that chemical patent word embeddings can be used to enhance existing natural language processing pipelines for patent analysis.

The old man stood in the open field, located specifically at somewhere in the middle of nowhere. It was empty save for meadow, sky and a single gravestone. Christine, it read, a single word etched into the smooth rock. This old man stared lazily at the gravestone, for his blue, cloudy eyes weren't really looking at anything. His hair shook slightly as a gentle gust came and pulled his peach beret off his head and onto the grass, but apart from that, the old man was still. His cane had been resting on the one spot for so long it had begun to dig into the earth. "Christine," he whispered from his frail mouth, the words coming out hoarse, yet beautifully melancholy if only for the weight with which he treasured the name. She had lived a happy life, he liked to think, yet despite the contentedness they had found in each other, he wished he could have given her more. He was only a boy when they had met, it wasn't any sort of perfect romance or even a tale of star-crossed lovers. Not anything of the sort. They had shared one class together in at the start high school, but no, not even there did their story begin. She sat at almost the opposite side of the room from him, with her group friends, while he..... he sat in the middle, not a social outcast, but not one of the cool kids. It was only towards the end of senior year they had gotten to know each other. They had both found themselves waiting at the bus stop, having left a friends party at around the same time. It was cold out, but unfortunately, or fortunately, this lost boy was a little too drunk to have realized he was supposed to offer his jacket to her. "Aren't you going to offer me your jacket, Eddie?" She'd asked him, in a light-hearted fashion. "But then I'd be cold." He told her, not catching that she'd said it simply to break the awkward silence. She looked at him, with one of those'You're so daft' kind of looks. Silence. He remembered. She had just turned her head to the street, anticipating the buses arrival any moment. That was when he had first looked at her. Not looked like he glanced past and she happened to be in somewhere in the frame of his eyes, but looked like truly looked at the girl who stood beside him. The gravestone grew blurry as a single tear floated into the eye of the old man. She had been as beautiful the day he saw him to the day he had held her hand while the doctors explained what they had found, and every day in between. Even the days they fought, like the one time he had to sleep at Paul, his friend's house, because Christine had been furious about his inability to help her around the house. They both worked, yet everyday he would come home and sit on the couch with a beer while watching the game while she would come home and start cooking dinner. Her food..... her food was home. Recipes passed down from her mother to her that remained the only traces of the little town they had grown up in after they'd moved to the city. One day she had had enough, and told him that if he didn't cook dinner or at the very least help cook it, he couldn't sleep in this house. Being the prideful, and stupid, and selfish man he was, he'd just walked out of the house. That was the first night they spent away from each other after being married, it wasn't the last. It wasn't a perfect marriage, but- the old man looked at the gravestone and chuckled a little, tears now streaming down his face from both eyes- "Perfection is overrated," she would always tell him. It really was, he thought to himself. His face a complete mess from the tears layered on his skin, and his eyes red on the edges, but he was smiling now. Smiling because he remembered that one time she had introduced him to Pearl Jam and how he hadn't listened to another band's music for almost 2 weeks, and that one time she had played piano for him in the dead of night when he'd snuck himself into her house while her parents were away, and he..... he'd just listened to her, and watched her fingers make some of the most beautiful sounds he'd heard, simply because of the weight with which he had loved the person creating them. And the night he had proposed to her, under the night sky, in front of the bus stop that he had first met her at. And then the old man was crying; crying because he remembered when the doctor had explained to them her arthritis, and the solemn look on her whenever she sat at the piano and struggled to make it sing for her. Crying because she had never looked as happy as he remembered since that day and crying because of the night years later that he had found her collapsed at the doorway, because of the morning after when the doctor told them what they had found in her breasts, and the months after spent sitting beside a hospital bed and today. Today. He stood staring at her grave. Unable to see under the tears piled on top his eyes. The materials, which can sense pressure as sensitively and quickly as human skin, have been outlined by two groups reporting in Nature Materials. The skins are arrays of small pressure sensors that convert tiny changes in pressure into electrical signals. The arrays are built into or under flexible rubber sheets that could be stretched into a variety of shapes. The materials could be used to sheath artificial limbs or to create robots that can pick up and hold fragile objects. They could also be used to improve tools for minimally-invasive surgery. In one approach, Ali Javey at the University of California, Berkeley, and his colleagues built up layers of criss-crossed nanometre-scale wires topped with a thin rubber sheet. Together, the stack acts as what is known as a thin-film transistor, or TFT, with a pressure-sensitive layer on top. The amount of electrical current running through the device is dependent upon how much pressure is exerted on the rubber sheet; more pressure allows more current to flow. The team demonstrated the flexibility of their TFT stacks by bending them to a radius smaller than that of a pencil without changing the skin's performance. "Javey's work is a nice demonstration of their capability in making a large array of nanowire TFTs," said Zhenan Bao of Stanford University, whose group demonstrated the second approach. The heart of Professor Bao's devices is micro-structured rubber sheet in the middle of the TFT - effectively re-creating the functionality of the Berkeley group's skins with less layers. "Instead of laminating a pressure-sensitive resistor array on top of a nanowire TFT array, we made our transistors to be pressure sensitive," Professor Bao explained to BBC News. "Our microstructured rubber can bounce back to its original shape much faster and enable higher sensitivity," she added. The overall flexibility of the Stanford group's skins appears to be lower, and Professor Bao concedes that to develop her group's approach further, better conductive rubber will be needed. Nevertheless, both groups demonstrate that their skins can register a pressure in a tenth of a second, over a large range - from five grams per square centimetre to 40 times that high. Those numbers rival the response of human skin, made with relatively inexpensive manufacturing techniques. John Boland, a nanotechnologist from Trinity College Dublin, praised the two approaches in a critique for Nature Materials. "Perhaps the most remarkable aspect of these studies is how they elegantly demonstrate that it is possible to exploit well-established processing technologies to engineer low-cost innovative solutions to important technical problems," he wrote. However, he notes that there are still "significant opportunities for further innovation," such as reducing the distance between the sensors in the arrays to maximise the detail they could "feel," as well as improvements that could make large-area arrays possible and affordable.

The sun was just starting to creep up in the horizon when they finished passing through the arid desert and started turning towards coastal land. Daniel rolled the windows down in the sedan with New York tags and took a breath as the air cooled. It smelt like the ocean, crisp and breezy. He turned and smiled to the passenger car. "We're almost there mum." She hadn't said it, but a year ago when she had grabbed his hand in the doctor's waiting room, and told him the news, he had started planning their last trip west on the drive to her home. He had hoped it would have taken longer, but the past year had taken its toll and two weeks ago, when they were sitting at the kitchen table eating breakfast, she had grabbed his hand and with an intensity in her eyes startling for a morning and said, "It's time." The woman in question didn't respond to his previous utterance, as she was laid back in the seat, head pressed against her jacket rolled up into a make shift pillow. The previous day's horse back ride through Joshua Tree and the desert had taken most of her energy. It had been an effort getting her awake and into the car before dawn but the visit had been worth it. His mother was born right in the land they were driving through, between the mountain canyons and the ocean on the west coast. She was a Katie, never Katherine, a painter, a story teller, a free spirit, and vagabond at heart. But even when she found his dad, fell in love and happily followed him clear across the country into Boston, then New York, making a home in the big cities of the east coast for fifty years, she still had a special love for her childhood home. He remembered how he had found her in the early morning, ten years ago, standing by the lighthouse in Montauk right after they'd buried dad. She had told him, "I always feel at home most, in wide open spaces, under the stars. I just needed a little bit of that feeling, now, you know?" It wasn't a surprise honestly, he clearly remembers the road trips the little family saved up for and took every couple of years. The three of them piling into a car and making the drive from New York to California. His dad was the type to stop at every roadside attraction, stretch his legs every rest station, and buy a t-shirt in every state, but his mum, she always tried to push him to hurry, with a buzzing energy that wouldn't let loose at least until they hit the midwest. "Daniel William Connor, the boiled peanuts in Indiana are going to taste exactly the same as the ones form the roadside stand in Ohio!" He remembers falling asleep across the backseat, watching his parents with drooping eyes, dad drawing out vowels and teasing in an impression of valley girl accent, "Hold your horses Katie, we're almost to Cal-eee-for-niiii-a." He pulled the sedan into a parking space just as the sun was halfway above the horizon, casting the horizon in a pink and golden dawn, but the sky above the ocean was still a deep blue. His mother had awakened. Yawning she cleared her eyes and sighed happily as she took in her surroundings. He barely had enough time to shut the car off and lock it before his mother took off along the boardwalk connecting the lot to the beach. Her shoes were kicked off well before her toes hit the sand. While she grabbed onto his arm for support, she walked with purpose up the shore. They'd made this trek countless times. He didn't speak much, letting his attention wonder. She'd point out when she'd see a particular beautiful seashell to scoop up, or call attention to a crab scuttling by. The sun was hanging above the horizon when she stopped their walk along the sand. She turned and led them toward the ocean, stopped and let her feet dig into where the waves lapped up onto shore, sand pulling at her feet, contented smile on her face. They stood with the sun warming their backs as the last remaining stars faded into the lightening sky and she leaned her head against his shoulder. "You know Daniel, as much as I love the city life we've made, I always feel at home most under the wide open sky, under the stars." He winced, but he felt compelled to answer for the both of them. "I know mum. We've always known." She continued right on smiling, "You know, if I have a boy, we can name him after you. But he should grow up in his own skin! Have a name to call his own along with yours." He knew the next line, as she had told him so many times before. "You call him Daniel all you want, but he'll be my Joshua, so he can always have a piece of my home with him."

Ten eggs were harvested from the last two remaining northern white rhinoceroses, potentially saving the species from extinction. Neither of the white rhinos can carry a baby to term, so scientists from Kenya and the United States implanted the eggs in southern white rhinoceroses. It's not the first time a northern white rhino egg has been fertilized in vitro, but it's the first time an embryo survived. The team injected the sperm of a northern white rhino male into the eggs. Although the male died in 2014, scientists were able to salvage some of his sperm. "Throughout their history, rhinos have recovered from the brink of extinction, so we hope that we can use this development to help the northern white rhino recover too," said Katsuhiko Hayashi, head of the BioResource Center at the University of Kyoto. "This is the first step in a long process," said Richard Vigne, CEO of the Ol Pejeta Conservancy. What are the perfect ingredients for a disaster that everyone would forget? 11 years later, would the public still want answers? Give it enough time and mysteries become myths. People don't want to know, it ruins the fun. And yet, here we are. Me and a tech kid I hired. He's German, speaks English like Stephen fucking Fry and has that kind of new romantic haircut that no one from my neck of the woods has worn since the 80s. God, he's pissing me off. He thinks I need him, just because he's got that tracker round his neck. I can read a data blip too, Hans. His name's not really Hans but I call him that because of his enormous hands. "We have to keep the pace up, Eoan. Pick up's 6 hours off." He pronounces my name perfectly, the prick. "I'm 50 years old, Hans. I'm not..... 14, or whatever the fuck it is you are." "I'll take that as a compliment." He's got a grin you could happily take an electric drill to. "The signal reads beyond the tree line up there," Hans tells me for the third time. "We'll make it within two hours if we keep pushing." "Fuck it." My legs are going a bit. "Ah, come on, Eoan, you Irish are used to a little adversity. One foot in front of the other, is that the saying?" "No, you must have translated that from one of the other hundred languages you know, Hans." Hans sighed when I said this, as if to say he's an engineer, he doesn't come from a culture where learning is mocked, he's to good to read too much into other people's sighs. Yeah, he's that kind of guy. But I always find it helps when you don't like them. What feels like 5 hours later is actually 2, and we are nearing the tree line. The views behind me are spectacular, presumably. Hans keeps looking behind him and gasping with typical Aryan vapidness. "Signal is strong here." Hans knows who I am. But he doesn't know exactly why I'm here. He thought he'd be coming with another tech or with a grizzled explorer-type. Not a greying, internet-explorer-type like me. We get up into the tree line and we see the ridge pretty soon. It's not as high as we thought, but the trees are huge. "How much further, Hans?" "You know Eoan, you keep calling me that and it might just stick!" Fuck you Hans, with your perfect use of idioms. "About 40 yards beyond the ridge, we should find something." "Okay," I'm glad this will soon be over, "the box will settle with sensors facing north, unless it is stuck in place. You're looking for a bright orange strip which will be facing upwards." "Yes, boss." Eurgh, why did he have to call me that. It's just going to make things harder. Over the ridge is a nice little flat clearing and then beyond that is a huge fuck-off waterfall. "This place is incredible, man. I'm surprised there aren't a few hotels." "Just look around, Hans. You'll get room service later." I sort of feel bad for the kid. Whole life ahead of him. "Orange!" He yells. Sealing his own fate. I look where he's pointing and sure enough, there it is. LEDs still going and everything. Thank God we found it before anyone else. I trudge over and grab the thing - it's about 6 kilos, just lying in some fern things in the clearing. I pick it up and head over to the waterfall. "Eoan, what are you doing? We're headed the other way. Don't go too close." "Come here, Hans, I want to show you something!" I'm shouting a bit against the spray. He hesitates. "Come on, kid, I want you to be here for this." His eyes glance down at the water and he takes a step before stopping. "Suit yourself, asshole." With that, I fling the box as far into the waterfall as I can, and it gets swallowed up instantly by the water. "No! What the hell?!" Hans is going crazy like a fucking puppy. Eurgh..... I do feel bad now. "It was my plane, Hans. So it's my box." "But, your wife. You'll never know what happened to her or all those other people? What is wrong with you? You'll never know.." "I already fucking know what the box will say, Hans." I am so glad to get this thing out of my pocket. The barrell has been chaffing at my leg for the whole hike. "Sheize." The first time he's slipped out of English. It takes a fucking gun. "Do you wan na walk closer to the edge for me before I do this, Hans, or are you gon na make me drag you?"

To date, most studies on spam have focused only on the spamming phase of the spam cycle and have ignored the harvesting phase, which consists of the mass acquisition of email addresses from the Internet. In this paper, we present a data set consisting of 12.5 million emails collected from a single spam harvester, spammed by almost 20,000 distinct spammers. We describe how the data set was collected and describe the spam harvester, as well as the spammers that used it. We then analyze the data set to gain insight into the methods used by the spammers and the spam harvester, as well as the characteristics of the harvested email addresses. We also compare this data set to a similar one that was collected from another spam harvester. In addition, we present a novel technique for detecting harvester-spammer relationships. Our results demonstrate that the data set is representative of the overall spam harvesting population and shows that spammers often use harvesting software that is similar to one another. We would like to thank the CMU Information Networking Institute and the Hewlett-Packard Research Laboratories for their financial support of this work. 10.1109ICDS.

Although strong selective pressure is believed to reduce genetic diversity, a significant number of species display remarkable variations based on genetics. Frequency dependent selection is frequently used by researchers to account for the continuation of variation. Our research aligns with an increasing amount of proof indicating that a multifaceted type of balancing selection could possibly clarify how color polymorphism has evolved and is sustained in a specific fish species. This research specifically shows that competition between males of the same species leads to the development of physically distinguishable males who display varying levels of aggression to eliminate other males as potential sexual competitors. The males who are more aggressive and dominant can bypass the female preference for attractive males. On the other hand, some males have subordinate behaviors that help them circumvent both male aggression and female mating preferences. The combination of recent and past findings suggests that males may develop unique mating strategies by taking advantage of various forms of social interactions, which contributes to the preservation of genetic diversity within populations.

At least 1.8 million more households will be looking to rent rather than buy a home by 2025, the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (Rics) claims. It has called on the government to build 3 million more homes in the next eight years to meet the growing demand. A survey of 370 chartered surveyors revealed that 42 believe renting will increase as a proportion of the total housing stock, with 40 predicting that it will fall. Mortgage interest rates have been at a record low, but Rics said that this would not be enough to encourage potential buyers to commit to buying a home. In a separate survey, 24 of respondents said that the cost of borrowing money had increased, while 42 said that the availability of mortgages had increased. In the past year, the number of people living in private rented accommodation increased by 8 to 8.4 million. Rics' spokesman Jeremy Blackburn said: "The number of households in the UK is expected to grow by more than 2 million in the next eight years and we estimate that at least 1.8 million of these will be looking to rent rather than buy a home. "A lack of new homes is driving demand for rental properties and with average incomes failing to keep up with rents, we will see a growing number of people unable to afford to buy a home." The government has already pledged to build 170,000 affordable homes by 2015.

Not every type of wine improves as it ages. For instance, a bottle-aged Bordeaux offers a vastly different tasting experience compared to a young Beaujolleshould only be consumed within three months. The Bordeaux matures between six months to five years in the bottle, whereas the Beaujoulais, typically released in early November, becomes unsuitable for consumption by late January. To learn more about this topic, visit [this link](URL0) or consult knowledgeable staff at your neighborhood liquor store; however, there is an inherent limitation. All wine contains alcohol (ethanol), which naturally converts to acetic acid over time. This transformation leads to spoiled wines that are generally not desirable for drinking. The rate of conversion varies based on how well the wine has been stored. Proper storage extends the period during which the wine remains enjoyable. Additionally, like any other perishable item, wine comes with an expiration date, indicating when the manufacturer believes the wine maintains its quality. Consuming the wine after this date is still safe but may result in diminished flavors.

We develop a general framework for proving rigorous guarantees on the performance of the EM algorithm and a variant known as gradient EM. Our analysis is divided into two parts: a treatment of these algorithms at the population level (in the limit of infinite data), followed by results that apply to updates based on a finite set of samples. First, we characterize the domain of attraction of any global maximizer of the population likelihood. This characterization is based on a novel view of the EM updates as a perturbed form of likelihood ascent, or in parallel, of the gradient EM updates as a perturbed form of standard gradient ascent. Leveraging this characterization, we then provide non-asymptotic guarantees on the EM and gradient EM algorithms when applied to a finite set of samples. We develop consequences of our general theory for three canonical examples of incomplete-data problems: mixture of Gaussians, mixture of regressions, and linear regression with covariates missing completely at random. In each case, our theory guarantees that with a suitable initialization, a relatively small number of EM (or gradient EM) steps will yield (with high probability) an estimate that is within statistical error of the MLE. We provide simulations to confirm this theoretically predicted behavior.

A pivotal innovation in 5G wireless communication is massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO). This technology offers considerable enhancements in network capacity. For optimal efficiency regarding costs and power consumption, it's essential to utilize low-resolution data converters within massive MIMO systems. Our study focuses on a downlink mmWave transmission setup, serving several users concurrently through massive MIMO using single-bit digital-to-analog (DA) converters. Specifically, we introduce an original precoding technique grounded in signal-to-leakage-plus-noise ratio (SLNR). This method reduces unwanted energy dissemination among users whilst considering distortions caused by one-bit quantization nonlinearity. Furthermore, we demonstrate how a renowned regularized zero-forcing (RZF) precoder can be viewed as a special instance of our SLNR-driven precoder, achieved when ignoring quantization effects entirely. Comparative numerical analysis reveals substantial performance gains offered by the SLNR-based precoder over traditional RZF or ZF precoders.

The Weston Cadet (model 852 introduced in 1949), Direct Reading (model 853 introduced 1954) and Master III (models 737 and S141.3 introduced in 1956) were the first in their line of exposure meters to switch and utilize the meanwhile established ASA scale instead. Other models used the original Weston scale up until ca. 1955. The company continued to publish Weston film ratings after 1955, but while their recommended values often differed slightly from the ASA film speeds found on film boxes, these newer Weston values were based on the ASA system and had to be converted for use with older Weston meters by subtracting 13 exposure stop as per Weston's recommendation. Vice versa, "old" Weston film speed ratings could be converted into "new" Westons and the ASA scale by adding the same amount, that is, a film rating of 100 Weston (up to 1955) corresponded with 125 ASA (as per ASA PH2.5-1954 and before). This conversion was not necessary on Weston meters manufactured and Weston film ratings published since 1956 due to their inherent use of the ASA system; however the changes of the ASA PH2.5-1960 revision may be taken into account when comparing with newer ASA or ISO values.

Jerry had never been to a funeral. He wasn't sure if he could handle it. His grandmother died at age eighty-five. He didn't cry at her funeral because there was no way to bring her back; he cried for the first time in his life, when they were about to have a little baby girl. The funeral director asked him why she would leave him. "We thought you'd be able to come up with something," he said. "But then we found out your mother did not like funeral service, and he has been very sick." "I'm sorry I don't understand. You're going to have to go through some things," Eliezer replied. If he wanted to hear another story about the funeral, he had to ask someone else. His aunt made several phone calls from the hospital, and he finally called, asking, "Did you know that she's still alive?" At the bottom of the dial, Eliezer felt a sense of relief. He knew he needed to call her now. She should make certain that she loved him. Had she not lost her brother? How could he possibly help her? He came into the office on the day after the funeral, and heard the conversation between Eliezer and her cousin. The doctor told him he wouldn't be able to see her until she got married. The doctor explained that Jerry had already arranged her marriage, so she might as well get married right away. This was the last thing he wanted to do. But he couldn't let this happen again. Eliezer calmly stuck out his tongue while the doctor talked to him. "Do you want me to take care of my sister first?" Eliezer whispered, hoping that his aunt, who was living off the pension, would appease his conscience by saying she'd love a new husband. "Yes, please," she answered softly. They sat together under a lamp, talking for a while. Then they decided which one would fill Eliezers' shoes: Eliezer, the grandson of a man named Carl Cavanaugh, or their father, who had worked directly for them. They seemed to agree. For this reason alone, they agreed that the family shouldn't be apart. It had always been their only interests. Oncoming cars overhead showed a white car with the details of their wedding ceremony on it. Eliezer was wearing a gray feather dress, the same black synthetic material they wore for their wedding. The silver hoop earrings were hidden behind a leather belt. The jewelry was dusted with wax, and Eliezer rocked a golden-colored gold ring and a bracelet. Eliezer sat down beside Carl, who wore a red silk scarf over his head. A large red velvet shirt hung around his waist, and the cap he wore matched the jewelry. Eliezer leaned forward, holding Carl's hand. Carl glanced around at his watch. He knew it every time he looked at it. It rose at 6:30 p.m., but he was afraid it took longer than it sounded. James walked down the row of rooms; they did not call them prison cells, since the occupants were not prisoners. The asylum was for mental health patients, and James'wing housed the violent offenders. Unlike all the other guards, James liked nights at the asylum, the inmates were quieter, usually sleeping. A night person since he was a little boy, James didn't mind the nighttime noises that emerged when the cacophony of daytime died down. The quiet padding of rats in the walls, the drips of a leaking pipe somewhere off in the distance, the way the wind whistled through the gaps in the stone walls. The sounds were all lost in the gaggle of mindless conversations that filled the daytime shifts. He ignored all the residents until he came to the last door on the left. The room was called the penthouse, since the window showed beyond the asylum walls, all the way to the city lights in the distance. He peered through the door and saw the room's lone occupant, crouched on his bed staring out the window at the darkness. James unlocked the door and went in, standing next to the bed staring out the window, shoulder to shoulder with the patient. It was a waning moon tonight, barely any light from the pale crescent, but the lights of the city still twinkled. The streetlights painted yellow circles on the road leading away from the gates, making the road appear to be a polka dotted belt leading away from the asylum. " Hello James " " Bruce " " It's a nice night out there. " " I know " " How's your wife James? " " Still dead Bruce. " This wasn't a new conversation; in fact, they had it almost every night. Bruce was the most dangerous resident at the asylum. It wasn't that he was larger or stronger than the other inmates, but his background in martial arts and the years spent surviving on the streets of the city had made him faster and more deadly with his bare hands than any one James had seen come through the asylum. In Bruce's first week at the asylum, he had killed two other patients in the recreation yard, claiming that they had " killed his parents. " No one knew much about Bruce's background, he was an orphan, picked up for petty crimes several times during his youth, put into different foster homes, but always managing to run away until finally at 16 he had simply disappeared from the system for ten years. The Bruce that re-entered the system at 26 had extensive martial arts training, was covered in scars and angry as hell at the world. James suspected Bruce had lied about his age and joined the military, but the military had no record of him. James had been a beat cop in those days, still fresh from the academy, still convinced he could change the city, make it better by arresting the bad people. It would be a few years until the reality of the situation would hit him like a ton of bricks. The justice system was broken; the only criminals it caught were the ones too poor to buy their way out, or too dumb to pay the right people. Bruce was one of the poor ones. In an out of jail, James had picked up Bruce several times for fighting, vagrancy, even auto theft once. Other cops had been terrified of Bruce, after seeing what he would do to the men he fought, and would subdue him with extreme force, but Bruce never fought back, never hit a cop, he always went with them willingly, apologizing for inconveniencing them, contrite for his actions. James usually just asked Bruce to get in the squad car, no handcuffs, no sucker punches, just a polite request, to which Bruce always complied. Then, five years later, something changed in Bruce. He snapped mentally, and started suffering delusions. Delusions of grandeur and war and violence, and he had ended up here, in the asylum. After years of hard work, only to see the same crimes committed by the same people over and over, James became disillusioned with his police job and quit, ending up at the asylum as a guard around the same time Bruce showed up, just on the other side of the locked door. Bruce had recognized him from his cop days and a dialog had started between the two men. The psychologist had encouraged James to continue to talk with Bruce, said that: " Expanding Bruce's world beyond the one he has created in his head is good; it shows him a little glimpse of reality " James didn't buy the psychologist babble, he thought Bruce had experienced some crappy things in his life, and whatever he made up in his own head was probably far better than the institutionalized reality. " Ready to go Bruce? " " I'm ready James, what's the plan tonight? " " No plan, just the usual place and time. " James led Bruce out the unlocked door, down a back staircase, through a set of maintenance doors, past the loading dock to the employee parking lot. James unlocked his old beat up sedan; it had once been a cop car, now it was just another black generic sedan with way too many miles on the clock. He got in the driver's seat, and as was his custom, Bruce got into the back, a remnant of the days when James used to arrest him no doubt. The drive in was quiet, Bruce usually stared out the window while James drove him into the city. The old sedan twisted through the dirty streets, splashing through puddles, the old suspension protesting with a thunk at every pothole. Eventually they reached their destination, an overpass near the center of the city. James pulled to the curb and shifted the car into park. " Meet you right here in..... " He glanced at his watch, it was ten pm " ...eight hours " He turned to confirm the time with Bruce, but his passenger was gone, the door to the sedan open, and the street around him empty. James hated it when Bruce did that. On the drive back to the asylum, James reflected on what he had just done. The idea had come to him after he witnessed Bruce's fight that first week. James had still been working day shift and had foreseen trouble before it even began. Bruce had spent the night screaming about a nightmare and some of the other patients did not appreciate their sleep interrupted. James had heard the whispers and tried to get Bruce put into the protective wing, but the transfer wouldn't happen until after breakfast. He'd gotten to the cafeteria just as the fight had started. He didn't remember the other two patients, just that they were big. The fight took slightly longer than ten seconds, and even the cameras couldn't capture exactly what had happened. One minute the two patients had cornered Bruce near the far wall, and then a few seconds later both were writing on the ground, one with his hand at his neck, slowly turning from red to blue and the other clutching his stomach dry heaving and then finally vomiting blood. The first had died of a crushed windpipe, the second from massive internal bleeding. Bruce had been moved to the isolation wing after that. James'remembered asking Bruce about why he had hit the two other men a few weeks after the fight: " So why'd you hit those two guys Bruce? " " I didn't hit them, I killed them " " How did you know that? " " Because I'm trained to kill " He had said this before, but, James had just chalked it up to his delusions, this was the first evidence he had that he wasn't just making it all up. " So why'd you kill them Bruce? " This was the type of question the psychologist would have shit his pants to hear a guard asking a patient, but he didn't really care. " Because they were bad men, they killed my parents, so I killed them. " " What about other bad men, are you going to kill every bad person you come across? " " Only if they deserve it. " The plan took a year to perfect and by now, almost four years later, it was more of a routine. James would drive Bruce into the city at night, he would strike terror into " bad people " and James would take him back to the asylum in the morning. In four years, crime had dropped so much that in the most recent year the police department shot more people than all of the criminals in the city, combined. There were grumblings about a serial killer, but to tell you the truth, police don't work very hard when the killer seems to focus on the worst the city had to offer. James was parked under the overpass as the sum came up. It was starting to get lighter a little earlier these days, they'd have to schedule the pickup earlier next week. He didn't hear the back door open, or even close, but suddenly, Bruce was staring at him in the rearview mirror from the back seat. " Let's go home James " " How'd it go tonight? " " A rapist, a murderer, a mob guy and a dirty cop. " " Dirty cop, that's going to raise some eyebrows. " " He was with the mob guy, both up to their eyeballs in shit. Hard to do one without the other. We may want to lay low for a few weeks " James turned onto the road out of the city, towards the asylum. " Good idea, maybe we'll come out again in three weeks? " " Let's see how the investigation goes. It should implicate the mob guy, but you never know. " The asylum was still quiet and the sun was just breaking the horizon as James pulled into the parking lot. Bruce followed James up the stairs to his room; he locked him in and signed out. His shift over, James walked back to his car, walking through the yard back towards the employee parking lot. As he pulled out of the gates, he turned onto the road, driving towards home, towards Gotham City, the Arkham Asylum gate fading from the rearview as he rounded the first bend.

Hypersensitivity is an immune response that damages the body's own tissues. They are divided into four classes (Type I - IV) based on the mechanisms involved and the time course of the reactions. Type I reactions involve an immediate, IgE-mediated response to allergens and can result in anaphylaxis. Type II reactions are antibody-dependent cytotoxic reactions in which antibodies bind to antigens on the surface of cells and activate complement, leading to cell destruction. Type III reactions are immune complex mediated responses in which antigen-antibody complexes deposit and cause inflammation. Type IV reactions are delayed, T-cell mediated responses that usually take several days to develop.

We propose a Las Vegas transformation of Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) estimators of Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs). We denote our approach Markov Chain Las Vegas (MCLV). MCLV gives statistical guarantees in exchange for random running times. MCLV uses a stopping set built from the training data and has maximum number of Markov chain steps K (referred as MCLV- K). We present a MCLV- K gradient estimator (LVS- K) for RBMs and explore the correspondence and differences between LVS- K and Contrastive Divergence (CD- K), with LVS- K significantly outperforming CD- K training RBMs over the MNIST dataset, indicating MCLV to be a promising direction in learning generative models.

It's not because of a crappy phone, it's the lack of shielding on the speaker.] (URL0)," "Older phones (well really older networks) used what is known as TDMA, or time division multiple access. They still transmit the signals using several hundred MHz (mega hertz) radio waves, like newer networks. This noise picking up on a speaker wouldn't do anything, and even if the speaker could play it, it's way beyond human hearing, too high pitch for any animal to hear. But what the TDMA means is each users get to talk over the frequency channel for small intervals. Person one gets a short amount of time to talk to the tower, then person two, and so on until it's back to person one. This swapping between users though doesn't occur at MHz frequencies though, it occur in the low kHz range. Speakers can play this range, and humans can hear it up to 20 kHz. So what you phone is going is emitting MHz radio waves, but pulsing them on an interval in the kHz so it only talks to the tower on its allowed interval. Combine this with poorly shielding speakersamps and the pulsing will get picked up and cause the speaker to vibrate with it, and hence causing you to hear the cell phone signal. Newer phones don't do this because they use different networks that don't use TDMA, and hence don't pulse radio waves at audio frequencies.

The Supreme Court of Sri Lanka stands atop the country's legal hierarchy due to the enactment of the constitution in that year. It holds ultimate authority within the nation's justice system, exercising its jurisdiction under constitutional guidelines. Decisions made by this esteemed institution are binding upon all subordinate courts. Sri Lankan law comprises elements from both common law traditions and civil law systems. Certain matters, like death sentences, can be referred to the President for mercy considerations. Nonetheless, when the Parliament has a two-thirds majority supporting the president, the Supreme Court's power wanes, since the president possesses the ability to remove judges from office per the Constitution. Consequently, during these periods, the influence of civil law diminishes significantly.

They read the briefs on their own, although they can confer informally whenever they wish, and there's nothing inappropriate there. Then during oral arguments they get an idea of what their colleagues might think based on the questions they ask. After orals they have a private conference where they discuss things, but (as far as we know) not typically in great depth. Then the Chief and the senior associate justice on the other side assign the majority and minority opinions. The assigned justices retire to their chambers and draft the opinion. It's here where the real work happens in earnest, as many opinions are redrafted and circulated, with justices who agree in bulk saying "I can't agree with this section" or "can you add a section addressing X?," etc., and justices on each side redrafting to respond to arguments brought up in the other side's earlier draft. And this continues until everybody's happy with their statements, and then it's announced publicly and the opinion is published.','As mentioned the justices tend to vote along their ideological (not necessarily political party) lines. These are well known before they are appointed so its no surprise. One cannot forget that they all have clerks who do most of the heavy lifting for them. Very often the process isn't "here are the facts of the case, everyone vote on it." The process is usually a judge's clerk building a line of legal reasoning consistent the judge's general ideological views on the topic. Clerks give the justice a plausible "excuse" to vote according to thier general views concerning a particular case. Sometimes, judges do look at the facts more objectively and vote based on the case's legal merits alone. Roberts decided for The affordable care act even though he's a conservative. It was more of a legal decision than a ideological one. Ditto with the recent vote to require a police officer to have a warrant before seaching a cell phone...all 9 voted the same way. A lot of the theater of the Supreme Court is more or less for show and for explaining the legal way they and their clerks have found to decide a specific matter. Same with the printed decisions. Its not that they are making stuff up because they aren't. There isn't just one possible way a decision can go. There is no ultimate objective "right" way to decide an issue. That's why there are usually split decisions....reasonable minds can disagree and use different interpretations to lead them down different legal avenues to reach their ultimate decision.', " Do they all sit in a room, discuss the issue, argue, vote, and then split up to write the decisions? That one. There's a conference a few days oral argument, in which they discuss the case, then vote on what to do and it's decided who's writing the majority opinion (whoever's the senior justice in the majority picks who'll write the opinion). After the conference, the justices, with help from their clerks, write draft opinions; justices can change their mind after conference, and ultimately whichever opinion gets a majority signing on to it becomes the official disposition of the case.,They typically are supposed to debate the court case and decide if ruling in favor of it would be constitutional or not. Ever since FDR, though, presidents have appointed justices with litmus tests, meaning that they will vote purely based on party lines, which effectively means that they already decided how to vote before the case even gets there. Scalia for example is the most conservative, so he will never vote for a measure that would ban the death penalty.

The global landscape can manifest in three possible scenarios: a single dominant nation, several influential nations, or an equal distribution of power among all countries. Let's examine the third scenario first, where every nation possesses equivalent strength. Due to inherent competition driven by political, economic, and security interests, achieving absolute equality among countries seems nearly impossible. Nations differ in their capacity and willingness to maintain parity, ensuring that disparities in power levels persist. Moving on to the second situation, featuring numerous superpowers, reminiscent of the Cold War era. In this case, only those countries capable and determined to vie for supremacy engage in intense rivalries, leading to prolonged standoffs like 'cold' wars. Such conflicts may involve varying numbers of countries; historically, the United States and the Soviet Union were key players in the latter part of the 20th century. Finally, let's consider the prevailing condition characterized by a single preeminent force – currently exemplified by the United States post-Cold War victory. Despite the cessation of direct opposition, the U.S. continued its robust defense expenditure to deter potential challenges to its supremacy. Some argue that a single superpower model is the most pragmatic choice, given the natural inclination of nations to contest one another and the risks associated with escalating tensions amidst the existence of nuclear weapons. The rationale behind this perspective suggests that if a dominant nation invests heavily in defense and global presence, it could potentially thwart the rise of new adversaries, thereby safeguarding international stability. Although imperfect, this approach appears feasible within the context of geopolitical dynamics.

The decision to dedicate part of the radio spectrum to a global flight tracking system was taken at a UN conference in Geneva on Wednesday. The conference aimed to improve on the current tracking system which relies on ground-based radars. MH370 disappeared in March 2014 with 239 people on board. Representatives from more than 160 countries decided to set aside a radio frequency for the satellite tracking of planes at the World Radiocommunication Conference (WRC), organised by the UN's International Telecommunication Union (ITU). The deal will enable satellites to receive transmissions, known as automatic dependent surveillance-broadcast (ADS-B), that aircraft currently only send to other aircraft and to ground stations. This will allow "real-time tracking of aircraft anywhere in the world," said Francois Rancy, head of the ITU's Radiocommunication Bureau. The disappearance of flight MH370 exposed weaknesses in worldwide air navigation systems. The current system leaves around 70 of the world's airspace uncovered. Soon after the plane disappeared, Malaysia's communication minister urged the ITU to help find new ways of transmitting flight data in real-time. The Malaysia Airlines flight was en route from Kuala Lumpur to Beijing when air traffic control staff lost contact with it. The plane is long believed to have crashed into the southern Indian Ocean. In July part of an aircraft wing was found on Reunion Island. Malaysian authorities later confirmed the debris to be from the missing MH370 plane. Following Wednesday's decision, ITU Secretary-General Houlin Zhao said the agency had "responded in record time to the expectations of the global community on the major issue concerning global flight tracking." The UN's aviation arm, the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO), has set a November 2016 deadline for adopting new tracking guidelines. These will include aircraft sending their position at least every 15 minutes, or more in case of emergency, reported Reuters.

When discussing 'regular' Mathematics, you likely mean 'pure' Mathematics, which focuses on comprehending various numerical values, ideas, and mathematical principles. In contrast, 'applied' Mathematics involves utilizing said theories and concepts within different contexts and practical scenarios, such as Engineering or Physics. To put it simply, 'regular' (or Pure) Mathematics pertains to studying math purely for the purpose of expanding our knowledge about it, while 'Applied' Mathematics uses mathematical tools to gain insright into actual situations and issues. 

In essence, Pure Mathematics revolves around exploring theoretical questions like "what can we deduce assuming certain premises hold true?", and then delving further by pondering "what minimal assumptions would allow us to arrive at similar conclusions?". On the other hand, Applied Mathematics deals with resolving tangible challenges related to fields like Mechanics and Statistics, reflecting its direct relevance to real-life situations. However, it's worth noting that the line between these two branches has blurred over time due to instances where seemingly abstract areas of Pure Mathematics, initially pursued solely for intellectual curiosity, found practical use in reality – an example being Number Theory's role in modern encryption methods. Occasionally, this intersection of pure and applied aspects is termed "applicable" Mathematics.

The current utilization of millimeter wave technology in commerce highlights several real-world challenges related to the design of user equipment (UE). As these waves have shorter wavelengths, their antenna gain patterns become more focused. Additionally, the success of the connection relies heavily on effective beamforming, making it essential to incorporate multiple antenna modules across various parts of the UE to ensure optimal functioning. Although increasing the number of antenna modules improves beamforming array gains, it also raises costs, increases power usage by RF circuits, and adds to the workload involved in managing beams effectively. Therefore, creating an efficient UE involves achieving consistent circular coverage through high array gains surrounding the device while minimizing complexity, expense, and management demands. This paper examines how two common millimeter wave UE configurations - one based on the face and another on the edge - impact overall spherical coverage. Our findings suggest that using analog beam codebooks can yield satisfactory results for both designs, with the edge configuration offering improved compromise concerning durable performance under obstruction, reduced overhead for beam control, simpler implementation due to antenna arrangement, and lowered costs.
