Arthur and the lads were crouched in the alley, looking out at the wharf. They were nervous, sweating, but their eyes were steady, keeping close watch to the ships. Sam Adams and his boys were going to be ready in just a moment and we needed to be ready. Timing would be everything. I looked at the boys again. They were so damned young. About a dozen total, and not one among them deserved to be involved in any of this. I took a deep breath, and addressed them one final time. "Boys..... no. No, today you aren't boys any longer. Men, I know you're scared. Hell, I've been in actual wars, charging damned savages and I wasn't as scared as this. It's been a long time coming and the moment of truth is here. We, good loyal British subjects, are about to commit a treasonous act of terrorism." Some of them shivered visibly at that. Spot on, lads. Spot on. "We've come too far to back out now. It's been months of planning to spark this event. First, Arthur used his connections at the Philadelphia Inquirer and we all know how that turned out. Seems like overnight people were mad about the "Stamp Tax." Arthur spoke up on that, incredulous, "Can't believe that worked. Stamp Tax is the first new tax in decades, and England's never collected from the American Colonies anyway. We pay less than any colony in the Empire." I allowed myself a wry smirk. Never bet against man's distaste for taxes. "But it did work. Then we used that Mistress friend of Luke's to place the idea in ol'Sam Adams' head that a monopoly on Tea was just like a tax, by a different name. Boy, Adams couldn't wait to bite at that one." Luke grin took a decided mischievous look. "He's lucky he didn't just sign over the deed to his house. When Sally hooks a man, he's practically under witchcraft, that damned Jezebel." I decided to power through that one. I can't say I approved of Luke's affiliations. "And then I used my connections at the Governor's office to have the Darmouth held up in the harbour. Which took some doing, let me tell you. But things are finally coming together. Fitz is out there, right now, rallying up the Sons of Liberty. He'll work them up into a damned lather, and then before you know, they'll be aboard the ships rioting, burning, looting and generally creating all sorts of havoc." Arthur fidgeted and said, "Apparently there's more tea on the Eleanor too. Should be a hell of a mess." "That'll work fine for our purposes. But remember, we're after the Beaver. She's on that wharf. That's where they're keeping the drug." The men visibly steeled themselves. That's what this was all about. The abomination that was the drug. The drug, I believe, was actually called Decreacies by the monsters who made it. It's terrible purpose, originally, was the subjugate negros more easily. It turned a man's mind to mush. Made him suggestible, placid, docile. It was made from a tree flower found in the heart of the Dark Continent. It was goddamn crime against God's creation and those heartless bastards, those "natural philosophers" meant to use it for profit. We meant to destroy their entire supply, under the chaos of the riot tonight. That's when we saw the first signs of the mob. "Act quick boys. And remember, what we do now may yet have us hung, but we do it for the honor and respect of God and Country." We snuck aboard the Beaver easily enough. All around us the riot raged. Sam Adams and his boys knew how to carry on, and Fitz seemed to have enraged them to an incredible degree. Since learning of the damnable drug and it's journey from Africa, the boys and I had had ample time to plan. In the months since, it seemed we'd all become masters of the Great Game. Manipulation, deceit and provocation were our weapons, and anonymity our calling cards. We'd become monsters to fight monsters, but I had long resolved that if any of us we're going to stop this terrible "science," it would not be with our souls intact. There'd been many objections of course. A great deal of fear. Some others questioned the practicality of it. Surely, the Empire could just get more? But I knew better. Only one trade company had a route to the flowers, and they'd risked no insurance on this boat. Burn their stock, cost them everything, and let the damned secrets of the drugs and flowers rot in the hell of Africa. Things were going well. We subdued the guards quietly, distracted as they were by the rioting. We worked our way through the mobs, though some were already on the Beaver. We reached the stock. It was a massive crate, far larger than I'd expected, of dark purple leaves. I lit a torch, and prepared to commit a criminal act in favour of a greater good. And that's when it all went wrong. "Hey Boys! Howabout a little Tea Party eh?" Screamed one of the rioters. A cheer went up! The men had seized on the idea. They began dumping whole crates of tea directly into the harbour, brewing all of Boston into a murky, sweet-smelling swamp. I tried to stop it, I really did. But the rioters were too incensed, and there were too many. The crate dumped into the Boston Harbour, drug and all. There was a chilled silence as we trudged home that night. Several of the boys were pale as ghosts. "How could we have let this happen..." mumbled Arthur. "We destroyed the stock, at least." said Luke. "Aye," I said, "But at what cost? That stuff's in the harbour now. Could affect the whole city." We all looked down at our feet. Arthur got a hopeful glint. It was heartbreaking, really. "But, it's diluted, it's mixed with tons of tea. Perhaps it will be ineffective?" I shook my head. "Perhaps. We don't know what a proper dose was supposed to be. We'll have to be cautious men. We'll have to watch closely. For signs of Colonists being affected. It might be subtle, but they" ll be signs. Look for men who are easily led astray, to anger and faulty reason. Look for people who will believe anything, buy anything, commit to anything without proof or justification. Look for men who seem reasonable one moment and act as though they've been struck dumb the next. " Arthur smiled, reassured. "Well, we'll be fine then. No way that could ever happen in America."

Studies indicate that individuals typically establish brand preferences during adolescence and early adulthood, which seldom undergo significant changes thereafter. Consequently, although influencing someone as young as 11 to perceive Audi vehicles favorably may seem premature, doing so with a 1EE-year-old presents a viable opportunity. In response to your query regarding whether marketing strategies aimed at kids are prevalent, it's undeniable. Marketers frequently direct their efforts towards children, who subsequently persuade their guardians to purchase desired items. Surprisingly, even preschoolers exhibit vulnerability to advertising tactics, prompting various nations to impose restrictions on such campaigns. Nonetheless, observing families navigating grocery store aisles accompanied by toddlers serves as proof of its efficacy. Car manufacturers specifically target youthful audiences due to two primary motives. After light waves hit the receptors in your eye, the receptors activate small electrical signals in the optic nerve. The optic nerve is basically a wire, carrying the signals further back into the brain. Once the signals reach the optical center in your brain, your brain starts trying to recognize patterns. Broadly speaking, it compares the signals it is getting now, to its memories of other signals it has gotten before, and the decisions that have been made based on them. This is done by electrical signals bouncing around everywhere. I'm going to anthropomorphize. Your optical center uses a complex network of associations, to notice where there is a large amount of any given color grouped together, and seperates everything out into objects. It compares apparent sizes of objects, and color intensities, and a thousand other little cues, and decides what is near and far, and big and small. A pattern-recognition part of your brain then tries to match the objects it has recognized in the sensory input to things in your memory: What have you seen before that may be similar to what you are seeing now? It primes any memories that are similar to this pattern of information, so that those memories are easier for your brain to find, and are ready to be triggered on a moment's notice. This is a long process, and involves a lot of logical leaps going from direct observations like "that is a blob of green" to decisions like "that is a blob of green shaped like a dress, therefore that might be a dress." When you recognize shapes in clouds, this is your brain making patterns out of nothing. Now that a selection of memories are ready to be triggered and you've recognized loosely what is going on, the patterns you've noticed are fed to the thinky part of your brain in an extremely summarized format. Instead of the entire long process of "Oh. That's a human. That's a green dress. The green dress is closer than the human. The green dress overlaps the human. The green dress moves when the human moves. The human is wearing the green dress. The human has red hair. The human is smiling. The human is familiar. The human has been seen before. The human's face is familiar. The human is Sarah." you just get "Sarah is wearing a green dress and smiling." There is a lot of data lost along the way: 99 of it is not important. As long as none of it was wrong. Sometimes this summary process means that you don't notice minor things that are in the background, because you haven't focused on them enough for your brain to process exactly what it is you're looking at. It's still stuck at the "There is a blob of color in the background" stage, rather than recognizing "There is someone in a horse mask behind her.,'To be honest, the processes inside the brain that go from, "Hmm, here is the light patterns the eyes received" to "Woah! this is my 2nd cousin patrick that I haven't seen in 6 years!" isn't all that well understood. We have theories with big gaps. [Visual Cortex] (URL0) is the part of the brain where [Visual Processing] (URL1) happens. Our current understanding of visual processing is called [Two-Streams Processing] (URL2).

A new method for estimating the relative positions of location-unaware nodes from the location-aware nodes and the received signal strength (RSS) between the nodes, in a wireless sensor network (WSN), is proposed. In the method, a regularization term is incorporated in the optimization problem leading to significant improvement in the estimation accuracy even in the presence of position errors of the location-aware nodes and distance errors between the nodes. The regularization term is appropriated weighted on the basis of the degree of connectivity between the nodes in the network. The method is formulated as a convex optimization problem using the semidefinite relaxation approach. Experimental comparisons with state-of-the-art competing methods show that the proposed method yields node positions that are much more accurate even in the presence of measurement errors.

In this paper, we introduce a regularized mean-field game and study learning of this game under an infinite-horizon discounted reward function. The game is defined by adding a regularization function to the one-stage reward function in the classical mean-field game model. We establish a value iteration based learning algorithm to this regularized mean-field game using fitted Q-learning. This regularization term in general makes reinforcement learning algorithm more robust with improved exploration. Moreover, it enables us to establish error analysis of the learning algorithm without imposing restrictive convexity assumptions on the system components, which are needed in the absence of a regularization term.

In this work, we explain the working mechanism of MixUp in terms of adversarial training. We introduce a new class of adversarial training schemes, which we refer to as directional adversarial training, or DAT. In a nutshell, a DAT scheme perturbs a training example in the direction of another example but keeps its original label as the training target. We prove that MixUp is equivalent to a special subclass of DAT, in that it has the same expected loss function and corresponds to the same optimization problem asymptotically. This understanding not only serves to explain the effectiveness of MixUp, but also reveals a more general family of MixUp schemes, which we call Untied MixUp. We prove that the family of Untied MixUp schemes is equivalent to the entire class of DAT schemes. We establish empirically the existence of Untied Mixup schemes which improve upon MixUp.

All 20 Leptospira isolates, recovered from patients in Andaman Islands, could also be typed by fingerprints generated with the M16 primer. Tablets and smartphones have revolutionized the way people interact with technology, offering a more intuitive and engaging experience. However, there is one common problem that affects most touchscreen devices - smears from the oils and sweat on our fingers. The issue with fingerprints on touchscreen devices is multifaceted. Not only do these smudges look unsightly, but they can also impair the performance of the device. The oils from our fingers can interfere with touch detection, causing the device to misinterpret our commands. Moreover, persistent smearing can damage the touch-sensitive coating on the screen, ultimately reducing the lifespan of the device. However, despite the significant drawbacks of finger smears, most people continue to use their devices without regular screen cleaning. According to a survey, only 9 of smartphone users clean their screens daily, with the majority admitting that they only clean their screens once a week or less. This reluctance to clean devices regularly is surprising considering that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends cleaning phones and tablets daily, considering them a potential source of viral transmission. To help tackle the problem of finger smears, device makers have come up with various solutions. One of the most effective is the oleophobic coating, a thin layer applied to the screen that repels the oils on our fingers. This works to a certain extent, but it can wear off over time and with regular cleaning. Moreover, the effectiveness of the coating varies between devices, with some performing better than others, depending on the manufacturer. Another solution is the use of multi-touch displays that can detect touches from a stylus or other object, rather than just fingers. This can be very helpful for people who struggle with smudging screens or who require greater precision in their work, but it doesn't solve the problem entirely. Not everyone wants to use a stylus, and sometimes fingers are simply the most convenient option. Other tips for reducing the appearance of fingerprints on a device's screen include keeping your hands clean and avoiding touching the screen too much, keeping the device out of direct sunlight, and using a microfiber cloth or screen protector to wipe away the smudges. In conclusion, touchscreen devices have transformed our lives and brought a world of convenience to our fingertips, but they do come with their own unique challenges. While finger smears may seem like a minor problem, they can affect the function and lifespan of our devices. Regular cleaning and maintenance can help keep our screens smudge-free, but it's up to us as users to take responsibility for our devices and ensure that they perform to the best of their capabilities.

The earliest references to "democracy" was Athens in about the 6th century BC, where all male citizens over the age of 20 were part of the legislative assembly, and so had the right to take part in the lawmaking process. But it's very likely that some form of democracy must have existed long before then; for example, through the appointment of ordinary citizens to city councils. Our modern European-style democracy wasn't so much "invented" as "evolved" over a long period of time, from the Middle Ages on. If you're American, you've almost certainly heard of the Magna Carta. This was a treaty that the unpopular King John of England was forced to sign in the 13th century, and which granted the barons certain freedoms and privileges, the aim being to curb the king's powers and make him more answerable to the rest of the aristocracy. King John actually simply ignored the Magna Carta, but later monarchs revived it, and it was an important event in the long, slow road to a modern democracy. (Americans are usually given the impression in history classes that it was the single most important stage in the process, but this is actually not true: many other steps were necessary, and the 1689 English Bill of Rights was actually far more important.) In other European countries, though, the process needed to be helped along with the occasional revolution, such as the famous French Revolution, although not all of them were really successful (the Russian Revolution, for example, replaced a despotic monarchy with a despotic government). Germany had a particularly unfortunate experience: after one attempt at a revolution had failed, the First World War basically finished off the monarchy and paved the way for the Weimar Republic; but the young democracy was swiftly subverted by the Nazi Party and it took another devastating war to get things back on track and even then it resulted in the partition of the country.

In this paper, we introduce a new method for generating an object image from text attributes on a desired location, when the base image is given. One step further to the existing studies on text-to-image generation mainly focusing on the object's appearance, the proposed method aims to generate an object image preserving the given background information, which is the first attempt in this field. To tackle the problem, we propose a multi-conditional GAN (MC-GAN) which controls both the object and background information jointly. As a core component of MC-GAN, we propose a synthesis block which disentangles the object and background information in the training stage. This block enables MC-GAN to generate a realistic object image with the desired background by controlling the amount of the background information from the given base image using the foreground information from the text attributes. From the experiments with Caltech-200 bird and Oxford-102 flower datasets, we show that our model is able to generate photo-realistic images with a resolution of 128 128 . We introduce an adaptation of Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) estimators used in Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs), which we refer to as Markov Chain Las Vegas (MCLV). This method offers probabilistic assurances while allowing variable execution durations based on chance. The MCLV technique incorporates a predefined termination criterion derived from the training data and is capped at a predetermined limit of Markov chain iterations denoted by K (termed MCLV-K). Our research includes developing a variant of the MCLV gradient estimator specifically tailored for RBMs, known as LVS-K. Additionally, we analyze how this estimator compares to its counterpart, CD-K, particularly within the context of the MNIST dataset. Results show that LVS-K substantially surpasses CD-K in effectiveness when it comes to training RBMs, suggesting that pursuing the MCLV path could yield significant advancements in the realm of generative model education.

We consider a dynamic variant of these systems and propose FreeStore , a set of fault-tolerant protocols that emulates a register in dynamic asynchronous systems in which processes are able to joinleave the servers set during the execution. These protocols use a new abstraction called view generators , that captures the agreement requirements of reconfiguration and can be implemented in different system models with different properties. Can somebody explain to me how supernovas can "explode" given that space is a vacuum? A conventional explosion is generally an expansion of gas caused by a chemical reaction, something that would not be possible in a vacuum. The explosion is inside the star, not in the vacuum. One way to look at it is this: a star is a very hot ball of gas, millions of degrees. It's hard to imagine, but that means that the gas is ionized: instead of the atoms being neutral (1 electron) they're mostly in a plasma state (free electrons and nuclei). Inside the star, the outward pressure of the gas is balanced by the inward pull of gravity. If the star collapses, the pressure will increase. The gas will heat up more, and the nuclei will start to fuse, releasing energy. If the fusion proceeds fast enough, it can counteract the gravitational collapse, and the star will stabilize. However, if it doesn't, the star will continue to collapse, and the pressure will increase even more. The gas will get hotter and hotter, and will fuse more and more, and the star will explode. The fusion reactions are not chemical reactions, they are nuclear reactions, and they don't depend on an atmosphere to propagate. Actually, a supernova is the explosion of the star, not the implosion. A supernova is the end result of a massive star that has run out of fuel (fusing hydrogen into helium, helium into carbon, carbon into iron, etc). When there is no more fuel, the outward pressure of the core is no longer enough to counterbalance the inward pull of gravity, so the core collapses. This collapse raises the temperature and pressure of the core, and the star explodes. This may sound like a contradiction, but it's not. Imagine a balloon. If the balloon is full, it will expand outward because of the pressure of the air inside. But if you let out all of the air, the balloon will collapse inward, because the pressure of the air outside is now greater than the pressure of the air inside. This is similar to the way a star works. The outward pressure of the core is balanced by the inward pull of gravity. But if the core runs out of fuel, the pressure will drop, and the star will collapse, just like a balloon that has no air inside. The collapse raises the temperature, and the star explodes. Supernovae and Novae: The distinction between supernovae and novae is the mass of the star that explodes. When a white dwarf star accretes matter from its companion, it can reach a mass of 1.4 solar masses (called the Chandrasekhar limit) and explode as a type Ia supernova. Supernovae of this type are useful because they always explode with the same mass, and so have the same intrinsic brightness. Novae are produced by the explosion of a white dwarf which is part of a binary system. The white dwarf accretes matter from its companion until it reaches a mass of 1.4 solar masses, the Chandrasekhar limit. At this point, the star can no longer support its mass and it collapses. The collapse heats up the material inside the star and ignites a runaway fusion reaction. The fusion releases energy, but not enough to unbind the white dwarf. Instead, the outer layers of the star are blasted off, leaving behind a dense, hot core. This core can continue to fuse and release energy for weeks or even months after the explosion, causing the nova to gradually fade away. Novae are much less luminous than supernovae and can take months to fade. I've seen a few answers saying that it's not a chemical explosion but a nuclear one. This is incorrect - it is a chemical explosion. A chemical explosion is defined as a reaction that releases energy in a very short time. As such, it is independent of the medium it is in. A nuclear reaction is also a chemical reaction. The reason that supernovae explode is because fusion produces energy. Fusion requires pressure and temperature, but it is not dependent on a medium. Thus, when the pressure and temperature is high enough, fusion can occur. The outward force produced by the energy released in the fusion is much larger than the inward force of gravity. The reason that the pressure and temperature are high enough is because of the collapse of the star. So, the collapse of the star is not caused by the lack of fusion

Data from levels.fyi was analyzed to find out how long it takes on average to become a senior or principal engineer, how much money do tech workers make, whether women get paid less than men in tech, and whether the tech industry favors the young or not. The data for the analysis came from 18.8k tech workers. On average, it takes about 18 years to become a distinguished engineer, and about four years to become a senior software engineer. There are fewer women as the level of career progression increases. Many women leave tech before they are promoted, at more than double the rate of men. The median yearly compensation for tech workers is 195,000 while the mean is 225,000, with very little difference between men and women. Stock grants are a common way to increase total compensation. Tech companies tend to favor younger employees, with older engineers' salaries having no correlation with their years of experience.

He went on to explain that this particular star had gone missing long ago and, since then, great misfortune had befallen his people. He said that if I could return the star to them, it would bring them good luck and prosperity. I was taken aback by his story and I felt guilty for having purchased the star without knowing what it meant to someone else. Despite the money being offered, I told the man that I could not sell the star and I returned it to him. As soon as he had left, I felt relieved and strangely content. The man never returned, but I often wonder if the star brought the people of his planet the luck they had hoped for. Regardless, I'm glad I made the right decision and honored their request.

The immune system protects organisms from infection with layered defenses of increasing specificity. In simple terms, physical barriers prevent pathogens such as bacteria and viruses from entering the organism. If a bacterium infects another cell or organ first, it usually means that the key to survival is retained; but if bacteria and viruses enter other cells, then the immune system can attack them. So what happens when these new types of immunity have been discovered? In the small intestine, there are two kinds of antibodies: one is an antibody called antigens, which is made up of an enzyme called lipids called polypeptides, which is found in complex molecules of food. This type of antibody binds to the active site on the surface of the cell that causes infection. But the problem is that bacterial cells don't always stay coated in this protective net against infections. Instead, they get released into the bloodstream. So when new forms of immunity emerge, those will need medicine - and some drugs. But none of this was possible without the help of antibiotics. When the immune system attacks specific proteins, or "guts" by going near specific receptors, its immunity is weakened. That means the immune system won't still be able to fight off infection. Even when antibiotic-resistant strains are introduced, only a few cells survive. That doesn't mean antibiotics alone aren't effective at preventing disease. It just means that most people who develop severe infections come out the other side of the hospital with no symptoms. Scientists estimate that between 1 and 5 of patients suffer from serious illnesses during their treatment for "infective" disease. (You may want to read a recent article about an American doctor getting sick because he used a secret drug.) Antibiotics can also keep viruses away from the body's non-pathogenic parts, like the liver and kidneys. But the human immune system has different strategies for keeping virus molecules inside the body. The simplest way to protect yourself is with a bacterial poison. Just as in the case of humans, colon cancer kills off all the good bacteria we had been making. However, researchers believe that a controlling agent, such as oral antibiotics, could also work. Both X.25 and Frame Relay provide connection-oriented operations. But X.25 does it at the network layer of the OSI Model. Frame Relay does it at level two, the data link layer. Another difference between X.25 and Frame Relay is their error correction process. X.25 uses a complex error correction protocol that ensures data integrity, while Frame Relay does not have this feature. Additionally, X.25 provides support for virtual circuits, while Frame Relay uses permanent virtual circuits to establish a connection between endpoints. Finally, Frame Relay is generally considered to be faster and more efficient than X.25 due to its simpler protocol and lack of error correction.

Here's an explanation in simpler terms: During reproduction, such as when a man and a woman conceive a child or two plants create seeds, their respective genetic material combines to form the offspring's unique set of genes. Genotypic interaction refers to how the parental genes mix during this process. Alleles represent various versions of the same gene responsible for specific characteristics, making each individual distinct yet belonging to the same species. 

When these parental genes merge to generate the child's genetic code, we get a combination called a heterozygote. Dominance then depends on whether the resulting heterozygote more closely resembles one parental gene type or another. To put it simply, imagine combining a mother's square-shaped gene with a father's octagonal-shaped gene; if the outcome leans toward square, the maternal allele takes precedence. However, dominance isn't always straightforward—it may vary depending on the situation and doesn't always follow a strict order.

The root cause of dominance lies within the biological mechanisms behind certain traits. As an instance, eye color could naturally manifest as either blue or green due to underlying genetics.

At midnight UTC 14 on August 28, 2014, the world suddenly went dark. In an instant, all internet connectivity was disabled across the globe. Without the internet, communication between countries and international business came to a standstill. Panic spread as people feared for their safety and the safety of their families. As time passed, some people began to adapt to the new reality, relying more heavily on local communication networks and resources. But most people felt lost without the internet. They missed being able to stay connected with friends and family around the world, access information at their fingertips, and be entertained with their favorite shows and movies. Days turned into weeks, and after 2 months of darkness, there was still no sign of the internet coming back. Many had given up hope and resigned themselves to living without it, while others held onto a shred of optimism that the internet would eventually come back online. It was then, on October 28th, 2014 - two months to the day since the internet had gone down - that people around the world suddenly heard a sound emanating from their computers, signaling the return of the internet. People rejoiced at the news and quickly logged on to check up on their loved ones. The cause of the blackout was never officially determined, but the global pandemic of 2020 brought forth theories linking the incident to a cyber attack by a secret organization. Whatever the reason, the world was thankful for the return of the internet, which had become so deeply entrenched in everyday life.

We introduce LETO, a novel hybrid approach combining Lagrangian and Eulerian methods for topology optimization. Central to LETO is a blend of particle-grid Material Point Method (MPM), which calculates elastic force balance. This technique transfers density data from mobile Lagrangian particles to stationary Eulerian quadrature points. These quadrature points serve as MPM particles within a coarser grid, enabling detailed structure representation at a lower computation cost. With both carrier particle densities and locations as optimization factors, LETO reformulates the Eulerian solution framework for topology optimization from a Lagrangian perspective. It also harmonizes the handling of both linear and nonlinear elastic materials. For substantial deformations and buckling scenarios in the nonlinear regime, this scheme seamlessly adapts. Furthermore, LETO integrates a contact-conscious strategy using a fictitious domain-based contact model within the static equilibrium resolver, leading to the identification of unique structures. Through comprehensive experimentation, we compared LETO with a standard Eulerian procedure, observing a mean quantitative enhancement of 20% (reaching up to 40%) in three dimensions and 2% (potentially 12%) in two dimensions. From a qualitative standpoint, LETEE reveals innovative nonlinear functional forms and autonomously navigates through self-contact-related structural discoveries.

We propose and study a task we name panoptic segmentation (PS). Panoptic segmentation unifies the typically distinct tasks of semantic segmentation (assign a class label to each pixel) and instance segmentation (detect and segment each object instance). The proposed task requires generating a coherent scene segmentation that is rich and complete, an important step toward real-world vision systems. While early work in computer vision addressed related imagescene parsing tasks, these are not currently popular, possibly due to lack of appropriate metrics or associated recognition challenges. To address this, we propose a novel panoptic quality (PQ) metric that captures performance for all classes (stuff and things) in an interpretable and unified manner. Using the proposed metric, we perform a rigorous study of both human and machine performance for PS on three existing datasets, revealing interesting insights about the task. The aim of our work is to revive the interest of the community in a more unified view of image segmentation.

A vertex-locating code within a graph G(V,E) refers to a set C belonging to V, where every element u from V will have a distinctive intersection between C and the r-radius sphere around u. Such r-vertex-locating codes have been previously examined in different lattice structures. Specifically, research has demonstrated the existence of an optimally dense 2-vertex-locating code in a hexagonal lattice with a density of 4/19, while also establishing that any 2-vertex-locating code cannot possess a lesser density than 2/11. More recently, Martin and Stanton (2010) enhanced the lower limit to 1/5. This study asserts the optimality of the aforementioned 2-vertex-locating code with a density of 4/19 in the context of a hexagonal lattice, thereby confirming the absence of a more efficient 2-vertex-locating code with reduced density.

Under a longstanding agreement with the city of New York, the museum must accept whatever patrons offer to pay. But signs at cashier desks appear to demand full price, the suit contends. The museum says its "recommended" policy has been place for 40 years and it makes no effort to deceive visitors. The lawsuit, filed in New York City on behalf of former patrons, contends that the world famous museum, which receives six million visitors a year, uses misleading marketing and cashier training to deceive unwary visitors. Lawyers say the signs in the lobby listing the price of admission with the word "recommended" below in smaller type violate a 1893 law mandating the public be admitted free of charge at least five days and two evenings per week in exchange for monetary grants and rent-free use of city-owned land. The suit, which lawyers hope will eventually represent a broad class of people who have visited the museum in recent years, seeks a change in the admissions policy and reimbursement for those who they say were misled. Confusion over whether visitors were required to pay the full 25 is "an issue with tourists travelling to the US from a foreign country," Michael Hiller, a lawyer for those who brought the suit, told the BBC. "They are violating the statute, plainly and simply," Mr Hiller said, referring to the 1893 law. "The museum was designed to make art accessible to the public." A former employee of the Met is expected to testify, Mr Hiller said. The witness, who trained cashiers from 2007-2011, alleges that signage was changed from "suggested" to "recommended" because administrators believed it would encourage people to pay more, Mr Hiller said. Harold Holzer, a spokesman for the museum, said the 1893 law had been superseded. New York City agreed to the museum's request in 1970 to charge an admission fee - so long as the amount was left up to individuals and the signage reflected that. About 40 of visitors pay full price, Mr Holzer said. He said gate proceeds allowed the Met to offer free admission to special exhibitions. About 11 of the museum's operating expenses were covered by admissions last year. As a non-profit organisation, the museum pays no income taxes. It is one of the wealthiest museums in the world, with a 2bn investment portfolio. Mr Holzer estimated the museum would receive 15-20 of its operating budget from the fees this year, with 11 coming from city grants. The Met believes its policy "guarantees access for people regardless of their ability to pay," Mr Holzer said. He noted other New York City museums charge steep admission fees. Entrance fees for prominent New York City art museums such as the Whitney, the Museum of Modern Art and the Guggenheim range from 18 to 25. Mr Hiller demands the museum stop charging entirely for admission and remove the cashier desks. "You have got to eliminate any effort to charge people," he said.

When this threat failed, Innocent excommunicated the king in November 1209. Although theoretically a significant blow to John's legitimacy, this did not appear to greatly worry the king. Two of John's close allies, Emperor Otto IV and Count Raymond VI of Toulouse, had already suffered the same punishment themselves, and the significance of excommunication had been somewhat devalued. John simply tightened his existing measures and accrued significant sums from the income of vacant sees and abbeys: one 1213 estimate, for example, suggested the church had lost an estimated 100,000 marks (equivalent to 66,666 at the time) to John. A floor stone dedicated to Larkin - who died in 1985 - will join the names of the country's best-loved poets including WH Auden, TS Eliot and William Wordsworth. It will be unveiled on 2 December 2016, the 31st anniversary of Larkin's death. The last poet to be honoured was Ted Hughes in 2011. With poems like The Whitsun Weddings and This Be The Verse - which contains his famous musings on "your mum and dad" - Larkin is widely regarded as one of Britain's finest 20th Century poets. The decision to honour him was made by the Dean of Westminster, the Very Rev Dr John Hall. "Philip Larkin is one of the great poets of the 20th Century in English and it's been pressed on me by a number of his colleagues and friends that it's the right time to memorialise him," Dr Hall told the BBC. Prof Edwin Dawes, who chairs the Philip Larkin Society, said Larkin's words were quoted more frequently than those of any of his poetic contemporaries. "The memorialisation of Philip Larkin in Poets' Corner will be warmly welcomed by his many admirers in all walks of life," he said. "We are delighted that in 2016 Larkin will take his place at the very cultural heart of the nation, in Westminster Abbey amongst Britain's greatest writers." Born in Coventry in 1922, Larkin studied at Oxford and had his first poems published in 1940. He took up the position of librarian at the University of Hull in 1955 and, in the same year, published his acclaimed collection The Less Deceived. His last collection High Windows was published in 1974. In December 1984, a year before his death from cancer, he was offered the chance to succeed Sir John Betjeman as Poet Laureate but declined, being unwilling to accept the post's high public profile. The posthumous publication of Larkin's letters gave an often unflattering insight into his inner life and led to accusations of racism and misogyny. Despite the dent to his reputation, in 2003 Larkin was chosen as the nation's best-loved poet of the last 50 years, in a survey by the Poetry Book Society. Poets' Corner became established at Westminster Abbey after Geoffrey Chaucer's remains were interred in a tomb there in 1556.

As in Brazil, the mandolin has played an important role in the Music of Venezuela. It has enjoyed a privileged position as the main melodic instrument in several different regions of the country. Specifically, the eastern states of Sucre, Nueva Esparta, Anzoategui and Monagas have made the mandolin the main instrument in their versions of Joropo as well as Puntos, Jotas, Polos, Fulias, Merengues and Malaguenas. Also, in the west of the country the sound of the mandolin is intrinsically associated with the regional genres of the Venezuelan Andes: Bambucos, Pasillos, Pasodobles, and Waltzes. In the western city of Maracaibo the Mandolin has been played in Decimas, Danzas and Contradanzas Zulianas; in the capital, Caracas, the Merengue Rucaneao, Pasodobles and Waltzes have also been played with mandolin for almost a century. Today, Venezuelan mandolists include an important group of virtuoso players and ensembles such as Alberto Valderrama, Jesus Rengel, Ricardo Sandoval, Saul Vera, and Cristobal Soto.

UKIP is looking for a new leader following the shock resignation of Diane James, who had succeeded Nigel Farage after the EU referendum. MEP Steven Woolfe, who had been seen as the frontrunner, quit the party on Monday. He had been hospitalised after a "scuffle" with fellow MEP Mike Hookem. Speaking to the BBC's Good Morning Scotland programme, Mr Coburn denied Mr Woolfe's claim that UKIP was in a "death spiral" and had become ungovernable. He said the incident between Mr Woolfe and Mr Hookem had been "regrettable" but had involved only two people rather than the whole party. Mr Woolfe has stood by his claim that he "received a blow" from Mr Hookem, though this has been denied by Mr Hookem. Mr Coburn said: "I keep saying it is country, party and self last. It is ideas that count, not individuals. What we are looking for is an agenda for the future, we are publishing it now and that is how we are moving forward. "Can I lead the party? Well, if I were asked by colleagues then of course I would do my best. But the thing is it is not about who is governing, it is to do with getting a group of people together, a collegiate group of people, who are going to run the thing." Mr Coburn said the party's libertarian politics meant people "can't be told what to do" but called on party members to "govern their own emotions and govern their own behaviour." He added: "What has happened is that we have had a charismatic leader for many years, who has kept a lid on things. "Now what you have got is you've got to choose a new leader. In that, you've lifted the lid off things a bit and it bubbles over." Mr Coburn, who is UKIP's only elected representative in Scotland, insisted there was still a reason for the party to exist despite achieving its core aim of having the UK leave the EU. He said he wanted to ensure the country was run "in the interests of the people not in the interests of big business or trade unions" and that he had joined UKIP because he wanted "radical change" to the way the country was governed, not just because he wanted to leave the EU. And he said he would "certainly not" be supporting First Minister Nicola Sturgeon's attempts to keep Scotland in the EU single market after Brexit. Mr Coburn insisted: "We decided during the Scottish referendum on independence that we are part of the United Kingdom and in terms of that we voted in the European referendum, that was as a United Kingdom. "We entered as a United Kingdom, we leave as a United Kingdom. We voted as a United Kingdom, everybody knew that beforehand." Nominations to replace Ms James as UKIP leader close on 31 October, with the new leader announced on 28 November.

Semantic grasping is the problem of selecting stable grasps that are functionally suitable for specific object manipulation tasks. In order for robots to effectively perform object manipulation, a broad sense of contexts, including object and task constraints, needs to be accounted for. We introduce the Context-Aware Grasping Engine, which combines a novel semantic representation of grasp contexts with a neural network structure based on the Wide Deep model, capable of capturing complex reasoning patterns. We quantitatively validate our approach against three prior methods on a novel dataset consisting of 14,000 semantic grasps for 44 objects, 7 tasks, and 6 different object states. Our approach outperformed all baselines by statistically significant margins, producing new insights into the importance of balancing memorization and generalization of contexts for semantic grasping. An advantage of the universal motor is that AC supplies may be used on motors which have some characteristics more common in DC motors, specifically high starting torque and very compact design if high running speeds are used. The negative aspect is the maintenance and short life problems caused by the commutator. Such motors are used in devices such as food mixers and power tools which are used only intermittently, and often have high starting-torque demands. Multiple taps on the field coil provide (imprecise) stepped speed control. Household blenders that advertise many speeds frequently combine a field coil with several taps and a diode that can be inserted in series with the motor (causing the motor to run on half-wave rectified AC). Universal motors also lend themselves to electronic speed control and, as such, are an ideal choice for devices like domestic washing machines. The motor can be used to agitate the drum (both forwards and in reverse) by switching the field winding with respect to the armature.

If a problem X is in C and hard for C, then X is said to be complete for C. This means that X is the hardest problem in C. The most famous example of this idea was given by Euler when he wrote down his formula for the first time: V I A cdot B vc, x where V is the solution in C, I is the initial value (that's why it's called a commutative matrix), A is some vector that determines if we are at zero or one, and B is our hardcode. So now we can easily compute this from other information available about how well we solved the original problem. It wasn't until much later, after many years, that the construction became widely popularized as solvers were built on top of it and parallel algorithm implementations proliferated. Right now you probably know enough algebraic geometry to solve any problem in C; but have no clue what all those vectors meant just five minutes ago! In fact, there seems to be quite a bit more going on under the hood than just arithmetic operations, such as encryption algorithms, that haven't even been invented yet! The image created by night vision is blackwhite. Human eyes are most sensitive to green light. Since you're in the dark and it takes your eyes time to adjust to lightdark, you only want to make the image as bright as necessary. So the image is given in green to make it more comfortable to view in the dark, possibly for long periods.,The human eye is most sensitive to green light. This is why the Bayer pattern used in many cameras has two green pixels, one red pixel, and one blue pixel per quad. Night Vision Goggles amplify low light to appear green so that the user can distinguish as much detail as possible while keeping the luminous flux (light intensity) as low as possible as to preserve their actual night vision.

In this letter we propose the Rao test as a simpler alternative to the generalized likelihood ratio test (GLRT) for multisensor fusion. We consider sensors observing an unknown deterministic parameter at one and same time, followed by a modulus distribution of the composite signal. The difference between the two tests is significant: on average, the non-invariant noise reduction in the composite signal has significantly reduced the errors obtained with the GLRT tests compared with the GLRT tests. This results strongly indicate that both tests can be used as basis for characterization of various hybrid distributions. The Rao test is a basic, well-known set of Ergion-like predictions which rely on a predetermined information to predict future behavior trends in a system. These predictions are then coupled with numerical computing techniques such as the pseudo-random number generator (PRNG). In some cases, such predictions could be applied to multiple systems using the Ergion-type prediction model. For example, a political prediction may be made based on Lorentz statistics or RSI equations. Other methods include the Huffman approximation method, and bounds-based axial projections. However, these methods do not have the advantage over the Ergion-type prediction model because their assumptions require more computations than the Ergion type prediction models. Furthermore, though they use random numbers instead of linear algorithms, they do not allow for generalization that does not depend on probability distribution estimation. We therefore want to show that the Rao test is reliable when applying the ERGion-type prediction model to multiple systems, whereas the ERGion-type prediction model is unreliable when using it only to several sites. We currently experimentally evaluate the Rao test against the ERGion-type prediction model in our simulation experiments. A simulation system is described in which different signals are measured simultaneously from different locations. Both types of measurement devices are used to measure motion, and no error was observed during measurement. By comparison, the Rao test performs better if the universe is composed of objects on a larger scale. However, the Rao test cannot be used to estimate the amplitude of any one component of an object due to the fact that the sizes of the components correspond to each other. Therefore we decided to provide a simple Routine Analysis of the Rao test that optimizes the accuracy of averaging. Specifically, the Rao test generates a prediction which is rated based on the mean value of all components of the object on which the Rao test measures the variance of the predicted value. Only after calculating the absolute values of all components of the object will the Rao test demonstrate the efficacy of averaging, thereby avoiding the risk in predicting the magnitude of other components of the object upon comparing them. Since only a small percentage of unknowns exist in a system with the Rao test, we are forced to reduce the Rao test to just one set of estimators. Due to the high cost associated with the Rao test, the Rao test should be able to obtain similar performance without compromising its efficiency. Furthermore, we intend to compare the Rao test against the ERGion-type prediction model to determine whether the Rao test achieves equal performance with either model. Finally, we plan to find an appropriate algorithm for performing the calculation of the Rao test. RESULTS Rao Test Results A Rao test represents two sets of data; the first set contains the most common components, and the second set contains the most advanced features. The Rao test produces a relatively accurate result because of the existence of a large amount of features which are not necessarily present in the original Rao test. Because of the greater number of possible effects of the Rao test compared with the OLP, we did not design the Rao test with the assumption that there would be any appreciable effect of the Rao test for every system. To ensure that the Rao test achieves optimal results, we tested the Rao test against the OLP using computer simulations in which subjects were asked to answer questions about the Rao test, and perceived changes in their perceptions of the Rao test's findings. As a result of this, we designed the Rao test to simulate what would happen if one of the participants performed a test that placed a higher emphasis on the laws of thermodynamics.

The Apollo program was conceived during the Eisenhower administration in early 1960, as a follow-up to Project Mercury. While the Mercury capsule could only support one astronaut on a limited mission duration, the Apollo program had a much greater opportunity for success after the Challenger space shuttle disaster in 1986, when astronauts Neil Armstrong and Edwin "Buzz" Aldrin were killed upon landing after their orbiter suffered an explosion that destroyed it at Earth's surface. Through the 1960s, NASA focused largely on research activities related to aeronautics, with its greatest accomplishments coming from the launch of the Saturn V rocket into lunar orbit, which eventually led to the moon landings of 1969 and 1972, respectively. As projects like the Apollo missions became less popular due to increased budgetary pressures, attention turned instead toward the development of space shuttles and capsules capable of carrying cargo. These new vehicles would carry crew members to the International Space Station (ISS), and then return them safely back down to earth. After several years of deliberations about how best to develop these spaceships, NASA ultimately selected a single design for each spacecraft type: the Gemini spacecraft, the Viking, and the Shuttle (called "Columbia. Each spacecraft vehicle developed by NASA proceeded through numerous revisions before being finalized. The Shuttle Columbia is still widely considered to be the most advanced and revolutionary spacecraft ever created; however, some subsequent designs have proven more successful than others. At any given moment, there are approximately five different types of manned spacecraft operating under contracts to NASA or overseas organizations. This number can fluctuate based on funding levels - but over the past few decades, this number has steadily fallen as NASA continues to retire older models while replacing them with newer versions. In fact, there are currently no manned spacecraft in active service carried out by NASA itself, aside from its commercial partners. In addition to rockets, satellites continue to play a large role in many parts of modern society, including agricultural output, weather forecasting, communications, navigation and other applications associated with space exploration. Although satellite systems remain relatively inexpensive compared to conventional methods of transmitting information across long distances, they do pose significant safety hazards since satellites often directly impact remote locations around the world where people live and work. To address this problem, various approaches have been proposed to control satellite collision collisions. However, despite recent advancements in technology, these proposals require sophisticated equipment, such as radar arrays, to track and monitor all potential future targets approaching the earth, even if those objects are not actively involved in any sort of collision. Therefore, there remains room for improvement within existing satellite collision avoidance technologies and systems.

In our study, we examine the anticipated length of blocks using variable-length encoding techniques on the binary symmetric channel (BSC), incorporating feedback without any noise. The initial concept was introduced by Horstein through a straightforward single-stage method aiming at reaching the BSC's full potential. Subsequently, Naghshvar et al. devised a distinctive sequential communication strategy based on the maximum external Jensen-Shannon (MaxEJS) distance utilizing a unique form of divergence called the extrinsic Jensen-Shannon (EJS). They also established a non-asymptotic ceiling for the estimated block length associated with MaxEJS. However, according to our simulations, although MaxEJS demonstrated shorter average block lengths compared to Horstein's original technique, the non-asymptotic restriction put forth by Naghshvar et al. proved too lenient, resulting in values higher than those observed in practical scenarios involving a low error rate. Thus, we present a fresh formula estimating the expected block length for MaxEJS, which closely mirrors the outcomes obtained from actual tests. This estimation arises from investigating a hypothetical 'genie'-assisted decoding mechanism (GAD) - its predicted block length surpasses that of MaxEJS and can be roughly calculated via two separate stochastic processes. Our hypothesis suggests that despite employing both estimates, the final result might still serve as an upper limit for the block length, consistent with our experimental findings.

Many large datasets exhibit power-law statistics: The web graph, social networks, text data, clickthrough data etc. Their adjacency graphs are termed natural graphs, and are known to be difficult to compress using traditional methods such as Huffman coding. The difficulty lies in the fact that the power-law degree distributions of these graphs generate long strings of same symbols, which traditional compression algorithms such as Huffman coding do not exploit efficiently. We propose a novel compression technique (called RLE2) to compress natural graphs by exploiting the structure of their degree distributions. RLE2 is based on a data-dependent context model which uses the previous symbol and the number of previous occurrences of the current symbol in its context. Using the web graph, we show that RLE2 beats gzip by 4X-6X and bzip2 by 12X-20X, while compressing with almost the same speed as bzip2. Power laws are ubiquitous in nature, from social networks to the world wide web. To compress such datasets, one needs to design compression algorithms which can exploit the long-range correlation in the dataset. "The Crime That Killed Humanity," it was called. When they discovered the Fountain of Youth. Sure, Ponce de Leon found it first. But we didn't know that until a crazy billionaire that was convinced that the Fountain existed staged a silly expedition into the middle of nowhere in Florida. There, he found the bones. What we used to know is that Ponce de Leon gave up the search and decided to keep on gallivanting around the world. What we now know is that there were a few men he left behind to guard his discovery. Turns out that when the discovery of the century was made, he was told off for searching for something that wasn't gold or of benefit to the Spanish Crown. So off he went, leaving a few men to guard the Fountain. There, they kept their promise, drinking the water. And when we found what was left of them, then we didn't believe them. Even though we encountered something that was life-restoring, but we didn't believe anything they wrote on whatever they could write on - rocks, trees, their armor and clothing. All in Spanish. Curses in Spanish, pleading of God to end their suffering. We didn't know why they wrote it. Only that they showed remorse for having indulged in living. We ignored the warnings, and we paid the price. The Fountain of Youth was opened a few years later. The crazy billionaire flaunted it, drinking it in public, saying that the Fountain was going to make America great again. He wasn't wrong. Those who drank the stuff had their wounds healed, their vision restored. Muscle dystrophy was treated, cancer was done in, the blind regained their vision, the deaf their hearing, it was a miracle - the water healed everything that wasn't right. The religious were chanting how the Fountain was their gift from God (as was he, chugging bottles of it and then cutting himself just to show how the water healed him), atheists were baffled, scientific experiments were conducted to find out why the water healed. That's where science decided to keep quiet. I'm not sure why, only that it did. The Fountain of Youth was never empty. In fact, it was very badly overcrowded. Each time an expansion was commissioned, the Fountain never underscored in attendance. The hardest part of expansion was how fiercely the local wildlife protected it - almost zealously, without giving up. But as soon as the expansion was made, up to a certain point, the wildlife gave up. Whatever animals were captured fought against their captors, baring teeth, claws, rabid. But after a few days they stopped. They reverted to their average behavior. The parrots, instead of shrieking and flying everywhere, resumed their calm melodies and mocking tones of the zookeepers. The crocodiles were crocodiles. Everything was fine with them after a week of drinking non-youth water. The water was akin to a drug in how the body handled the it. First it released a huge amount of dopamine. Then adrenaline. Then it healed any wounds or afflictions. And then it went straight to the bladder within five minutes. That was the concentrated mix, derived straight from the fountain and had flavors added. The consumer version was diluted twentyfold, but was half as effective as the concentrate. But it was tastier, considering how many flavors could be added to it. Health-Juice was monopolized world-wide. And hence why only one company was ever blamed for the genocide. Not like the company exists now to keep taking the blame like a champ. They say, by the time seven years have passed, that all cells from seven years ago are gone and have been replaced with newer versions within your body. The water that was left within your body after you drank it left some minor healing effects, that much was apparent. Then the Fountain ran dry, five years later. By that time, five hundred billion consumer bottles have been sold. Considering that the consumer version was diluted twentyfold. The company was rich, the billionaire was rich, most investors were rich. And everyone was chugging the stuff. Those that didn't chug right away set up stockpiles. When the Fountain ran dry, there was a rapid spike in prices - each bottle, instead of costing ten bucks, cost two hundred. Assuming that the bottles weren't tampered with and then diluted even further until the water's healing effects were on par with the body's own regeneration. The well ran dry not because of overconsumption, but because the water's effects were adjusted by the body. After six months of drinking one bottle a day to heal a bone that was being broken continuously, five bottles were needed to do the same job per day. After another six months, two tonnes of the stuff was needed to heal anything per day. The madness and the quest for eternal youth never stopped. By 2027, humanity was dead. Because of the body's adjusted healing effects, the water became unnecessary. One could make do like Deadpool and heal any injury. Five years after drinking the last drop (for the average human), the healing effects stopped for most people. In fact, due to the immune system's new state of being obsolete, the body rejected it. The water's adding effects did the job better. And then the healing ran out. Wounds that could heal within seconds festered. Bones didn't heal. Those who regained vision and hearing kept their senses, but weren't so different from the rest of humanity when everyone shared a festering gangrene papercut. Whoever didn't stop healing within five years stopped within six. Those who stockpiled their shares were often robbed for it. Vaccines, by virtue of not being needed, killed whoever was injected with them. Humanity couldn't do anything, not even the weakest of injections. Because even the tiniest virus could undo everything. Viruses never go away. Even in the body, they remain dormant while waiting for the right conditions to start the incubation period. And then they strike. That's what happened. The common rhinovirus, a common little cold, something everybody shared..... killed humanity. Few people survived, and only because they were careful to watch their steps. I watched mine. I knew where we were heading. Accelerated healing and youth have a terrible price. A price I never cared to pay. I watched most people I know die, but I didn't care because of how delusional they were, thinking there was no catch to endless healing, tasty water, and eternal youth. I only had a few bottles in my entire life - one to get me up on my legs from the wheelchair that plagued me for twenty years, one to heal my poor eyes, and another for alcohol poisoning. All within four years. Not like I care. I can do what I like, now that no one's here. Now that I think about it, I know why we never weaned off the water. We liked health too much to think about giving up a little bit of living just to experience invulnerability from the common cold.

Negotiations over who will run the PS200m Metrobus network have stalled as bus companies are reluctant to run the service on a completely commercial basis. Metrobus admits public subsidies might be needed to provide a service in the south of the city. The Department for Transport insisted the Busway "is not a public service." A Department for Transport spokesman said the service was open to both bus operators and other users. It said a public subsidy would only be paid if a "commercially-viable service" was not provided. The city's new mayoral cabinet met on Friday to discuss the future of the busway, which has been operating without a dedicated operator since January. It is understood that the cabinet has approved a bus operator submitting an outline business plan for a service, however the Tories have called for a full council meeting to discuss the future of the busway. The DfT said the council could still apply to be the service's operator, or "run the service through a service provider." It said the service would only be eligible for a subsidy if "commercial operators were not able to provide a service which is economically viable." "The cost of operating a service on the Busway is very high, but there are a number of different ways the council can subsidise it," the DfT said. "Therefore, if a council does decide to provide a service, it will be able to consider a number of different funding options." The council's cabinet will meet again on Monday. The Busway, which was part-funded by the former Conservative-led council, opened in January but only two operators - Stagecoach and First - are currently running services on it. An agreement between the two companies saw them share the workload of running the service. However, the cabinet agreed to pay Stagecoach 100,000 a month to run 12 services, with the money coming from the city's budget and public subsidies. The council also agreed to pay the operating costs of 10 buses, which would have run empty between the existing Stagecoach services. The council's cabinet also decided to withhold payments from Stagecoach until they had signed a contract to provide a "commercially viable" service. The DfT has said it will decide whether to provide a subsidy for the busway in early July. It said it would be up to the council to run the service if it was determined there was no commercial operator. Councillor Keith Wakefield, the council's deputy leader, said the council would keep "all options on the table." "The busway has been in operation now since January 2011 and we have had discussions with the operator and also with other operators and we are now at the point where we are going to have to look at whether there is any other option," he said. "The council has never said it is going to run the busway service itself. "We have been very clear about that from the start and it is now time to take a decision about what we are going to do. "The council has to make a decision in the next few weeks about what it is going to do." Both Stagecoach and First have declined to run the service independently because of the high costs involved. Mr Wakefield said he was not in a position to reveal the number of council employees working on the busway, but it was "very few." "We are not talking about thousands of council employees running the busway," he said. "We are talking about a very small number of people and also a small amount of money. "The funding for the busway is not coming from the council's general fund. "It is coming from the Government grant that the council receives for the busway." "This is not about providing a service to people for free. This is about providing a service that is viable for the operator." The Cabinet agreed to pay Stagecoach 100,000 a month to run services on the busway, but the company has not signed a contract. Stagecoach previously said it would not take on any more services until a financial deal was reached. The company's UK chief executive Richard Watson said: "We are in discussions with the council and the Department for Transport and are continuing to work with them to reach a commercial agreement for the provision of services on the Busway. "Until we do, we are unable to comment further." A spokesman for First said it was "still in negotiations" with the council and the DfT.

A small number of individuals contest the outcome of the government elections held on July 17th, 193EE in Spain, where the left-wing Popular Front secured victory. Those opposing this result transformed into rebel factions, commonly known as Nationalists or Fascists, comprising both military personnel and civilians. Their attempt to seize major cities across Spain ultimately led to a protracted civil conflict after failing to swiftly capture Madrid and Barcelona. Key figures among these rebels included commanders such as José Sanjurjo, Francisco Franco, and Emilio Mola. Following Sanjurjo's tragic death in a plane crash on July 20th, Franco assumed control for the remainder of the three-year war period (1936-1939). During this tumultuous era, neighboring countries Britain and France chose to remain neutral yet enforced an arms embargo preventing weapon sales or transfers. Conversely, Italy and Germany flouted the embargo, providing essential resources and manpower to bolster Franco's forces. Although the Republican government received some assistance from the Soviet Union and international volunteer fighters, the Americans joined the cause under groups like the Abraham Lincoln Brigade and the John Brown Anti-Aircraft Battery, alongside renowned authors Ernest Hemingway and George Orwell. Scientists have developed a new gene-editing tool that is more accurate than CRISPR-Cas9. Prime editing can mend about 89 percent of the 75,000 or so harmful mutations in the human genome - even correcting for glitches at very specific places where DNA breaks occur, known as "hot spots" on chromosomes near genes in our body cells and tissues, such as the brain. The scientists behind this discovery consider it proof of concept: It works better with bigger genomes (humans currently make up 20 percent to 25 percent of the Earth), but they believe that their work could be adapted to other organisms by simply changing one simple parameter. The team will report its findings online today in Nature Communications. CRISPR was invented two decades ago to quickly tweak single strands of DNA using an enzyme called Cas9, which has been engineered from bacteria, and then snipped out to create a piece just like itself. Scientists use CRISPR to alter all sorts of traits in plants, animals, and microbes; for example, they used it last year to edit eggs inside mice, making them produce healthy embryos when fertilized by sperm containing diseased genetic material. But many biologists dislike CRISPR because it requires complex biological machinery designed specifically to target specific sections of DNA within each cell. Moreover, it tends to cause unintended edits elsewhere along the genome. Instead of targeting precise segments, researchers have tried different ways to cut off stretches of DNA in fish or fruit flies without affecting nearby regions. One group made proteins called zinc fingers that bind tightly to DNA and disable genes above certain levels. In some cases, these methods worked far better than conventional CRISPR, allowing researchers to fix only a small fraction (a few hundred) of allele defects. Another approach uses chemical enzymes called nuclease proteins whose activity depends partly on how much oxygen is present around them. A third method involves chemically modifying the structure of DNA before altering it. This technique allows researchers to insert fragments into specific points of existing genomic sequences rather than systematically cutting away entire chunks. According to the research team, this method eliminated hot spots in Drosophila fly embryos after seven tries. They also confirmed that they were able to correct both disease-causing genes and benign changes associated with aging. To test whether their method would actually do a good job on larger genomes, the Harvard team created three-dimensional structures of yeast cells showing exactly what hot spots remain intact if you turn off most of the cellular machinery required for protein synthesis. The scientists found that PrimeEdit targeted 90 percent to 95 percent of those hotspots, depending on which version the engineers had created. And while PrimeEdit did still result in errors across the genome during normal development, it appeared more stable once the organism reached adulthood. It seems likely, says geneticist Michael Deem, who studies evolution alongside Deem's collaborator, Emmanuelle Charpentier, professor of evolutionary biology, that genetic engineering may soon become standard practice among biologists. She predicts that any alterations caused by prime editing will eventually disappear over time by themselves. That means people might someday be able to get rid of cancer-causing variants - though there are big ethical questions surrounding splicing disease-fighting genes into babies, she notes.

Historical interpretations of John have been subject to considerable change over the years. Medieval chroniclers provided the first contemporary, or near contemporary, histories of John's reign. One group of chroniclers wrote early in John's life, or around the time of his accession, including Richard of Devizes, William of Newburgh, Roger of Hoveden and Ralph de Diceto. These historians were generally unsympathetic to John's behaviour under Richard's rule, but slightly more positive towards the very earliest years of John's reign. NASA will test drive a robot underneath Antarctica's sea ice in preparation for a mission in the subsurface oceans of Jupiter's moon, Europa. Buoyant Rover for Under-Ice Exploration, or BRUIE, will spend three weeks in Antarctica's McMurdo Dry Valleys, an ice-free region, as part of the 2019 field season for the McMurdo Long Term Ecological Research (MCM LTER) project. The researchers will test BRUIE's endurance, durability, navigation, power systems, and communications. "We've found that life often lives at the interface, both the sea ice and the water beneath it," said MCM LTER Project Manager Jack DiTullio. "If there's an environment on Europa where there's an ocean that might be similar to Antarctica, this would be a good way to start to understand what kind of life could possibly survive there." Understanding the biogeochemical and geophysical interactions between ice and water in the Antarctic Dry Valleys, which is similar to conditions on Mars and the icy moons of Jupiter and Saturn, is a primary focus of the MCM LTER. Ice-covered moons in the outer solar system, such as Europa, are of interest to astrobiologists because they may contain liquid oceans. A NASA mission to Europa, tentatively scheduled for the 2020s, would attempt to look for evidence of extraterrestrial life in the moon's subsurface oceans. The BRUIE has a buoyant cylindrical body that is 3.3 feet (1 meter) long and has a diameter of 1.7 feet (0.5 meters). The buoyancy allows the rover to roam under sea ice for extended periods without having to manage the power necessary for surfacing and submerging. BRUIE is equipped with two thrusters that propel the vehicle forward or backward. It also has a camera, lights, a communications system, a water sampler, and a sediment corer. The BRUIE will not carry instruments to detect life, because scientists do not want to contaminate the environment they are trying to study. "We don't have life detection instruments, because this is a platform for us to go investigate the area under the ice," said MCM LTER Scientist Kirsty Tinto. "It's about going back to the same place over multiple years, which is how you start to understand what type of life is there, how it's surviving, and how it's adapting to its environment." Tinto is the principal investigator of the Benthic Rover project and has been working on it for several years. She recently joined the MCM LTER team as the field season support scientist. Tinto and her colleagues in the Benthic Rover team at JPL will spend two weeks in Antarctica testing BRUIE. They plan to deploy the rover under the sea ice in McMurdo Sound, where the average ice thickness is 6 feet (2 meters). They will guide the rover back and forth as it autonomously samples and records data. BRUIE will be the first instrument to carry out a science mission under sea ice in Antarctica. The rover is designed to stay under the ice for weeks at a time. It will carry a communications system and an electric heater to prevent the electronics from freezing. "We hope to get it to go under the ice, maybe 10 to 20 meters, stay there for a little while, and then come up and resurface through the ice," said Tinto. The BRUIE will be equipped with a radio antenna, GPS unit, and a Wi-Fi modem for communications. It will also be equipped with a pair of sonars to provide real-time data about the ice and water conditions around the rover. The BRUIE team plans to test its navigation system, as well as the camera and lights. The navigation system is based on an algorithm developed at JPL called the Anywhere-on-Ice algorithm. The algorithm works with information from the GPS and the sonar to determine the rover's position in the ice. "We're not going to have a rover that can go anywhere, but we are going to have a rover that can go anywhere under the ice," said Tinto. In the initial years of producing records from vinyl discs, the sound was captured directly onto the "master disc" within the recording studio. Around 1950, this practice began to shift towards recording performances initially on audio tapes, allowing for processing and editing before being transferred onto the master disc. This transfer involved using a record cutter to inscribe the grooves onto the master disc. Initially, the master discs were made of soft wax but were eventually replaced by harder lacquer materials. Mastering required skillful manual adjustments by operators to accommodate variations in sound frequency throughout each rotation's groove width. Some larger record companies adopted this technique earlier than smaller ones.
