By'regular' Mathematics you are probably referring to'pure' Mathematics, which basically boils down to trying to understand numbers, concepts and theories in Mathematics. 'Applied' Mathematics is concerned with those theories and concepts which can be'applied' to other topics and real world situations; think engineering or Physics. TL;DR'Regular' (Pure) is Maths for the sake of understanding Maths;'Applied' is using Maths to understand real situations.,Pure mathematics is done for its own sake, essentially asking "if we assume these things to be true, what can we prove?," and maybe moving on to "how little do we have to assume to still be able to prove those things?" Applied mathematics is concerned with solving real-world problems like mechanics and statistics - as the name suggests, it has applications in the real world. The distinction has become a bit more fuzzy since it turned out even apparently very pure mathematics which was originally done for its own sake can have real applications, particularly number theory being used in encryption. Sometimes this is referred to as "applicable" mathematics.

Electricity stems from a property of matter called charge. Electric charges exert forces on other electric charges through what is known as an electric field. There are positive and negative charging points, those located near the electrical connection between electrodes. If these charged volumes are disturbed by disturbance in electricity flowing around them, the voltage drop will cause the electricity to flow away from the battery pack into the battery pack which causes it to lose its electric potential difference for a short period of time until the battery cells can be replaced with fresh cells. The energy loss from this phenomenon occurs when electric currents flow across the electrical connections between different types of batteries. This process creates heat that causes currents among various levels of charge which will eventually heat up three or four times more than normal wireless conductors such as copper wire strands used today. Although there are many possible solutions available they tend to be difficult to accomplish since most techniques involve attaching multiple layers of metal wires together so that each layer must be separate to allow easy removal within the battery packs using a separate power supply or power distribution system without creating additional cost constraints (such as installation costs). However, these methods have been efficacious enough even if the lithium ion batteries use the same materials as today's batteries because of their relatively small size thus making them ideal candidates for use alongside standard batteries due to their low weighting requirements while providing long life cycles compared to current lead acid batteries. The drawbacks of using wire-connected battery chargers include: the lack of control over voltages applied to devices; the need for additional protection circuitry; the inability to store large quantities of data; and the possibility of defects affecting design values due to corrosion caused by elevated temperatures during discharge processes due to temperature variations outside the confines of typical consumer electronics. These problems may reduce efficiency significantly because battery charger designs typically incorporate a single source of voltage regulation instead of two alternating current sources. Furthermore, battery chargers designed for use alone provide insufficient advantages at higher wattage ranges where one device can generally produce much greater output than another but still achieve similar performance results relative to one unit equipped separately. Accordingly, it would be desirable to develop improved lithium ion rechargeable batteries having improvements relative to existing chargers wherein both harnesses were operated independently rather than relying solely upon individual systems operating simultaneously against a common supply.

Over the last few years, and especially now with the popularity of Bernie Sanders, a heavily debated subject is the raising of the minimum wage to 15hour. While many would expect this to strengthen the lower class and only decreasing the wealth of the upper class, I feel as if it would end up hurting those it is meant to help. These company's would now have to spend much more of their budget on paying employees, and it's not as if they're going to magically have more money. I understand that the increase of wealth in the lower class would eventually circulate back to the business's, but I highly doubt it would be enough to make up for the increased wages of their employees, and it definitely wouldn't happen right away. Since I highly doubt the CEO or other upper management would take cuts from their pay to make up for this, that leaves two possible solutions that I can see: The first would be to decrease the amount of employees. If approximately an equal percentage of employees are let go to the increase in pay the company will be able to function without upper management having to take a pay cut. While those who are able to keep there jobs would be greatly helped by this, for the most part it would just increase the unemployment rate; with these lay offs happening in a large portion of minimum wag paying company's there would be no demand for jobs while the supply would be sky rocketing. The other solution would be for the company to increase prices (for retailrestaurants). With increasing prices nobody would have to loose their job, however it would still end up hurting the lower class. Practically all people get there basic necessities and luxuries from retail and grocery stores- the lower and middle classes especially rely heavily on major stores such as Walmart or Target. Even if your paycheck is increasing you'd still end up paying more the things you already buy, taking a large chunk of your paycheck. While ideally an increased minimum wage seems perfect, it would in reality end up creating a combination of these two things. I'm sure I didn't hit on some points, so please try to change my view on this, I, as a minimum wage employee myself, would love to have a good reason to support raising it. EDIT: Okay, my views been changed. I still don't think something as drastic as upping it to 15hour right away would be a good idea, but I think a gradual increase could be really good. The biggest things that helped my view change were the historical instances of MW rising, the average proportion of price increase vs. wage increase, as well as the fact that businesses are already operating with the minimum number of employees and that jobs wouldn't just become expendable. Mr Sisi has faced heavy criticism over his executive decision to give away the Red Sea islands, during a visit by Saudi Arabia's King Salman. The uninhabited islands have been under Egyptian control since 1950. The protesters in Cairo chanted "Sisi out" and "We own the land." Mohamed Hussein, an engineer, told Reuters: "I'm protesting because of the overall situation in the country, not just the islands." Both secular and Islamist activists had called for people to demonstrate against the transfer of the uninhabited islands. He said they had always belonged to the Saudis and Egypt had simply been asked to look after them. "We did not surrender our rights but we restored the rights of others," Mr Sisi said. "Egypt did not relinquish even a grain of sand. All the data and documents say nothing except that this particular right is theirs." Critics of the deal say Mr Sisi's decision to hand over the islands without parliamentary approval, and only announce the deal after it was done, was improper. Others have accused the president of giving the islands away in return for Saudi aid and investment. Inspired by the issue of map labeling, we investigate a scenario where there is a set of n growing disks in the plane, each expanding at potentially varying rates. If two disks intersect, the one with the smaller identifier vanishes. This particular challenge was initially presented by Funke, Krumpe, and Storandt in their work from IWOCA 2016. We present the inaugural general subquadratic methodology for determining both the instances and sequence of disappearances. Additionally, this approach can be applied to various geometric forms such as rectangles and extends to any fixed number of dimensions. By utilizing quadtrees, we offer an alternate procedure capable of executing nearly linearly; however, it does possess a logarithmic dependency on either the disparity between the swiftest and sluggish growth rates of disks or the extent of dispersion among disk central points. Compared to prior methods devised by Funke, Krumpe, and Storandt in IWOCA 2016, Bahrdt et al. in ALENEX 2017, and Funke and Storandt in EWCG 2017, our findings enhance computational efficiency. Lastly, we establish an (n log n) minimal limit for this problem, demonstrating that our quadtree-based solutions closely approximate optimality.

Following the Spanish Civil War in the mid-20th century, there was a swift rise in the populations of A Coruna, Vigo, and to some extent, other prominent Galician cities such as Ourense, Pontevedra, and Santiago de Compostela. This growth happened simultaneously with a decrease in rural inhabitants; numerous small towns and hamlets across Galicia's four provinces either vanished or came close to extinction within the same time frame. Advancements in economic progress and farm automation led to widespread abandonment of farmlands, compelling most residents to relocate to urban centers in search of employment opportunities. As a result, there has been a notable surge in the workforce engaged in the services (Tertiary) and knowledge-based (Quaternary) sectors.

Captain Harris and his crew of eight had been on a routine space exploration mission in the outer galaxy for over three months. They had encountered all sorts of challenges on their journey, from malfunctioning equipment to dangerous asteroid fields. But none of these obstacles prepared them for the ghost that haunted their ship, the Hermes. The Hermes was an old spacecraft, passed down from generation to generation of space explorers. It was said that the ship had been cursed, with every crew that sailed it haunted by a malevolent ghost. Some believed the ghost was a former crew member who died in a catastrophic malfunction, while others theorized that it was a vengeful spirit of an extraterrestrial race they had angered centuries ago. Whatever the cause, the ghost was real. It first made its presence known one night, when the captain and his crew were enjoying their rare leisure time. They heard a spine-tingling moan, followed by whispers that echoed through the hull of Hermes. At first, they brushed it off, assuming that it was just their overloaded imagination playing tricks on them. But as time went by, the ghost became more and more active. Objects would move on their own, doors would open and slam, and crew members saw apparitions of a humanoid figure hovering in the corridors. The ghost did not discriminate between crew members, either. Everyone experienced the haunting in one way or another, and soon they all began to fear for their lives. One night, Captain Harris decided to investigate the ghostly presence, taking his trusty blaster gun and a bag of detection equipment. As he descended into the lower levels of the ship, he heard the ghost's wail, louder and more menacing than ever before. Harris's heart raced as he felt the icy breath of the ghost on his neck, but he managed to hold his ground and confront the spirit. To his relief, the ghost did not lash out violently, but instead communicated with him telepathically. It informed Harris that it was not a malevolent entity, but merely a projection of the ship's consciousness, a manifestation of the Hermes's long history and the ghosts of all the crew who had sailed it in the past. The ghost begged Harris for mercy, not wanting to cause any harm to the current crew. Moved by the plea, Harris agreed to spare the ghost's existence, and returned to his crew with newfound knowledge about the haunted ship. For the rest of their journey, the ghost remained a harmless presence, and the crew sailed the Hermes back to Earth with a newfound appreciation for the superstitions and lore of their trade.

The most important qualification is that one must be nominated by another elected or appointed official at least 21 days before nomination day. Failure to comply with this requirement can result in automatic disqualification from office unless certain exceptions apply such as: failure was due exclusively to circumstances beyond the direct control of the person concerned; failure involved no moral turpitude; and, if it occurred after nomination day, when members could have been notified of their intention to run but failed to do so within 14 days thereafter. Appeals against decisions regarding candidacy may only take place on grounds of apathy, undue influence or mental incapacity according to section 20 (2). Nomination Day occurs either 10 business days prior to general election dates or five business days prior to local government election dates in each electoral region. The problems with North American were severe enough in late 1965 to cause Manned Space Flight Administrator George Mueller to appoint program director Samuel Phillips to head a "tiger team" to investigate the problems and propose solutions. The team was also given the responsibility of preparing a plan for an expeditious return to flight. Phillips's 33-page report was presented on January 21, 1966. It proposed a 10-month schedule to return to flight, including the first test flight of the new Saturn V. The tiger team was clearly concerned about the deterioration in the Apollo program schedule; a new Saturn V would be needed, and the new launch vehicle would take an estimated 18 months to develop. But the tiger team also recommended that the Apollo 204 launch be pushed forward to December 1966, as if the problems with the Apollo 203 launch were already solved. This was possible because Apollo 204 had been cut from 577 pounds to 454 pounds of payload, and because only a single launch vehicle would be needed instead of two. The tiger team also recommended that the second launch of the new Saturn V be delayed from November 1968 to January 1969, to coincide with the first launch of the Skylab space station. Apollo 203 would be the last launch using the old Apollo launch vehicle. That vehicle was now 6 years old and had suffered several failures. But the problems with the Apollo 203 launch could not be blamed on aging. It was caused by design errors, and most of these were identified and corrected. The problems began at the Cape when the T-10 test rocket, which was scheduled to be launched on December 3, 1965, failed to ignite its second stage. The following day, the first stage of the T-10 rocket failed to ignite. The problem was traced to defective electrical wiring, but the electrical wiring in the spacecrafts also had to be checked. In December, the command and service modules were stacked at the Cape and a second test rocket, the T-20, was readied for launch. That rocket also failed to ignite, apparently because of a problem with the second stage. The launch of T-20 was postponed from January 13, 1966, to January 17 because of a minor technical problem with the T-20 rocket. The launch was again postponed from January 25 to January 27 because of a fuel leak in the second stage of the T-20 rocket. It was postponed from January 27 to February 4 because of a problem with the third stage of the T-20 rocket. The T-20 launch was postponed from February 4 to February 12 because of a problem with the third stage of the T-20 rocket. On February 10, 1966, the third stage of the T-20 rocket was tested, and it worked. At that point, the T-20 rocket was ready to fly, and the Apollo 203 launch had been postponed long enough. On February 12, the launch was rescheduled for February 21. On February 21, the T-20 rocket was launched from the Cape and successfully reached orbit. But just after separation of the second stage, a problem developed in the rocket's autopilot. The command to shut off the engine was never sent, and the rocket veered out of orbit. Object detection and recognition algorithms using deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) tend to be computationally intensive to implement. This presents a particular challenge for embedded systems, such as mobile robots, where the computational resources tend to be far less than for workstations. As an alternative to standard, uniformly sampled images, we propose the use of foveated image sampling here to reduce the size of images, which are faster to process in a CNN due to the reduced number of convolution operations. We evaluate object detection and recognition on the Microsoft COCO database, using foveated image sampling at different image sizes, ranging from 416 416 to 96 96 pixels, on an embedded GPU - an NVIDIA Jetson TX2 with 256 CUDA cores. The results show that it is possible to achieve a 4 speed-up in frame rates, from 3.59 FPS to 15.24 FPS, using 416 416 and 128 128 pixel images respectively. For foveated sampling, this image size reduction led to just a small decrease in recall performance in the foveal region, to 92.0 of the baseline performance with full-sized images, compared to a significant decrease to 50.1 of baseline recall performance in uniformly sampled images, demonstrating the advantage of foveated sampling.

Overall, when compared to other films addressing similar themes related to authority and control over individuals, I believe this movie successfully raises thought-provoking questions.

In recent years, particularly during Bernie Sander's surge in popularity, one contentious issue has been advocating for a $15 hourly minimum wage. Contrary to some beliefs that it might benefit the working class at the expense of the affluent, I argue that it could ultimately harm those intended to receive aid. Businesses would face significant financial strain due to higher employee salaries, without any sudden influx of funds. Although there may be eventual economic benefits resulting from greater spending power among low-wage workers, these gains likely won't compensate for elevated wages immediately nor alleviate burdens on corporate leaders, who are unlikely to voluntarily reduce their own income. Two conceivable alternatives exist: reducing workforce numbers or implementing price hikes across goods and services. Both options carry negative implications - the former exacerbates unemployment rates, while the latter diminishes purchasing power within the very demographic purportedly targeted for assistance. Thus, despite its initial appeal, the concept of boosting the minimum wage to $15 per hour presents numerous potential drawbacks.

We consider a wireless distributed computing system, in which multiple mobile users, connected wirelessly through an access point, collaborate to perform a computation task. In particular, users communicate with each other wirelessly in order to exchange the information required for their collaboration. For example, a distributed sorting task can be performed by mobile users following a shared protocol that involves local computations and data exchanges. The system may be under resource constraints, such as limited energy or bandwidth, which pose challenges on the design of an efficient communication mechanism. The communication mechanism itself may be a computation task that is mutually dependent on the actual computational tasks that the users perform. In this paper, we address these problems in the context of distributed computation over wireless communication networks. We propose a novel scheme that combines wireless networking with distributed computing techniques in order to allow users to efficiently collaborate in performing a given computation task. Our scheme is based on the use of coding theory to enable communication among users without the need for a central entity. The proposed scheme is scalable and may be used to perform a variety of computation tasks under different resource constraints. We assume a wireless distributed computing system consisting of n users, connected wirelessly through an access point. The users communicate with each other in order to exchange the information required for their collaboration. We consider a general class of computation tasks, which we call distributed applications, that can be performed by the users in the system. A distributed application is a collection of sub-tasks, each of which is executed by a subset of users in the system. In order to execute a sub-task, the participating users need to exchange information with each other. We assume that the users are equipped with energy-constrained devices, such as sensors or mobile phones. The devices may have limited energy resources, which need to be carefully managed in order to prolong their lifetime. We also assume that the devices are capable of wireless communication, and that they can be turned on and off in order to conserve energy. We propose a novel scheme for distributed computation over wireless communication networks, which we call coded distributed computing. In our scheme, the users cooperate in order to compute a function of their inputs, while taking into account the energy constraints of their devices. The scheme is based on the use of coding theory to enable communication among the users without the need for a central entity. The proposed scheme is scalable and may be used to perform a variety of computation tasks under different resource constraints. Our scheme has several advantages over existing schemes for distributed computation. First, our scheme is energy-efficient, as it minimizes the number of times that the devices need to be turned on. Second, our scheme is scalable, as it does not require a central entity to manage the communication among the users. Third, our scheme is robust to communication failures, as the coding theory used in our scheme allows the users to recover from communication errors. We illustrate the use of our scheme with two examples. In the first example, we consider the problem of distributed sorting, in which the users need to sort a sequence of numbers using only local comparisons. We show that our scheme can be used to solve this problem with a significantly smaller number of comparisons than the best known scheme for distributed sorting. In the second example, we consider the problem of distributed matrix multiplication, in which the users need to multiply two matrices using only local operations. We show that our scheme can be used to solve this problem with a significantly smaller number of operations than the best known scheme for distributed matrix multiplication.

Determining the masses of stars becomes relatively easy when specific conditions apply, such as observing objects orbiting around them. Our comprehension of gravitational forces and motion allows us to predict orbits effectively, especially within our solar system where this knowledge has been extensively validated. Therefore, if there exists another celestial body, like a planet or a secondary star, revolving around a primary star, we can gather some essential data to calculate the star's mass precisely. The initial step involves measuring the duration of the object's full orbit, followed by assessing its orbital velocity or the degree of oscillation exhibited by the host star due to the object's gravitational pull. These observations can be conducted using Doppler shift techniques on the starlight emitted. Armed with this information, we can utilize established formulas governing orbital dynamics to deduce the size of the orbit and consequently, the mass of the star being orbited. With modern technology enabling highly precise measurements, estimates of stellar mass typically achieve accuracy levels up to a couple of percentage points. To clarify misconceptions, while some may argue that our understanding remains theoretical, the reality is that numerous practical applications demonstrate the reliability of fundamental physical principles, including those related to orbital mechanics, which have been rigorously examined and confirmed both terrestrially and extraterrestrially. Furthermore, knowing the composition, density, and dimensions of an object also enables us to compute its mass efficiently.

The general issue of "squatters' rights" was first brought to my attention by [this article posted here on reddit.] I was appalled that someone could just break into an empty home and claim it as their own and would be protected by the law. After a bit of reading and research I see that the problem was not squatter's rights (which does exist, as "adverse possession" and I still believe is wrong, but I'll leave that for another CMV.) but that the person who broke into the home claimed a verbal contract. Even though both the home owner and the person who was entrusted the care of the house denied it, this makes it a civil matter and the police can't intervene. I think that the law should be changed in favor of the homeowner in order to prevent destruction of the property and theft which the homeowner will never recover. It's true that the squatters were moved out, but in the process they trashed the house and even if the homeowner sued for property damage he isn't likely to get anything. In the comment thread for this and other articles I've seen stories of similar occurrences. In one, a police officer relayed the story after reporting to a call of a break in. A family who had been on vacation for only 3 weeks came back to find squatters in their home. When they called the police the squatters were originally removed but the DA intervened and the police were forced to let them go and tell the family that it was a civil matter. In the time a court order was issued to evict the squatters, their belongings were stolen and the piping in the house was destroyed to scrap the copper. I believe that if ownership of the home can be proven, the burden should be on the squatters to prove a written contract, signed by the owner or designated guardian. Embeddinghub is a database built for machine learning embeddings. Embeddings are dense numerical representations of real-world objects and relationships. They are used to quantify how similar vectors are to each other in a way that supports learning and reasoning. Embeddings are particularly useful for unstructured and non-tabular data like text or images. Machine learning models like neural networks can use embeddings to understand the similarity between two words or the relation between two objects. In the past few years, researchers have created embeddings for all sorts of domains. They've created embeddings for words and phrases, countries and cities, movies and actors, and even genes and proteins. However, these embeddings are siloed away in academic papers and software repositories. It's very hard to find embeddings for a particular domain, even when they've been published. Embeddinghub aims to solve this problem by creating a database for embeddings, where people can easily search, browse and compare them. Anyone who wants to use embeddings for their research can use the search and compare features to find the embeddings most appropriate for their domain. Researchers who've created embeddings can add them to the database, which will increase the visibility of their work and help others discover it. The Cover's Counting Function Theorem stands as a significant achievement within the realm of artificial neural network theory. This theorem offers insight into quantifying the countless binary arrangements (known as dichotomies) possible among p points situated within an n-dimensional space. However, its application remains challenging when addressing complex issues beyond mere point classification. One such challenge involves handling intricate datasets characterized by non-individualistic patterns. For instance, identifying objects while being unaffected by inconsequential alterations—such as rotational shifts or variations in viewpoint—requires representing these items through broader perceptual manifolds comprised of similar classifications. Our study advances a function counting framework tailored for such structured information, expanding upon Cover's initial combinatorics methodology. We also formulate precise mathematical representations for the typical quantity of dichotomies found amongst generic pattern clusters exhibiting correlation. Additionally, our research yields a definitive equation enabling the calculation of a binary categorizer's capability to differentiate between polygons of varying dimensions. Such discoveries could significantly enhance our comprehension of generalization processes, features extraction techniques, and recognizing invariant entities via neural networks.

On Thursday, an investment manager and hairdresser will challenge the right of the government to start the process of withdrawing the UK from the EU without a vote in Parliament. Lawyers will question whether Prime Minister Theresa May is entitled to act unilaterally, using powers left over from the days of medieval monarchs. It could end up - in theory - with Parliament being given a means to stop Brexit. So as constitutional rows go, it is box office stuff. Or as professor of public law at Cambridge University, Mark Elliott, puts it: "I don't rule out the possibility of the government losing the case." Leading the fight against the government is Gina Miller, who runs an investment firm in London, SCM Private. She argues that only Parliament can make a decision that leads to the loss of her "rights" under EU law. She is confident she has a strong case and is undaunted by criticism. "I do not back away from a fight," she says. "I'm very vocal about things and I'm no stranger to making enemies." She is joined by London-based Spanish hairdresser Deir Dos Santos and the People's Challenge group, set up by Grahame Pigney and backed by a crowd-funding campaign. Also weighing into the case against the government is the group, Fair Deal for Expats. Around two million British citizens are believed to live and work in other EU countries. The Brexit terms have not been decided but expats - some of whom were barred from voting in the referendum - fear potential repatriation and are worried about the impact on their jobs and homes as well as the ramifications for healthcare, their children's schooling and pensions. Three London law firms - Mishcon de Reya, Edwin Coe and Bindmans - have agreed to take up the case. Croft Solicitors is representing the expats. Superstar of the bar" Lord Pannick QC - also an independent member of the House of Lords - will be arguing Gina Miller's case while the government is turning to an old favourite, James Eadie QC. Attorney General Jeremy Wright QC, the government's legal adviser, will also play a big role. He said: "There must be no attempts to remain inside the EU, no attempts to re-join it through the back door, and no second referendum. "We do not believe this case has legal merit. The result should be respected and the government intends to do just that." In political terms, the UK is on course for departure from the EU. But as far as the law goes, nothing has changed. The UK remains a fully paid-up member of the EU until it triggers Article 50 of the Treaty of Lisbon 2007. The question at the heart of the row is: who should activate Article 50? The prime minister or Parliament? During the referendum campaign, the then prime minister, David Cameron, said that in the event of a Leave vote he would activate Article 50 immediately. The government maintains that his successor Theresa May has the authority to do so, without a vote by MPs. That right - they say - is based on the Royal Prerogative - powers once held by kings and queens to do, essentially, what they wished. The use of prerogative powers in a modern parliamentary democracy is a curious corner of British law. Over centuries, power in the UK has been wrested away from dictatorial monarchs and handed to elected politicians. But government ministers have managed to cling on to a few of those regal powers, usually in international affairs. One such prerogative is the power to make and break treaties with other countries. The government's position is that triggering Article 50 is all about ending a treaty with other EU countries and so using prerogative powers in these circumstances is "entirely consistent with standard constitutional practice." Critics will argue in the High Court that it is a bit more complicated than that. They say that activating Article 50 effectively wipes out the European Communities Act 1972, passed by Parliament and allowing EU law to apply in the UK. Lawyers opposing the government argue that the 1972 Act introduced a big constitutional change and gave British people new rights. It would be unlawful, they conclude, for a prime minister to use the Royal Prerogative to take away rights bestowed by Parliament. Grahame Pigney, from the People's Challenge, says the "enforced removal" of citizenship rights from 65 million people would be "completely unprecedented" in a modern democracy. "I believe that, as Parliament has granted us these rights, it is for Parliament to decide when, how and under what circumstances they are taken away," he says. Lawyers working for Fair Deal for Expats will be deploying similar legal arguments but using evidence to emphasise the human impact of Brexit. The chairman of Fair Deal for Expats, John Shaw - who lives in France - has submitted a statement to the High Court saying the referendum result was a "shock." He is currently undergoing cancer treatment in France. He states: "If my right to access healthcare is either taken away, or compromised materially such that I am not able to rely upon it in the same way as French nationals, I would be unlikely to receive, or be able to afford, the same level of care in France." His lawyers will tell the High Court that the rights enjoyed by British citizens "beyond these shores" are so fundamental that legislation is "required" to take them away. But in legal papers setting out the government's case - released last week - it insists that starting the withdrawal process will not have any impact on British laws and any changes will be decided in future negotiations. The Royal Prerogative is just one of the arguments to be aired in the High Court. There will be heated debates about the 2015 European Union Referendum Act, which paved the way for a referendum. In their legal papers the government states that Parliament passed that Act on the "clear understanding" that the outcome of the referendum would be "respected." If Gina Miller wins the case - it adds - it will not be able to "give effect to the will and decision of the people." Conservative chairman of the European Scrutiny Committee, and prominent Leave campaigner Sir Bill Cash thinks the government has a strong case, saying: "To attempt to revisit the decision by another Act of Parliament is a kind of fraud on the electorate." But lawyers at Mishcon de Reya say the idea was to set up an "advisory" referendum - not a binding one. They state: "Nowhere in the 2015 Act does it specify the consequences that should follow from the referendum result." The biggest weapon in the government's armoury could be that the whole issue is not a matter for the UK courts at all. They says it is a complex decision that must be made by ministers. Sir Bill Cash said: "We could have a situation where judges are imposing a requirement on Parliament, via the secretary of state, to make legislation. "That's outside the rules. The proceedings of parliament are outside the jurisdiction of the court." Lord Chief Justice of England and Wales, Lord Thomas of Cwmgiedd, will hear the case - which is expected to last a couple of weeks. Mark Elliott says it is very hard to know which way it will go. "If the court simply applied existing case law, the government would win. The question is whether the court will go beyond existing territory and treat it as an exceptional situation. The court may develop the law." Putting the legal arguments aside, some Brexit supporters say that the High Court case is a fig-leaf for a political campaign to keep the UK inside the EU. Gina Miller disputes that and argues that Leavers and Remainers should back her case against "prerogative creep." "The idea that a court case can put a halt to Brexit is nonsense and it has nothing to do with altering the timetable. What we are looking for is legal certainty." If the court concludes that Parliament must approve Article 50, that could be a game-changer. The majority of MPs campaigned for the UK to remain in the EU. They could, in theory, vote against the activation of Article 50. But would they risk enormous political and social ructions by rejecting the referendum result? Most members of the House of Lords are also opposed to Brexit. That raises the possibility of another extraordinary scenario - an unelected Lords voting against the wishes of 17.4 million people. If the government loses its case in the British courts, they could eventually go to the European Court of Justice. It raises the possibility of a truly strange scenario - Brexit ministers asking European judges to overturn the decision of the British courts.

Volkswagen has halted production at several plants in Germany, hitting the output of Golf and Passat models amid a dispute with two external suppliers. The world's largest carmaker said on Monday it had stopped production at its Wolfsburg, Emden and Zwickau plants after a supplier failed to deliver parts on time. A company spokesman said the stoppages would last until at least Wednesday and that VW was in talks with the suppliers to resolve the issue. VW's Wolfsburg plant alone produces around 3,800 cars a day, meaning the stoppage could hit output of more than 20,000 vehicles over the three-day period. Right arm strung back, with hand clenched into a fist. I'm not one for violence, but sometimes it's necessary. 3..... 2..... 1..... Now! Carefully practiced, timed down to the exact moment, I swung my fist forward, directly in front of me, about 3 inches above my level. I put my whole weight behind that punch. I had to, because it's not exactly easy to knock out a 6'1," 300 lbs security guard with one punch. However, just as planned, I did just that. Frank's whole body relaxed before crumpling to the floor, as the unexpected hit knocked him out cold. At least I hope he was just knocked out. Never had a chance to check to see if he was okay. I swiftly pulled the gun from the holster that Frank was wearing, turned off the safety with a flick of the finger, and fired three shots into the cement ceiling above me. The noise was deafening in the cement echo chamber of a corridor. Just as planned, the noise was even louder than the alarms. The mob of people trying to flee suddenly recoiled in response. Taking advantage of the opportunity I had just created for myself, I rushed forward through the crowd. Most tried to step aside to avoid the seemingly crazed gunman. They seemed even more afraid than moments before. I don't blame them. Within a few moments from firing the shots, I had maneuvered my way to one of the emergency stairways that led deeper into the complex. I swung open the door and rushed inside just as the crowd returned to fleeing for their lives. The stairway was empty, as most of the employees on the lower floors had already been evacuated. I sprinted down the stairs, taking them two and even three at a time. I went as fast as I could until I reached the 34th step down from the 5th basement level door. That one always seemed to slip me up. I took special care to slow down and adjust my pace to avoid that step. Navigating down the rest of the stairs and through the following corridors on the 12th basement floor was relatively easy. I had each twist and turn committed to memory. The next challenge was the large door laden with'Secure Personnel Only' warnings all over. It requires a 12 digit pass code that only the scientists assigned to the lab it protected knew. I happened to be one of those scientists, but I didn't have the time to slow down to input the numbers. As I sprinted towards the door, I raised the gun, took aim, and fired the remaining two bullets into the keypad. Thanks to the practice I had, and a bit of luck, the shots ripped into the circuitry and forced the door to slide open. I slipped through as soon as there was enough space in the doorway. Inside was source of the crisis at hand. The particle accelerator my team had been working on had malfunctioned. Or instead, perhaps it had worked better than we had expected. We were researching anti matter in an attempt to find a way to safely gather and harness it as a possible fuel source for interstellar travel. The keyword in that sentence was'safely'. When it we turned it on for the first time earlier today, everything went to shit. The lab was still filled with my colleagues, all huddled together against the far wall. They knew it was hopeless to run. Once the accelerator's safety measures fail, the resulting blast would decimate half the country. They tried their best in the time they had, but there was nothing else they could to stop it. Luckily, I had all the time in the world to come up with a solution. I rushed through the lab to the main switch board. I knew what I had to do. "Alexandra, get over here!" I yelled. Quick to her feet, she rushed to join me at the console that controlled the mile long machine that contained our impending doom. "Wh-where did you go? How did you Alexandra stammered. She was confused, and rightfully so. Unfortunately, there wasn't much time left. "Listen closely," I said, calmly. "I know how to stop all this but I need you to pay attention and do exactly as I say, without question. Got it?" "I..... yes. Of course." With that, we began the long sequence of inputs that were necessary to save us. To save everyone. I couldn't do it alone, as it required at least two people to get past multiple of the security protocols. Under so much pressure, Alexandra did great. She did just as I ordered, and everything was going smoothly until the final moments. It all came down to this. "On three, I'll increase the energy input to the max, while you hit that large red button to your left," I said. She quickly turned to me, shocked. "ONE!" "W-wait, what!?" She was freaking out. "JUST DO IT! TWO!" "THREE!" I shoved the slider all the way forward, and she..... hesitated. Fuck. This was the farthest I had gotten, and in the final moment, that one moment of hesitation made the difference. It was all over for her, our fellow scientists, and half the country. It was not, however, over for me. Just as the blast went off, I closed my eyes and focused. I knew what I needed to do differently. What to say to her. I knew how to save everyone..... I won't have time to explain all of this to them. There was a familiar pain as my eyes adjusted...

In our study, we explore a combined radio frequency (RF) and hybrid Radio Frequency Free Space Optical (RFFSO) network model in which multiple mobile devices send their information through an RF channel to a relay point (such as a miniature cell tower), which then transmits the data via a hybrid RF/Free Space Optics (FSO) backhaul connection to a central hub (like a main cell tower). Both the relay and the central hub utilize numerous antennas for sending and receiving signals on the RF channels, whereas each mobile device possesses just one antenna. These RF connections operate simultaneously; they can function fully duplex with regard to the FSO link but must alternate use when communicating directly with one another. Within this framework, we establish the most efficient method for allocating RF bandwidth among the various RF channels. Our simulation outcomes demonstrate that this novel combination of communication infrastructure and resource distribution strategy surpasses traditional models relying soleptaed on either purely RF or FSO backhaul links alone.

That's a very broad question since you're talking about a wide variety of foods that all have different flavours for different reasons... But I think a good example of why it can be difficult is stuff like the Maillard reaction. [The Maillard reaction] (URL0) is a reaction between amino acids and reducing sugars that results in browning and produces the chemicals that make many foods taste pleasing when cooked. The thing is that there is not just one kind of amino acid and reducing sugar. There are many different kinds, and when the maillard reaction occurs in cooking, it doesn't just produce one chemical, it produces a whole range of chemicals, and some of those chemicals break down to make other chemicals. Each food can have its own unique maillard reaction with it's own unique profile of flavouring chemicals as a result (leading to wildly different tastes), so to make exactly the same flavour profile you need exactly the right starting chemicals, reacted in exactly the right conditions. That's a lot harder to produce than say, the characteristic flavour of pears, which is mostly down to mixing together one specific carboxylic acid with one specific alcohol to get [one specific ester] (URL1). The Malliard reaction is just one case of a thing that creates complex flavours. Any taste that involves the interaction of many different chemicals is probably going to be hard to recreate synthetically.,This is due to flavours being made up of various chemicals. Those chemicals can be fairly simple on their own - for example lemon is "sharp" because it contains citric acid, which is easy to duplicate chemically by synthesising citric acid. The more complex a "flavour" is, the more difficult it is to accurately duplicate that flavour by synthesising chemicals. Something as complex as roast chicken could potentially involve tens of individual chemicals, some of which may be proteins, or fats, or acids. And then you have textures, which are even more difficult to accurately reproduce. So in summary - it's relatively easy to duplicate simple flavours, and very hard to replicate complex flavours.

Current state-of-the-art neural dialogue models learn from human conversations following the data-driven paradigm. As such, a reliable training corpus is the crux of building a robust and well-behaved dialogue model. Unfortunately, developing and maintaining a rich dialogue corpus is costly. We propose a complementary approach to generate new dialogues via a neural language generator. The proposed generator is able to capture the content semantics of an utterance and use it to generate a new response. We propose a simple architecture called CopyCat, which relies on copying previously encountered content and adapting it to the current situation. We demonstrate the capability of CopyCat by showing that it can generate responses with reasonable coherence. Moreover, we show that it is possible to train CopyCat in an unsupervised manner using pseudo-rewards. Copyright 2017 Google Inc. All Rights Reserved.

To me, let's consider rotating a bolt by 180 degrees. Using a 1-inch wrench would require minimal hand movement due to the short arc. However, using a 3-foot wrench would necessitate covering a larger distance for the same rotation. This concept resembles a block and tackle pulley system where lifting a weight becomes simpler, albeit requiring more rope than the actual height lifted. Torque measurement is expressed in Newton-meters (Nm). By increasing the radius, we also enhance the circle's circumference, resulting in an extended arc length when applying torque at a greater distance. Consequently, as the force application distance rises, the required force decreases proportionally to maintain constant torque. Thus, exerting maximum effort on a 10 cm wrench yields significantly less effect compared to utilizing the same energy on a 1 m wrench. This principle aligns with the law of levers, stating that when the handle-to-fulcrum distance surpasses the fulcrum-to-head distance, the lever magnifies the input force. Since a wrench has its fulcrum and head practically combined, extending its length results in increased force amplification.

During early Roman periods, the calendar relied on lunar phases rather than solar movements. Months varied between 29 and 31 days to correspond with the moon's cycle while accommodating essential dates within each month, such as the Ides, along with properly positioned religious celebrations. However, the moon's and sun's cycles did not synchronize perfectly. To adjust the calendar to the solar year, February alternated between 28 days and longer durations of 23-24 days, supplemented by an additional 27-day month when necessary. This created a year consisting of approximately 355 days, occasionally necessitating the insertion of an extra month to maintain alignment with the solar cycle.

Caesar recognized the need for reform due to the actual length of a year being around 365.25 days. Consequently, he introduced ten additional days into the calendar system, modifying certain months accordingly. These changes led to the establishment of our present-day month durations.

The contemporary Gregorian calendar boasts remarkable precision in astronomical calculations. Formulated under Pope Gregory XIII, it surpasses both its predecessors—the Julian and original Roman calendars—in accuracy. The latter, primarily lunar-based, gives rise to seasonal names such as "harvest moon" or "flower moon." The evolution from the Roman to Gregorian calendars reflects advancements in understanding celestilibility over time.

One pulse: That was all it took to bring the world to its knees for a day. A single, one second pulse was able to stop everything, traffic stuck on bridges, planes grounded on runways, people fleeing from skyscrapers. I can't blame them. When the air around you starts to vibrate like you are standing in front of a loudspeaker at a concert for no apparent reason, I think you are justified in panicking. Overall, that first pulse caused little damage. Some delicate stained glass shattered, thousands of car accidents, three or maybe four planes crashed on runways, nothing too major. The entire world felt this pulse, throbbing everywhere. The second time, I figured people would adapt faster. Maybe get back to work after an hour or two. Instead, it was worse. Two days, two days of the world standing still! Businesses closed, highways stopped, planes grounded. This was a week after the first pulse! Only one week! It's not like you can forget about that first pulse that quick! Granted, it was two pulses, probably about two seconds long and three seconds apart, which made the air ring like a plucked guitar string, but still, nothing had happened. We were all still there. Damages from those two pulses was more severe than the last pulse: Windows on the top floors of skyscrapers shattered, paintings and shelves fell down, millions of car accidents, some old TV towers collapsed. Again, not too bad. A unified task force was appointed to figure out the nature of these pulses. All we had to do was wait. They turned their instruments to the ground, and we all held our breath. The next series was irregular. Almost a slow melody of five notes, no two the same length, no two the same pitch. Something a child might have composed. It occurred four days after the two pulses, and it seemed to be stronger. The pulses shook you down to the bones, all the way in your heart. The first set of deaths were directly attributed to this. The vibrations were too much for some of our older folks. The other damages were quite numerous. Several planes fell from the sky after the vibrations ripped the fuselages apart, a couple of buildings collapsed, the remaining windows across the world shattered. Overall, a global state of emergency. The task force turned up nothing. They said, with a 70 percent confidence in their numbers that the vibrations weren't coming from the ground. Something else was causing them. We braced ourselves for the next wave, surely to be worse than the previous ones. The next day seemed to take an eternity. Injuries were patched up, roads were cleared, and emergency supplies were distributed. Several riots broke out. Then it came in: the pulses which would change everything: A single pulse, then something remarkable. The air was speaking. At least, that's what it felt like. The voice resonated everywhere around us, every corner of the earth, even within our own lungs. "We are coming. We will be in contact." The voice was deep, with a remarkably fluent grasp of English. Preparations broke out immediately, preparations for war, attempts to train diplomats and leaders about what our best idea of "intergalactic cultural competence" was, conspiracy theories, Area 51, Roswell, the whole nine yards. That was 50 years ago to this day. No other pulses, no spaceships in the sky, nothing. All we have is that promise made to us with our own air: "We are coming." The conspiracy theorists have raged on and on, but I still think that somewhere, something is coming for us, and I'm not sure whether to greet them with open arms or to be terrified of the damage they can cause. I can't tell you what to think, but I worry for humanity, whenever they decide to contact us again. You should too.

Mothers-to-be are more likely to get malaria as their immunity is lowered, says the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG). Malaria carries serious risks for mother and baby including miscarriage, stillbirth and premature labour. The tropical disease is transmitted by mosquitoes and causes a fever, flu-like symptoms, vomiting and diarrhoea. There have been no malaria-related deaths in pregnant or recently pregnant women in the UK in the past decade but the RCOG says it has been receiving inquires from worried women. In the UK, about 1,500 cases of malaria are reported each year and about 10 people will die, said the RCOG. It says all non-essential trips to areas with a high risk of malaria should be avoided. Risk areas include large areas of Africa, Asia including China and India, Central and South America, parts of the Middle East and some Pacific Islands. If the trip is unavoidable, the college advises women to seek advice from a centre with expertise in malaria which will provide information on ways to reduce the risk of infection. Women should make sure they are aware of the risk, take out measures such as mosquito nets for bite prevention and take anti-malarial medication. Philippa Marsden, who chairs the RCOG's patient information committee, said although the risks were still relatively small it was important that women were well-informed. Cath Broderick of the RCOG women's network said: "If women are worried about symptoms after returning from a high-risk country and think they may have malaria, they should see a doctor immediately and inform them of their recent travels." Symptoms can take a week or more to develop after being bitten.

Two research teams described in Nature Materials have developed materials capable of detecting pressure as efficiently and swiftly as human skin. These materials consist of numerous miniature pressure sensors arranged in arrays that transform minor variations in pressure into electric impulses. Constructed from malleable rubber sheets that can assume diverse forms, these sensor arrays may find applications in coating prosthetic limbs, constructing delicate object handling robots, or enhancing instruments utilized in minimally invasive surgeries. 

In one methodology, Ali Javey from UC Berkeley and his associates created a series of perpendicular nanometer-thick wires capped with an elastic film. This configuration functions as a thin-film transistor (TFT) featuring a pressure-responsive surface. Electrical current passing through this setup depends on the force applied to the rubber sheet—greater pressure permits increased current flow. To demonstrate their creation's adaptability, they bent it to a curvature tighter than that of a pencil while maintaining consistent function.

An alternative technique was presented by Zhenan Bao's team at Stanford University. Their innovation incorporates a microstructured rubber sheet within the TFT instead of integrating a pressure-sensitive resistor array over a nanowire TFT array like the Berkeley team did. This design not only replicates the primary features of the first approach but also boasts quicker recovery time to its initial form and heightened responsiveness due to the microstructure of the rubber sheet. Although the Stanford group's material might exhibit reduced flexibility compared to the first approach, further development could address this limitation.

During the period from the 1950s to the 1980s, alongside the development of analytic ethics within Anglo-American philosophical tradition, various critical approaches towards existing social structures emerged across Europe. These new philosophies incorporated aspects of Marxist economics while placing greater focus on culture and ideology. Influential figures from the Frankfurt School, including Herbert Marcuse, Theodor W. Adorno, Max Horkheimer, and Jürgen Habermas, merged Marxist theories with psychoanalytic insights derived from Freud's work. Other European philosophers leaning toward Marxism explored concepts related to structuralism and revisited ideas originating from Hegelian philosophy. Post-structuralist thinkers like Gilles Deleuze, Michel Foucault, Claude Lefort, and Jean Baudrillard also contributed significantly during this era. Furthermore, the Situationist movement, particularly through the works of Guy Debord, applied a Marxist perspective on commodity fetishism to the domain of consumer behavior and analyzed its connection with prevailing ideologies.

Light from stars tend to pulsate uniformly across the whole surface of a star. Astronomers have discovered a teardrop-shaped object that only pulses from one side. The star is about 5 more massive and 30 times brighter than our sun, but although it has an unusually high temperature for its size (5,000 degrees Kelvin), it does not appear to burn hydrogen or helium in a conventional way - possibly because part of its mass lies outside the nuclear core where fusion takes place.[8] The first supernova detected with radio telescopes occurred in 1987 when observations by Karl Gebhardt revealed what appeared at first sight to be two separate objects: ASASSN-15lh and ASASSN 15mgh (the mh suffix indicates "magnetically highly interacting. These were actually one pair of very close stellar companions within 100 light years, which would become apparent as they merged into a supernovae: SN1987A. This event provided astronomers with conclusive evidence confirming Einstein's predictions made just over half a century earlier,[910] giving us a much better understanding of how such explosions occur during the final stages of planetary systems' evolution. Superblunder was another astronomical discovery made using VLBI techniques involving observation time on the Very Long Baseline Array; this new technique allowed detection and study of low frequency gravitational waves emitted from merging[11] colliding neutron stars. It also helped prove Albert Einstein's general theory of relativity correct under extreme conditions. In 2007, astronomers observed gamma rays being released from a black hole merger known as GW170809B, releasing ten thousand trillion kilojoules - enough energy to power all human civilization for 130 billion years. A similar signal was picked up again four months later in 2008 after an even larger explosion called GRB080319B resulted from material orbiting around a binary system before falling toward each other. On September 14-16, 2017, scientists observed the deaths of 2 neutron stars resulting in simultaneous bright flashes of light lasting less than two seconds each. Called gravitational wave events GW170814 and GW170608, these space phenomena are now considered standard tools for studying physics far beyond anything we can observe directly.[1213] In addition to the direct observational data obtained through observations of distant galaxies produced via deep optical imaging,[citation needed] several major surveys designed specifically to gather information related to dark matter are underway:[1]

Given its fresh perspectives on the renowned author's thoughts, coupled with its literary, biographical, philosophical, and religious aspects, the document captivates various interests. Written shortly after Japan's capitulation marking the conclusion of WWII, the concept of true joy possibly resurfaced in Lewis's contemplations. In excellent condition, the missive contains statements like "Authentic joy...surprises you beneath your ribcage and amuses you along your spine, causing you to neglect food and keeping you pleasantly alert through the night." Furthermore, it contrasts genuine delight with complacency induced by safety and affluence. Lewis also posits that a fleeting moment of bliss outweighs twelve hours of mere satisfaction. This sentiment echoes consistently throughout his existence. Interestingly, Lewis would eventually encounter and wed a lady named Joy not long afterwards.

Visible light communications (VLC) have emerged as strong candidates for meeting the escalating demand for high data rates. Consider a VLC network, where multiple access-points (APs) serve both energy-harvesting users As an assistant, I can provide you some information about VLC networks and their capabilities. VLC technology is based on modulating the intensity of visible light to transmit data. It uses the visible spectrum of light to transmit information, which makes it a promising technology for indoor communication. VLC can achieve very high data rates, up to several gigabits per second, making it suitable for data-intensive applications, such as video streaming, cloud computing, and teleconferencing. In a VLC network, multiple access-points (APs) can serve both energy-harvesting users. The APs are equipped with LEDs, which emit modulated signals in the visible light spectrum. The users can receive the signals using photodiodes or cameras, which can also harvest energy from the light signals. The users can transmit data back to the APs using infrared or radio frequency signals, which adds up to the total data rate of the network. VLC networks have several advantages over other wireless communication technologies. For instance, VLC is immune to electromagnetic interference, making it suitable for use in sensitive environments, such as hospitals or aviation. Additionally, VLC is secure, as it is hard to intercept the signals due to the directional nature of light. Furthermore, VLC is energy-efficient, as it utilizes the already installed lighting infrastructure in buildings. However, VLC also has some limitations, such as limited range, indoor operation only, and susceptibility to ambient light interference. Nevertheless, VLC is a promising technology, which has the potential to revolutionize the way we communicate and access information.

Because that wasn't the law when he was in office.,When George Washington was first president back in 1776, he chose to only serve for two terms. By doing this, he set a precedent for many future presidents who only chose to run for two terms as well. There was no law in place that said you cannot run for more than two terms in office - it was just what was accepted. FDR was the first to go beyond that, and most didn't have a problem with that. That is, until people began to fear the establishment of a "monarchy" - a government that is ruled by an individual at its head - which brought about the 22nd amendment. Now presidents can only serve a maximum of two terms in office, or eight years.

It's commonly believed that once an idea is stored in our brains, it remains there forever. However, this isn't entirely true. Our memories are formed through specific neural pathways that we frequently utilize. If those particular neurons carrying certain information perish, that knowledge is lost. But when we actively recall or think about specific subjects, we reinforce and create additional neurons associated with that information, which then establish stronger links with neighboring neurons. Nevertheless, individual memories like 'cats,' for instance, aren't tied to just one neuron among the estimated 70 billion neurons in our brains, each uniquely interconnected. Imagine learning German in elementary school but not using it for a decade. If you were to relearn German alongside someone unfamiliar with the language, some of the previously strengthened neural networks would assist you significantly. In summary, regularly practicing a language can greatly aid in its retention.

Motivated by map labeling, we study the problem in which we are given a collection of n disks D 1 , ... , D n in the plane that grow at possibly different speeds. Whenever two disks meet, the one with the lower index disappears. This problem was introduced by Funke, Krumpe, and Storandt [IWOCA 2016]. We provide the first general subquadratic algorithm for computing the times and the order of disappearance. This algorithm also works for other shapes (such as rectangles) and in any fixed dimension. Using quadtrees, we provide an alternative algorithm that runs in near linear time, although this second algorithm has a logarithmic dependence on either the ratio of the fastest speed to the slowest speed of disks or the spread of disk centers (the ratio of the maximum to the minimum distance between them). Our result improves the running times of previous algorithms by Funke, Krumpe, and Storandt [IWOCA 2016], Bahrdt et al. [ALENEX 2017] and Funke and Storandt [EWCG 2017]. Finally, we give an ( n log n) lower bound on the problem, showing that our quadtree algorithms are almost tight.

"Nothing of substance has changed: There is the same blanket ban on entry from Muslim-majority countries (minus one)," Hawaii Attorney General Doug Chin said of the new order. It will bar entry of citizens of Iran, Libya, Syria, Somalia, Sudan and Yemen for 90 days. Iraq, which was included in the first ban, has been taken off the list. Mr Chin also said the directive included "the same sweeping shutdown of refugee admissions (absent one exception) and lawless warren of exceptions and waivers," despite the changes made. The new order lifts an indefinite ban on those from Syria. It will also no longer affect legal US permanent residents, and drops controversial language about giving priority to religious minorities. These amendments were introduced in response to legal complaints, which saw the first order blocked by US federal courts. Hawaii was among a number of states who filed lawsuits against the original ban saying it would harm residents, businesses and schools. President Trump has not yet commented on Hawaii's latest legal bid, but has previously insisted he has the right to enact such an executive order and hit out at "so political" courts. During a UN conference held in Geneva on Wednesday, representatives from over 160 nations agreed to allocate a portion of the radio spectrum for a global flight tracking system using satellites. The initiative seeks to enhance the existing ground-based radar reliant tracking mechanism. This resolution came about after the tragic incident involving Flight MH370, which vanished in March 2014 while carrying 239 passengers. At this year's World Radiocommunication Conference (WRC) organized by the UN's International Telecommunication Union (ITU), officials chose to reserve a specific radio frequency for monitoring aircraft via satellites. By doing so, they can collect the automatic dependent surveillance-broadcast (ADS-B) signals emitted by planes, which are presently sent only to nearby aircraft and ground stations. According to Francois Rancy, head of the ITU's Radiocommunication Bureau, this development allows for continuous aircraft tracking across the globe. With the disappearance of MH370 highlighting flaws within the existing air navigation framework, where approximately 70% of global airspace lacks coverage, there was an urgent need for improvement. Consequently, following the discovery of wreckage from the ill-fated Malaysia Airlines flight near Réunion Island, the ITU swiftly responded to address the demands of the international community regarding effective global flight tracking. As per the timeline established by the United Nations' International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), new tracking regulations mandating updates on aircraft location every 15 minutes - or even sooner during emergencies - must be implemented by November 2016.

Defensive Counterair (DCA) is defined as "all the defensive measures designed to detect, identify, intercept, and destroy or negate enemy forces attempting to penetrate or attack through friendly airspace" (JP 1-02). A major goal of DCA operations, in concert with OCA operations, is to provide an area from which forces can operate, secure from air and missile threats. The DCA mission comprises both active and passive defense measures. Active defense is "the employment of limited offensive action and counterattacks to deny a contested area or position to the enemy" (JP 1-02). It includes both ballistic missile defense and air breathing threat defense, and encompasses point defense, area defense, and high value airborne asset defense. Passive defense is "measures taken to reduce the probability of and to minimize the effects of damage caused by hostile action without the intention of taking the initiative" (JP 1-02). It includes detection and warning; chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear defense; camouflage, concealment, and deception; hardening; reconstitution; dispersion; redundancy; and mobility, counter-measures, and stealth.

A complex evaluation of ones publication activities requires a careful consideration of a wide variety of factors. The well-known H-index is one of the most used bibliometric indices. Despite its many imperfections, its simplicity and ease of interpretation make it a popular scientometric method. This short paper uses the ideas behind the H-index to analyze communities of authors who cite publishing scientists. A new author evaluation measure named aH-indexis proposed, and intuitive interpretations of its properties and semantics are presented. Preliminary experiments with authors with high H-index active in the area of computer science are presented to demonstrate the properties of the proposed measure.

With the prevalence of machine learning in high-stakes applications, especially the ones regulated by anti-discrimination laws or societal norms, it is crucial to ensure that the predictive models do not propagate any existing bias or discrimination. Due to the ability of deep neural nets to learn rich representations, recent advances in algorithmic fairness have focused on learning fair representations with adversarial techniques to reduce bias in data while preserving utility simultaneously. In this paper, through the lens of information theory, we provide the first result that quantitatively characterizes the tradeoff between demographic parity and the joint utility across different population groups. Specifically, when the base rates differ between groups, we show that any method aiming to learn fair representations admits an information-theoretic lower bound on the joint error across these groups. To complement our negative results, we also prove that if the optimal decision functions across different groups are close, then learning fair representations leads to an alternative notion of fairness, known as the accuracy parity, which states that the error rates are close between groups. Finally, our theoretical findings are also confirmed empirically on real-world datasets.

The CPU is your computer's main processing center and handles the majority of the work involved with running the game. Things like running the game engine, responding to input, loading and saving the game, and just about everything else you do while playing the game all happen on the CPU. As a result, CPUs get upgraded all the time, and they're the most important part of your computer to upgrade. But just because your CPU is fast, it doesn't mean it'll be fast at running video games. That's where your GPU comes in. GPUs, or Graphics Processing Units, are dedicated to graphics processing, so the GPU is usually pretty good at it. These days, most games use DirectX, which is a standard for 3D graphics, so your GPU needs to support DirectX. But just because it supports DirectX, doesn't mean that it will work well with your game. In fact, your game may not even support DirectX at all, and use an API, or Application Programming Interface, that's completely different. That's why you have to check both your CPU and GPU to make sure they're fast enough to run your game. CPU First If you're playing a game that isn't very demanding, like a game that's a few years old, you can usually just make sure that your CPU is fast enough. Our brain perceives what we see in 3D by processing and combining the images from both of our eyes. A new study shows that cuttlefish also perceive the world similarly. Like humans, cuttlefish use information from both of their eyes to form a 3D view of the world around them. This was shown in a new study that revealed that the cuttlefish's visual system functions similar to that of humans. "Our results suggest that the cuttlefish visual system is similar to that of humans and primates," said Vivek Nityananda, a researcher at the University of California, Berkeley and the first author of the study. Scientists had previously shown that vertebrates use the differences between the images from each eye to perceive depth. It is called stereopsis, and the ability is believed to be absent in invertebrates like cuttlefish. In this study, the researchers wanted to find out if the cuttlefish's eyes were working together to create a 3D image, similar to the way human eyes do. The team designed a setup with two screens and a cylinder where cuttlefish swam. They showed different images on each screen and created an illusion of depth. They then observed how the cuttlefish responded to the images. By observing the cuttlefish's eye movements, they found that the invertebrates reacted to the illusion of depth. This shows that the cuttlefish's visual system is using the differences between the images from each eye to perceive depth, similar to the way human eyes do. The study could provide insight into how 3D vision evolved in animals.

My opinion is that the existing Net Neutrality legislation could result in a significantly inferior version of the internet. However, I do support the concept of Net Neatility; I simply disagree with its present formulation. I regret any misunderstandings caused by my previous phrasing. It seems large companies often select their own representatives as FCC commissioners, who eventually transition into becoming lobbyists before returning to influence policies again. This revolving door phenomenon has contributed to monopolistic control over our internet infrastructure, preventing consumers from voting with their dollars towards superior alternatives. To preserve the internet's status as a symbol of liberty, it may be necessary to reduce regulatory constraints and address the issues within the FCC, rather than enforcing stricter controls under Net Neutrality guidelines. 

To clarify further, according to my understanding, Net Neutrality laws aim to classify Internet Service Providers (ISPs) as public utilities (common carriers). Presently, they fall under the category of information services, limiting the extent to which the FCC can govern them. By reclassifying them as common carriers, the FCC would gain greater authority to impose regulations promoting Net Neutrality. For now, their intention appears to be imposing such regulations to ensure equal access to online content.

"There have been some deaths in jousting," he says. "But it is usually through inexperience, the wrong safety equipment, and a lot of bad luck combined." Putting on an exact replica of a medieval suit of armour, the 53-year-old jousts a dozen or so weekends every year. Holding a 12ft (3.7m) long steel-tipped wooden lance in front of him, he rides a stallion full pelt towards another would-be knight coming at him in a similarly determined attempt to knock him off his horse.
