The most unnerving part of Aurora's day was catching a glimpse of herself in the mirror. She had long ago grown accustomed to seeing the identical faces of women and men that lived today. It all started many years ago with customer dissatisfaction. People would all wander into a supermarket with their different faces, different hands and different shades of skin and they'd spend their precious minutes looking for a perfect banana or a perfect tomato. Scientists threw hours into making these minutes less stressful by creating tomatoes that were identically beautiful. Then they did the same for bananas. Soon people wanted their faces to have the same treatment as well as their children's. It wasn't long until the gentle erosion of time had etched the old faces away entirely. Everyone looked the same and that was going to be the end of it. Every few years, an unfortunate day arrived and the process wouldn't go perfectly with, say, a child born with a single large, unusual freckle under their right eye or, god forbid, eyes green like a long extinct species of sour apple. With Aurora, one of the most extraordinary differences had occurred. When she emerged into the world, she had the traditional blue eyes, the blonde hair, but her skin was a deep brown, like the forgotten soil. Her parents, with their identical peachy faces looked to one another like a confused person in a mirror. They had signed the form much like every other parent, knowing but not considering the risk that old, strong genes could manipulate the process and leave them with a truly unique baby. Parenting a unique baby used to be a difficult road but with the Museum open and a rising interest in these "deformities," a couple could stand to make a great sum of money from the simple sale of their child. This was preferred to raising the accident themselves and many simply funneled the funds back into another attempt at the process, hoping blindly that the genes wouldn't warp the identical face they desired once again. Aurora spent her childhood by herself in a tiny playpen in a large hall of the museum. She never saw children like herself because every living soul who passed through the room looked exactly the same. Children parroted their parents' excitement. "Have you ever seen skin like that in real life?" they'd exclaim. "The poor thing, all alone," a pair of women would lament. From Aurora's side, it was impossible to tell who was mother and child, sister and sister, sometimes even brother and mother looked frightfully similar if dressed the same. Even more impossible to imagine was the concept of family itself. The only ones closest to her were the ones who fed her and even she had trouble telling if they were the same person or not with each passing day. As she grew older, she began to take stock of her room. She examined the bed as they studied her. She grew frustrated at receiving the same meal every morning, noon and night with the same identical fruit from the uniform markets that had grown very popular. She knew very little of the surrounding rooms but knew the doors to them well; heavy as they were, people hungrily threw them open every other minute or so. She couldn't speak because no one had ever taught her, but she knew that she was the brown girl. That's what people called her and the words hung proudly above her pen. Her body grew more unique every day. Her curls were difficult for people to wrap their confined minds around. She had freckles that littered her face, each like a hidden star on a foggy night. She elongated, her neck longer and more beautiful than anyone in her crowd of clones. Her curves expanded from her over the years with seismic energy, new mountains and valleys unlike any seen in years. In all this time, no one had taken a genuine interest in her. Not more than a few half-hearted glances or the occasional long stare like one might experience at a zoo. The young boy who first called her Aurora looked like all the others. Apart from his museum uniform, it'd be hard to spot him in the crowd if not for the way his eyes never let go of her. Their strong grip. When she slept, she usually slept alone behind locked doors, smothered in air conditioning. Waking to the sound of shuffling feet, she hears murmurs about the brown girl and starts her day. The day he called her Aurora, she had stirred early. Even though she'd spent her whole life being watched, this felt different. It was like he had taken his eyes and touched her skin with them. In stolen moments, they would begin the day. For the first time in her life, she was able to learn about the inside of a person. And Jon's insides were the same color as hers as far as anyone knew, but who knew what color his soul was. When she finally spoke her first words, they were questions and Jon told her what she wanted to know. He explained the girl with no eyes in the room to her left, the incredibly small boy with black hair in the room to the right. He avoided the subject of what laid outside the walls of the Museum and practically ran from the room to escape the conversation about the sum of money that she was worth, the price of admission, and what it would take to buy her freedom. He would put his finger to her mouth and tell her not to let anyone know that she could speak. Maybe he feared losing her or maybe he feared losing the easy money the Museum offered. Once the pair had gotten close, it became difficult..... exploring new emotional terrain when forced to stay on separate sides of the room. They shared those traditional blue eyes, but her soil skin kept her behind a fence and rotten fruit had begun to take seed beneath those pores. She resented that she could close her eyes and love his insides but, upon looking at him directly, could only see the waves of identical faces that jeered at her for years. In the mornings, she wouldn't want to wake early to see him anymore and separately they would cry identical tears. He was a child and so was she. She told him that she knew he had to marry another girl who looked like him and have babies who looked like him. He told her that he loved her and she knew he only loved the skin. Her life hadn't given her the opportunity to explore the same rooms that welcomed his face. So when he left the job and her behind, it was a surprise that she wished to keep the name. One day, after white face and white face washed over her, she would say her name aloud to her audience. Confused spectators would read the plaque in front of her pen, wondering how she learned to speak. Children pointed their sharp fingers and remarked loudly that they didn't want a speaking exhibit. The employees brought Aurora new fruit to shut her up, but this made her speak louder. Eventually patrons no longer wished to see the Brown Girl and having earned them a sizable amount of revenue, the Museum happily opened her pen and said "Good Luck." Pulling the door open, she tiptoed past the blind girl who would never read the banner above her tiny cell. Another heavy door led to a room where a tired creature with two blonde haired heads rested clumsily. Siamese was printed in beautiful calligraphy across the wall. Room after room of people behind tiny little fences. Finally she reached the entrance and made her way outside where the world looked like it was covered in fresh snow. Everyone looked at her like she was gon na melt their world with her heat and she worried deeply that she'd never know another person's insides again for even she was frightened by her own face.

A problem is regarded as inherently difficult if its solution requires significant resources, whatever the algorithm used. The theory formalizes this intuition, by introducing mathematical models of computation to study difficult problems. Demonstrate an understanding of how the theory of computation is used to model and analyze the computational complexity of algorithms and problems. Given a natural language problem description, understand how it can be translated into a mathematical model of computation. Know the classes of problems that are considered to be inherently difficult, and the complexity classes that correspond to these classes. Know what are the main limitations of the P vs NP problem, and what are the implications of these limitations. Have a basic understanding of the relationship between the complexity of an algorithm, and the resources required by the algorithm. Be able to use this theoretical knowledge to improve algorithms and algorithms' analysis. This is a theoretical course, with a large practical component. In the practical part, you are expected to experiment with different models of computation, such as the deterministic Turing machine, the random Turing machine, and the nondeterministic Turing machine. You are also expected to create a complexity class for your own problem description, and to study this class by solving instances of it, and studying the best known algorithms for this class. You are also expected to give a talk, based on the work you do in the practical part.

Modelling the physical properties of everyday objects is a fundamental prerequisite for autonomous robots. We present a novel generative adversarial network (Defo-Net), able to predict body deformations under external forces from a single RGB-D image. The network is based on an invertible conditional Generative Adversarial Network (IcGAN) and is trained on a collection of different objects of interest generated by a physical finite element model simulator. Defo-Net inherits the generalisation properties of GANs. This means that the network is able to reconstruct the whole 3-D appearance of the object given a single depth view of the object and to generalise to unseen object configurations. Contrary to traditional finite element methods, our approach is fast enough to be used in real-time applications. We apply the network to the problem of safe and fast navigation of mobile robots carrying payloads over different obstacles and floor materials. Experimental results in real scenarios show how a robot equipped with an RGB-D camera can use the network to predict terrain deformations under different payload configurations and use this to avoid unsafe areas.

In this paper, we consider the expected blocklength of variable-length coding over the binary symmetric channel (BSC) with noiseless feedback. Horstein first proposed a simple one-phase scheme to achieve the capacity of BSC. Naghshvar et al. used a novel extrinsic Jensen-Shannon (EJS) divergence in a sequential transmission scheme that maximizes EJS (MaxEJS) and provided a non-asymptotic upper bound on the expected blocklength for MaxEJS. Simulations in this paper show that MaxEJS provides lower expected blocklengths than the original Horstein scheme, but the non-asymptotic bound of Naghshvar et al. is loose enough that lies above the simulated performance of Horstein scheme for a BSC with a small crossover probability. This paper proposes a new expression for MaxEJS expected blocklength that is a tight approximation of simulated performance. This expression is developed by exploring a genie-aided decoder (GAD) whose expected blocklength will always be larger than MaxEJS and can be approximated by two random walks. We conjecture that even with these two approximations, the expression may still be an upper bound on blocklength as suggested by the simulation results.

These electrons pass through these various pathways until they leave the organelle to complete their trip back out to the outside environment where they will be used again. So what's going wrong if you're unable to get enough oxygen? In theory there shouldn't really be any problem since there's plenty available around us thanks to Earth's atmospheric pressure. However, research has shown how poor quality air pollution leads to problems like asthma attacks due to decreased levels of oxygen at the surface level. If this continues over time our bodies can't help but suffer its effects. In terms of related health conditions, low airborne concentrations of nitric oxide, nitrogen dioxide and carbon monoxide have been associated with increased mortality rates among cardiorespiratory patients treated in hospitals. A 2016 study showed that breathing 150 parts per billion of NO2 for 21 years led to decreased lung capacity while another published in 2017 revealed that constant exposure to sub-lethal concentrations of vehicle exhaust pollutants was significantly associated with reduced exercise performance and declining maximal oxygen uptake. As we know all too well, smoking cigarettes damages lungs more than other forms of tobacco use do so people who smoke may find themselves compromised even further by chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). However, studies suggest that hypobaric hypoxic therapy could offer some benefits against COPD symptoms without improving lung functions nor preventing lung infections. Hypoxaemic individuals benefit greatly from therapeutic altitude increases above sea-level populations, not only because of improvements in blood gases (oxygen saturation), however also protection against inflammation, cancer and cardiovascular death. This applies particularly to those suffering from heart failure, hypertension andor end-stage kidney disease. By way of illustration, a 2012 meta-analysis compared outcomes between 18 studies involving 4,400 participants with stable coronary artery disease undergoing moderate altitude treatment (1,500-2,200m). Three-fourths had angina pectoris symptoms and half were men. Following two weeks of moderate elevation treatment four hundred twenty-three experienced significant improvement in pain scores, resting oxygen saturations improved slightly (by 0.6) and peak oxygen consumption remained unchanged although treadmill times declined sharply. There are infinitely many primes, as demonstrated by Euclid around 300 BC. There is no known simple formula that separates prime numbers from composite numbers. However, the distribution of primes, as well as some properties of prime numbers, have been extensively studied and there are many important results in number theory related to primes. For example, the famous prime number theorem provides an estimate for the number of primes less than a given number, and the Riemann hypothesis proposes a complex formula that gives the exact distribution of primes. Additionally, many cryptographic systems rely on the fact that it is computationally difficult to factor large composite numbers into their prime factors.

In the 1910s, New York-based filmmakers were attracted to Jacksonville's warm climate, exotic locations, excellent rail access, and cheap labor. Over the course of the decade, more than 30 silent films shot in or around our city are known today as "lost" movies. Jack Dreyfus takes a look at them this week: After the Civil War, Jacksonville was an emerging railroad hub with lots of space for new tracks. The first train arrived here on October 1st 1871 from Chicago. By 1888 when Florida became its own territory, there were nearly 100 miles of track that stretched along what is now downtown St. Johns County - all owned by Jacksonville Transportation Company Limited. In 1889, JTCL merged with other companies into Atlantic Coast Line Railroad (ACLR) which would become one of the country's leading railway systems. On September 26th 1899, ACLR chartered the T.P.B.J., named after Thomas Payne Brown Jr., who led their efforts during Reconstruction. Later that year they bought out local competitor Stuart Jones owned lines, creating Greater Jacksonville Railway Company in 1901. As trains moved steadily through this area, so did film crews. The 1920s saw many great silent movie stars make appearances in the Sunshine State. Tallulah Bankhead starred opposite John Gilbert in 1917's "Heavenly Twins." Charlie Chaplin, Buster Keaton, Orson Welles, Mae West and Binnie Barnes made cameos throughout the decade while Mary Pickford filmed her last role alongside Douglas Fairbanks Sr. in 1926 before moving back to Hollywood permanently. But it wasn't just famous faces behind the cameras; it also put some of America's top directors on location too. Some like Allan Dwan stayed close to home shooting 'We Live Again' starring Walter Huston near Miami but others went further north opening up Jacksonville for shoots including Frank Capra whose 1931 drama "I Married A Witch" about a witch-shunning family that moves to Florida has long been considered lost. Others followed suit making movies including "A Fool For Love" (1925), "Night Nurse" (1928) and "Dynamite Dick" (1929). All three feature films about athletes premiered in theaters across Duval county. As the Great Depression hit, production slowed down drastically. But even though many studios had closed shop, many independent producers continued to shoot localized features locally using screenwriters from places like Pittsburgh who knew how to tell stories set outside major cities. Renowned director C. Aubrey Smith moved his office to Main Street in 1924 where he wrote over a dozen scripts for productions shooting in town. He directed two here including 1932's "Barbary Coast" featuring Betty Grable who lived nearby. By the mid 1930s, things started looking up again thanks largely to Warner Bros. Pictures. They began buying rights to popular novels such as "Tarzan Of The Apes" which allowed them to create easily marketable series. It didn't hurt either that Florida proved itself another favorite destination for filmmakers especially ones working on Westerns. There were several here including 1935's "Small Town USA" based loosely on Cecil Fielding's book "Lady Chatterley's Lover" starring George O'Hara and Louis Calhern among others. The studio experimented with different genres filming both comedy and horror shorts here. One of those comedies was 1937's short titled "Wackyland" featuring Laurel And Hardy playing circus clowns. According to the Yesteryear blog, the majority of these early films never found distribution due to poor sound quality which is why many remain completely unknown today only appearing occasionally on TV airings. During World War II, military bases like Macdill Air Force Base provided ample support roles, stunt work and extras needed to complete big budget projects. Many of these soldiers returned home with experience under their belts giving rise once again to the growing number of independent film companies headed by veterans of Hollywood. With renewed interest in the industry rising nationwide, along with increased funding, major corporations wanted in on the action. One of those, Paramount Pictures formed the Screen Gems Motion Picture Corporation in 1942. The company produced over 70 pictures each year until 1951 when they sold off their remaining interests to GulfWestern Enterprises paving the way for 20th Century Fox to emerge as king at the box offices. Soon enough, the state of Florida became fertile ground for setting countless productions including hits "Gone With Wind" and "All Quiet On The Western Front" plus classics like "Singin' In The Rain." Counter-argument: While the Golden Rule and its derivatives may provide a useful guideline for moral behavior, they are not the only sources of morality. Morality is a complex and multi-faceted concept that cannot be reduced to a single principle or rule. Furthermore, the Golden Rule can be subject to interpretation and may not always apply in all situations. For example, the rule to treat others as you would like to be treated may not be applicable in cases where the needs or desires of others differ significantly from your own. Therefore, it is important to consider a variety of factors and principles when making moral decisions, rather than relying solely on the Golden Rule.

The idea of countries bound by music was admirable, but flawed. When the majorities had to band together to prevent misuse of magic, those on the outside were tossed aside. We're not alone in our own denial that we have lost touch with nature and creativity. In this post, I point out how some artists continue to work hard for their songs despite all the negativity they get from the media. There are examples of artists who utilize "celebrity influence" as a marketing tool-such as Elvis Presley-with little success. So why do so many artists still choose to use their fame over people's feelings? If you write a song about your life, you can say exactly what it tells them about themselves, but if you don't tell them your story, they will be drawn to you by an image you created of yourself. You don't care about how long it takes to finish, as long as you keep writing. Even when it is your own private demons - like the fear of rejection or hate-filled emails - you only put it on paper once - you start thinking about you. It makes sense for musicians who want to share their experiences with thousands of readers each month. However, for everyday celebrities, it's much more difficult. The chances of getting noticed are much higher than just being seen. That's why the popularity of pop culture has doubled since 1984-not because any celebrity was popular enough, but because anyone could become famous without having to commit themselves to making money. Music is the one thing that gives us happiness every day; it is the one creative outlet we can afford to waste time chasing after comedy gold. In fact, artists always offer us something that helps. Galicia was spared the worst of the fighting in that war: it was one of the areas where the initial coup attempt at the outset of the war was successful, and it remained in Nationalist (Franco's army's) hands throughout the war. While there were no pitched battles, there was repression and death: all political parties were abolished, as were all labor unions and Galician nationalist organizations as the Seminario de Estudos Galegos. Galicia's statute of autonomy was annulled (as were those of Catalonia and the Basque provinces once those were conquered). According to Carlos Fernandez Santander, at least 4,200 people were killed either extrajudicially or after summary trials, among them republicans, communists, Galician nationalists, socialists and anarchists. Victims included the civil governors of all four Galician provinces; Juana Capdevielle, the wife of the governor of A Coruna; mayors such as Anxel Casal of Santiago de Compostela, of the Partido Galeguista; prominent socialists such as Jaime Quintanilla in Ferrol and Emilio Martinez Garrido in Vigo; Popular Front deputies Antonio Bilbatua, Jose Minones, Diaz Villamil, Ignacio Seoane, and former deputy Heraclio Botana); soldiers who had not joined the rebellion, such as Generals Rogelio Caridad Pita and Enrique Salcedo Molinuevo and Admiral Antonio Azarola; and the founders of the PG, Alexandre Boveda and Victor Casas, as well as other professionals akin to republicans and nationalists, as the journalist Manuel Lustres Rivas or physician Luis Poza Pastrana. Many others were forced to escape into exile, or were victims of other reprisals and removed from their jobs and positions.

Quantum Clustering is a powerful method to detect clusters in data with mixed density. However, it is very sensitive to a length parameter that is inherent to the Schrodinger equation. In this paper we develop methods for removing the sensitivity of Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) by increasing the range over which local minima are searched and extending the number of iteration steps used to find them. We show how these modifications can be performed without introducing new errors. The Westin is a good option if you want to get away from the mega hotels and ringing casinos on the strip. The other benefit of staying at this location is that you do not have to walk the gauntlet of poker machines, table games and old ladies puffing on their cigarettes to make it to the check in desk. Following closely behind in popularity among Parisian museums, the Musee d'Orsay showcases an extensive collection of 19th-century French artwork, particularly by Impressionist and Post-Impressionist painters. This prestigious gallery occupies what used to be the Orsay train station during the Universal Exposition of 1900. With over 3 million attendees, the Musee du quai Branly claimed the title of France's fourth-most visited national museum that year. It features art pieces originating from Africa, Asia, Oceania, and the Americas. Fourth in line amongst Parisian attractions, the Musee national du Moyen Age, otherwise known as the Cluny Museum, exhibits Middle Ages artistry, including the renowned tapestry series "Lady and the Unicorn." Another prominent cultural site, the Guimet Museum, which specializes in Asian artifacts, boasts one of Europe's most comprehensive Asian art collections. Additionally, there exist several museums dedicated exclusively to specific artists such as the Musée Picasso, Musée Rodin, and Musée national Eugène Delacroix.

There is a vast amount of research that supports the idea that triggers are a real thing and that they can significantly affect individuals. Countless people experience physical, emotional, or psychological reactions stemming from specific situations or events that remind them of past trauma, causing them to feel overwhelmed or triggered. While it is essential to work on personal growth and resilience to manage triggers, it is not always possible to control them when they occur. Refusing to acknowledge the reality of triggers dismisses the lived experiences of those who have experienced them and downplays the importance of mental health and emotional well-being. Instead, we should strive to understand and support those who are triggered and encourage healthy coping mechanisms.

Rank position forecasting in car racing is a challenging problem, which is featured with highly complex global dependency among the cars, with uncertainty resulted from existing exogenous factors, and as such not easy to handle. In this paper, we design an approach for ranking of drivers based on their performance during races. The proposed method uses initial probability distribution functions (IDF) at each race start to forecast the remaining 20 of the winning probabilities. We apply our method to one-make endurance races, and its accuracy reaches about 30. Author Bio: Dr. Haiyun Zhang is a researcher of Department of Mechanical Engineering and National Institute of Information and Communications Technology under Ministry of Education, Republic of China. He obtained his Ph.D degree in Computer Science Automation from University of California Berkeley in 2015. His research interests include artificial intelligence in time series analysis.

The issue isn't caused by a faulty phone; rather, it stems from insufficient protection around the speaker.] (URL0). In older mobile devices, TDMA (Time Division Multiple Access) technology was utilized. These devices operate using hundreds of megahertz (MHz) radio waves similar to modern networks. However, the interference captured by the speaker would be inconsequential since these frequencies are outside the audible range for both humans and animals. Instead, TDMA allows users to communicate through the frequency channel during brief periods. For instance, user one has a limited duration to interact with the network, followed by user two, and so forth, before returning to user one. Although the switching among users occurs within the kilohertz (kHz) spectrum—a range detectable by humans and capable of being reproduced by speakers—older phones emit MHz radio waves pulsed at specific intervals in the kHz range, allowing communication only during allocated times. When combined with substandard speaker shielding, this pulsing may resonate with the speaker and result in audible sound. Modern smartphones have overcome this problem by employing alternative networking technologies that no longer rely on TDMA, thus eliminating the emission of radio waves at audio frequencies.

" Okay. Interesting. How expensive is it and what results have you come up with? " she asked bluntly. " It is very expensive. " But although the shield was very resistant against blunt force impact, it was easy enough to cut open. So in 2004, we did. We accounted for everything, and prepared for the worst. Even if the cube had been made out of antimatter, the bunker would have contained the explosion. At first, after we opened the sphere, it was rather anticlimactic. " Well, after we had closed up the gold shell, we detected an extremely small vibration from inside. It turns out, that the substance contained micro machinery which was drilling through the gold. But after a few months of being in the same container, it suddenly started making its microscopic holes in the gold like it was drilling through butter. A small thermal gradient, and vibration energy from a motor running nearby. " " A thermal gradient? " Hillary asked with one eyebrow raised. Now she had let him talk uninterrupted for long enough. Until the early 1980s, industry was a major source of water pollution. Although many plants and factories can be found along the Rhine up into Switzerland, it is along the Allee des Neues Darmstadt in Germany that most of this septic waste goes down stream to the sea. The river is also heavily polluted with the solid waste generated by people who live or work near the river banks such as manure, excrement and a variety of garden products. The industrial sector has developed very rapidly since the early 1990's when new technologies were introduced which made it possible for large industries to operate in areas lacking adequate sewage treatment systems. Results from municipal sewerage studies show that in Berlin there are approximately 3 million residents living within 1 kilometer of a major wastewater treatment plant while in Munich over 2 million reside close enough to the wastewater plant to have significant environmental impacts from seepages and overflows. Industrial effluents flow directly off site through sewers into storm drains and will eventually continue their journey through the environment at an accelerated rate. Industrial waste contains about 70 percent dissolved organic matter (DO) which poses serious health risks to humans, animals and aquatic life if not processed prior to discharge. If untreated these pollutants may cause harmful effects to rivers, lakes and oceans. The majority of industrial activities occur on riverbanks where people spend much time during the day due to the proximity to waterways. Overfishing, loss of habitat and other social problems associated with human activity around water bodies create pollution challenges. The River Severn is marked by the presence of numerous industrial sites including chemical production facilities, textile mills, paper mills, glass manufacturing units and power stations. Researchers have discovered a new Linux backdoor called Symbiote that uses novel evasion techniques to conceal its presence. It is able to scrub any sign of infection from the file system when it is running and also uses steganography to hide its malicious code inside .PNG image files. The Symbiote malware was discovered by researchers from security firm ESET. It is designed to inject its code into legitimate processes on a compromised machine. The malware consists of a backdoor module that runs in the background and a dropper module that injects its code into a legitimate process, in this case, the xrdp process that is used to allow remote desktop access. The xrdp process is run as root and is designed to interact with the xrdp daemon using the D-Bus inter-process communication (IPC) mechanism. "After being injected, the malware hooks into the D-Bus interface for the Xrdp process. This allows the malware to control the xrdp daemon," the ESET researchers said in a report. The malware communicates with a command-and-control (CC) server over a non-standard HTTPS port. Symbiote doesn't use any polymorphic code obfuscation techniques, but its steganographic capabilities and the fact that it can scrub all signs of its presence from the file system might make it difficult for users and security products to detect. "One of the main reasons this malware is hard to detect is that it hides its presence in the file system," the ESET researchers said. "During the infection process, the malware creates a tmpfs (RAM-based) file system in the runuser1000gvfs directory." The malware creates a file called .cache on this RAM-based file system. The contents of the .cache file are encrypted with AES-256-CBC, but this is done to hide the malware's configuration data and not the malicious code itself. "The malware code is executed directly from this tmpfs file system," the researchers said. "It also stores all the log files generated by the malware in the runuser1000gvfs directory." When the malware is done executing, it wipes the contents of this directory and unmounts the tmpfs file system. This effectively removes all traces of its presence in the file system. ESET malware researcher Lukas Stefanko believes that the malware is most likely used in highly targeted attacks. He noted that the CC server identified so far is only reachable from IP addresses in Brazil. "However, the malware is not 'Brazil-exclusive, he said. "It can be easily adapted to attack any region in the world." In a blog post, Stefanko also noted that the xrdp RDP server is enabled by default on many Linux distributions, making it an attractive attack vector for malware writers. The Great Dividing Range, a mountain chain extending along Australia's eastern seaboard, forces humid air from the ocean to ascend through a process known as orographic lifting. As the air elevates, it cools and forms precipitation, enabling lush forests to flourish on the coastal side of the mountains. Conversely, the region west of the range experiences significantly less rainfall due to its position within the continent's interior. Without an equivalent mountain barrier, the west coast receives minimal moisture from maritime winds, resulting in arid conditions unsuitable for forest development. Additional factors like varying temperatures, rock compositions, and soil types further hinder forest formation in these drier regions. However, the presence of the Darling Scarp near Perth does promote localized rainfall, supporting small pockets of vegetation in southwest Australia. While certain parts of the country do receive substantial rainfall during seasonal monsoons, the extreme wet-dry cycles make them unfavorable environments for persistent forest ecosystems.

John perceived the interdict as tantamount to a papal proclamation of hostilities. To retaliate, he sought to penalize Innocent on a personal level and create division among the English clergy, separating those who supported him from those aligning closely with Rome's authority. John confiscated property belonging to clergy resistant to performing religious duties, as well as land associated with Innocent; he detained priests living immorally, releasing them only upon receiving monetary compensation; he took possession of property owned by clergymen who left England, while offering safeguarding assurances to those remaining faithful to him. Often, specific religious organizations managed to broker agreements regarding the administration of their assets and profits derived from their lands. However, by 1209, the conflict remained unresolved, prompting Innocent to threaten excommunication against John unless he accepted Langton's appointment. After the king disregarded this warning, Innocent proceeded to excommunicate John in November 1209. Despite its potential impact on John's credibility, the excommunication didn't seem to cause much concern for the monarch. This is because two of King John's influential associates, Emperor Otto IV and Count Raymond VI of Toulouse, had previously faced similar sanctions, diminishing the weight of such a penalty. Consequently, John intensified his previous actions and accumulated substantial wealth through the proceeds of unoccupied bishoprics and monasteries: for instance, a 1213 estimation indicated the church had forfeited approximately 100,000 marks (around 66,666 back then) to John. Records indicate that roughly 14% of the annual earnings generated by the English church went into John's coffers every year.

The term utopian socialism was first used in 1840 by the English socialist John Stuart Mill to describe what he saw as the extreme and impractical proposals of Robert Owen and other thinkers of the early 19th cent. Utopian socialism refers to a wide range of works and proposals, all of which have one thing in common: their authors look to the future and offer their vision of a perfect society. The term utopian socialism is usually used to describe a number of different doctrines and proposals in the socialist tradition. Utopian socialism can be broken into three broad categories: religious utopianism, scientific utopianism, and literary utopianism. The task of creating a perfect society would require the destruction of the old society, the creation of a new one, and the reeducation of the people in that new society. To accomplish this, a number of different plans were offered. A number of authors even proposed a violent overthrow of the old society. Religious utopianism was not a major part of the utopian socialist movement. It did, however, have a significant influence in the thought of such writers as William Morris and Edward Bellamy. Regarding your query about peculiar place names, are you American? In Europe, particularly older regions, settlements developed organically without centralized planning or naming conventions. Streets often received names based on prominent local landmarks or characteristics, like Chancery Lane near the High Court of Chancery. Jewish quarters became known as Old Jewry, while bustling markets earned names such as Cloth Fair or Haymarket. Some streets even reflected less savoury aspects of life, being dubbed Cock Lane or Gropecunt Lane due to the presence of prostitution. Over time, cities evolved, altering names along the way; however, many retained their original titles. For instance, Elephant & Castle derives its name from an ancient inn featuring an emblematic elephant carrying a castle—a nod to the Cutlers' Guild crest, symbolizing elephant ivory utilised in handle production. Similarly, Blackfriars refers to Dominican monks who relocated their monastery from Holborn during the 13th century. Their distinctive black habits inspired the name, stemming from the French word 'frère,' ultimately transforming into 'friar.' Another interpretation suggests proximity to Ludgate, adjacent to Fleet Street, although the origin of Ludgate remains uncertain, possibly linked to the Old English terms Hlidgeat or Ludgepta, signifying various types of gates.

Commons Leader Chris Grayling said the change, also applying in some cases to Welsh MPs, would bring "real fairness to our constitutional arrangements." SNP leader Nicola Sturgeon called the plan "staggering in the extent.... of its hypocrisy and incoherence." Labour said it was an "outrage" that ministers wanted to rush into making "profound constitutional change." Shadow Commons leader Angela Eagle said the plans risked creating two classes of MPs and accused the Conservatives of a "cynical" attempt to "manufacture itself a very much larger" majority in the Commons. Under the proposals, all MPs would continue to vote on all key stages of legislation. But English MPs - and in some cases English and Welsh MPs - will have a veto in Westminster when debating matters that have been devolved to the devolved administrations. MPs will debate the changes on 15 July, Mr Grayling said, and the system will be changed using the rules - known as standing orders - that dictate how Parliament conducts its business. With more powers set to be devolved to the Scottish Parliament after September's independence referendum, Tory MPs have said it is not right that MPs representing Scottish constituencies can continue to determine laws affecting England only. Mr Grayling told MPs that Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland were getting a "stronger voice" and that it was "only fair" to do the same for England. The Speaker will be asked to certify which bills or parts of bills relate to England or England and Wales only, he said. There will be no changes in the House of Lords, Mr Grayling said. But where Lords amendments are certified as England or England and Wales only, a "double majority" system applies, meaning it will need a majority of both the whole House of Commons and MPs representing English or English and Welsh constituencies. Tablet computers will be used to count MPs' votes as they walk through the voting lobbies so officials can instantly register whether they have used their veto in votes where the "double majority" rule applies. To jeers from opposition benches, Mr Grayling said "Today we are answering the West Lothian Question," a reference to the constitutional anomaly that lets Scottish, Welsh and Northern Ireland MP at Westminster vote on measures that only apply in England. English votes: What's going on? The SNP's Pete Wishart described the English votes policy as a "cobbled together unworkable mess," and said it was "totally unacceptable." He said this policy showed that the Tories were doing their best to ensure Scotland would become an independent country. His party leader Nicola Sturgeon said: "The Tories have produced a constitutional shambles - staggering in the extent of its hypocrisy and incoherence. "Under these plans - which are all about cutting Scottish MPs out of votes which impact on Scotland and our budget - the Tories are proposing an'English veto' and'double majority'. "I have been very clear that, at least in part, the level of support for independence will be determined by what the Tory government at Westminster does, as well as what the SNP Government does. And there is no question that the great disrespect shown to Scotland in these proposals is likely to have more people asking whether Westminster is capable of representing Scotland's interests at all." Labour's Sir Gerald Kaufman, the father of the house, said the title of the motion, English votes for English laws, "sounds racist." He added: "This government is undermining the whole basis of British democracy, right through from when the Magna Carta was signed."

A and B refer exclusively to floppy disk drives used during earlier times before the advent of hard drives. These designations originated in the MS-DOS era and persisted into contemporary computing systems. Drive A represents the primary floppy drive, while Drive B is designated as the secondary floppy drive. In contrast, Drive C denotes the primary hard drive, with subsequent drives (D through Z) representing additional hard drives or similar devices. Historically, these labels were applied to floppy drives, such as those found on an IBM PC XT circa 1983, featuring a single horizontal slot for a 5.25" floppy drive—the A drive typically contained the operating system or applications, whereas the B drive served as storage for user data. Hard drives became commonplace only after this period. To summarize, A and B denote traditional lettering conventions assigned to floppy disk drives in the nascent stages of personal computing, prior to the integration of hard drives.

For most teens, getting enough physical activity is easier said than done; some students find it fun but others never want to go out with friends or do sports themselves unless it involves working up a sweat and sweating off any extra calories. Try making a point of walking together regularly while shopping, cooking dinner or going to school. Being active can help improve mood, decrease stress levels and even boost workout motivation. Even just 15 minutes of light exercise daily could have long-term benefits for teens. [substeps] Getting plenty of movement boosts cognitive performance and prevents infections from viruses that thrive on sedentary lifestyles. It also makes your teen less likely to develop chronic illnesses such as diabetes, high blood pressure and obesity, all known risk factors for heart disease, stroke and type 2 diabetes. 4) Establish healthy eating habits. A lot of parents think having a meal plan, menu card or grocery list means that kid's meals come out perfect every single day. But if everyone follows these basic guidelines, your kids' diets won't be filled with junk food: Avoid added sugar. Sugar spikes insulin production in our bodies a couple times per hour, leaving us feeling hungry longer afterward. Studies show sugary drinks contribute nearly 20 percent of total calorie intake among U.S. adolescents aged 12-17 years old.[substeps] Cutting back on soda pop and other sweetened beverages will not only make your kids healthier but save money by preventing weight gain. Make lunchtime supervision optional. Kids who don't feel controlled by adults tend to eat junkier foods and skip breakfast. Don't expect your teen to take care of everything in his life right now. Instead ask him to pitch in around the house. It's been a bit of an annus horribilis for the internet and all of us who frequent it. In the past year, the world wide web has faced several challenges that have impacted our daily lives, from cybersecurity threats to misinformation and online censorship. One of the biggest threats to the internet this year has been the rise of cyberattacks. In just the first six months of 2021, there were several high-profile hacks that affected millions of people around the world. From the Colonial Pipeline ransomware attack to the Microsoft Exchange Server breach, these cybersecurity incidents have caused disruptions in supply chains, energy systems, and governments, and have highlighted the need for stronger online security measures. Misinformation has also been a major problem on the internet this year. The COVID-19 pandemic sparked a deluge of fake news, conspiracy theories, and hoaxes that have been widely shared on social media platforms. This information can be dangerous, as it can influence people's perceptions and behavior, and can harm public health efforts. Social media companies are struggling to keep up with this onslaught, and are being pressed to increase their content moderation practices. Another issue affecting the internet, particularly in countries with authoritarian regimes, is online censorship. Governments in countries like China, Russia, and Iran have increasingly used the internet to control information and suppress dissent. This has led to the blocking of websites, censorship of social media platforms, and even the arrest of online users who criticize their governments. Despite these challenges, there have been efforts to make the internet a better place. Online activism and social movements have gained widespread attention through platforms like Twitter and Instagram. Advocacy groups are working to protect users' privacy rights and push for responsible tech policies. And tech companies are developing new tools and approaches to combat online harms such as misinformation and cybercrimes. As we approach the end of 2021, it's clear that the internet remains an essential part of our lives, but one that we must continue to monitor and safeguard. By holding tech companies accountable and demanding responsible policies from our leaders, we can help ensure a safer and more secure online world for all.

What is the value of $x$ in the equation $\frac{4}{5} \cdot x = 16$?
response>
To find the value of $x$, we need to isolate $x$ on one side of the equation. We can do this by dividing both sides of the equation by $\frac{4}{5}$. Here are the steps:

Given equation:
$$\frac{4}{5} \cdot x = 16$$

Divide both sides by $\frac{4}{5}$ to isolate $x$:
$$x = \frac{16}{\frac{4}{5}}$$

Invert the divisor ($\frac{4}{5}$) and multiply:
$$x = 16 \cdot \frac{5}{4}$$

Simplify the right side:
$$x = 4 \cdot 5$$

Therefore, the value of $x$ is:
$$x = 20$$

Huge amounts of digital videos are being produced and broadcast every day, leading to giant media archives. Effective techniques are needed to make such data accessible further. Automatic meta-data labelling of broadcast media is an essential task for multimedia indexing, where it is standard to use multi-modal input for such purposes. This paper describes a novel method for automatic detection of media genre and show identities using acoustic features, textual features or a combination thereof. Furthermore the inclusion of available meta-data, such as time of broadcast, is shown to lead to very high performance. Latent Dirichlet Allocation is used to model both acoustics and text, yielding fixed dimensional representations of media recordings that can then be used in Support Vector Machines based classification. Experiments are conducted on more than 1200 hours of TV broadcasts from the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC), where the task is to categorise the broadcasts into 8 genres or 133 show identities. On a 200-hour test set, accuracies of 98.6 and 85.7 were achieved for genre and show identification respectively, using a combination of acoustic and textual features with meta-data.

Internal combustion engines are very complex and giving a simplified ELI5 answer really doesn't do it justice. Remember that when a manufacturer reports horsepower, they are reporting peak horsepower, meaning the most power the engine makes over it's rev range. To avoid getting too heavily into technical terms, imagine this.... Try flooring your car at 1500rpm, then try it again at 4000rpm, since your car most likely has a power curve that makes more power at higher RPM's, you will accelerate more quickly when you floor it at 4000rpm. That is because your engine is making less power at 1500 rpm. Saying that two cars make "300hp" is not very telling if one makes 300hp at all revs, and the other produces 300hp at a very high rev and doesn't make much power at other times. There are many reasons why some manufacturers choose to use large displacement engines. One of the best reasons is what we just went over, often times a large displacement engine can produce a more even power curve. This is not always true, but it is easier to make an engine with a large displacement have a balanced power curve. This is great for all kinds of driving because being able to accelerate quickly from a low rpm is useful for road driving and racing. Another reason is simplicity and weight. Weight? What? I thought that bigger displacement meant heavier! Not quite. Smaller displacement engines often use turbo chargers to help boost their power and efficiency. This is good, but turbo chargers add their own weight, take up space, and usually come with supporting units like inter coolers that take up more weight and space and will affect the car's center of gravity as well as a host of other driving characteristics. The third reason why large displacement engines are used is because they usually place less stress on components. Without diving into the combustion process, understand that making a small displacement engine produce the same horsepower as a large displacement engine makes it more "high strung." Components are exposed to higher pressures and higher stresses. This with the added complexity of turbo chargers means that they can wear out more quickly (2.0L turbo charged Mitsubishi Evolutions are a good example of this) and be less susceptible to adverse conditions. Since the components are less stressed in a large displacement engine, they can also be made cheaper, making service cheaper. Furthermore, a relatively unstressed engine is easier to modify to produce more power while an already high strung engine might be at the peak of its abilities without heavily sacrificing reliability. Large displacement engines have drawbacks, they often use more fuel and produce more emissions. A turbocharger that they might lack increases efficiency. However, do not confuse large displacement with exterior weight or size. There is much more to this. Notice that I try to use "usually" as much as possibly because there are very many exceptions. Engineering an engine is a complex process and like all engineering, compromise is the key. Source: Automotive Mechanical Engineer', "There is a lot more involved in horsepower than just displacement. For example, a smaller engine with a turbo charger can produce as much if not more horsepower than a larger engine without a turbo because the turbo increases the amount of oxygen being taken in by the motor. If you delve deeper into the mechanics of an engine there are even more differences in the quality of the parts being used and the specific tuning. Another example is the type of motor used in Nascar. They use a 358 cubic inch engine that puts out nearly 900 horsepower. Meanwhile, there are consumer level motors with the same displacement that struggle to produce 300 horsepower. Nascar engines don't use turbos or super chargers, but their parts are more finely tuned and of a higher quality. Their parts are lighter, stronger, and there is no concern for emissions. In contrast, consumer engines are made to be cost effective and low emission (although the two often contradict eachother). The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) is a scientific intergovernmental body under the auspices of the United Nations, set up at the request of member governments. It was first formed as an independent organization in 1990 and re-established in 1997 after a period of internal turmoil within its membership. On January 1st 2007 the IPCC expanded to include the European Union's climate services following the launch by the executive body of the European Commission of the "Climate Action Plan." On April 21st 2011, the IPCC met for the third time since forming, with most countries signing onto the Paris Agreement on Climate Change (policies formulated by 194 governments, which were adopted in December 2015). The meeting agreed that a new assessment of emissions must be issued every five years from now until 2028; this will indicate whether global warming has slowed or sped up, according to scientists' estimates.

In our study, we introduce a combined parallel programming technique for resolving a two-dimensional acoustic wave equation numerically through an implicit difference method applicable to a solitary machine. This process involves employing an implicit finite difference approach wherein the original differential equation is first converted into its equivalent implicit finite-difference form. Subsequently, we apply the Alternating Direction Implicit (ADI) method which divides the equation into dual sub-equations. An approximation of the solution is attained via the cyclic reduction algorithm. Ultimately, we adapt this algorithm for parallel computation across various platforms including GPUs, GPUOpenMP, and Hybrid (GPUOpenMP+MPI). Our primary objective is enhancing the efficiency of these parallelized algorithms with respect to their execution duration. Demonstrative evidence is provided showing comparable accuracy between the hybrid model and traditional processor cores, as well as existing CUDA and CUDA+OpenMP configurations when conducting identical simulations.

Since it requires double the bandwidth when compared to 720p resolution. Broadcasters like cable, satellite, and terrestrial signal providers have a restricted amount of total bandwidth determined by their allocated frequency range. Although theoretically possible, streaming 1080p content without increasing the channel's bitrate from its original 720p level would result in significantly worse picture quality due to increased compression. This occurs because although there are twice as many pixels to transmit, there isn't twice as much available space for transmission. As a consequence, broadcasters might need to reduce the number of channels offered or raise prices. Similar limitations apply to both cable TV and terrestrial services, striking a balance between desired image quality and customer willingness to pay. With regards to 4K resolution, there are four times as many pixels as 1080p, equating to eight times more than 720p. Consequently, one 4K channel may prevent the broadcast of six to eight 720p channels due to bandwidth restrictions. Radio frequency spectrum availability is finite, making it impossible to simply begin using new frequencies for broadcasting purposes without potentially causing interference issues. Transmitting ultra-high definition videos via the internet tends to be simpler since it doesn't rely on traditional broadcast methods; instead, only individual streams are sent rather than simultaneously sending all channels.

" Oh, what a lovely balloon! " Aenea exclaimed. " I've never seen one like that before. Did you make it? " Christopher beamed; " Yep! " He was very proud of his balloon. It was very pretty; red, and blue, and sparkling inside. " It's so... big! " she said. " You must have a very deep breath! " Christopher nodded vigorously, and continued on his way. He had to find father, and quickly. His balloon was quite big, to be sure. But, he'd not breathed that much life into it. No more than the last one. He kept it hidden, most of the time. Father had warned him not to show anyone. At least, once he'd been convinced there was something odd about it. That in and of itself had taken some time. " Some balloons grow, " his father had said. " It's perfectly normal. Don't worry. They all stop after a few million years. " Except it hadn't stopped. Not even a little. If anything it was gaining momentum. And it was getting heavier. It still floated, of course, but occasionally, the string seemed to tug at his hand, as if it were trying to escape. He hadn't told his father about this yet. He'd already had to hide his balloon where he could only see it once in a while. He didn't want to risk losing it forever. Suddenly, a hideous sound ripped through space and time. It was coming from the balloon. " Ack! " Christoper gasped, and rushed to find the new leak. He pored carefully over every tiny surface, slowly, intently. All the while the hiss of escaping dimensions expanding assaulted his ears. They weren't meant to interact this way. " Huh! " Christopher found the problem, and the solution, together. Upon his discovery, the hissing ceased, and the balloon adopted its much more pleasant, silent, tone. His father was not going to be happy. The leaks were a recent development. He would ask father if, once balloons reached a certain age, they leaked to maintain their size. But he already knew what the answer would be. Sure, balloons grow. Balloons change colour. Balloons do some wonderful things. But no balloon had ever leaked before. And Christopher knew what it meant. It meant he was in trouble. " Father! Father! " Christopher cried. " What is it, Ch...- oh. What are you doing with that thing again? I thought I told you to hide it. " " I did hide it! I just, you know, went to check up on it. " " Is it still growing? It looks pretty big now, " his father said, flatly. " Well, yes, I think so. But, um, I think we sh....- " Christopher was saved from having to explain the situation by a new leak appearing, suddenly and violently. " Ugh! " His father said. " What is that sound?! " Immediately Christopher went to work, studying carefully, trying to find the new piece of knowledge that had appeared inside the balloon. It never took him long. The sound subsided, and Christopher stood, looking at his father, looking at him. " What. was that? " his father asked. " Yeah... that's what I wanted to show you. There's been lots of those. " " Lots? " " That I've seen. There could have been more when I wasn't around. Somewhere the balloon opens up, and if I find out why, then it closes. I think it's gotten too big. " His father looked perplexed. " If you... find out why? That doesn't make any sense. " " I know! Except, it keeps happening, and, I was wondering if maybe..... - " " What did you find out? " " Just... you know... some stuff about light and time, " Christopher said, cringing. His father abhorred light. He'd told him not to put it in his balloon. " Sure, it'll be pretty, " he had said, " but light's a troublemaker. Always doing strange things, never behaves the way it ought to. " Christopher had ignored him, of course. And when his balloon had started sparkling, and shining red and blue, his father had been convinced to allow his son to keep it, despite his own misgivings. " They're related, you know. " His father stared. " Yes, " he said, after a time, " I know. What happens if you don't find out? " " No idea, " Christopher said. " I've never let it go. The sound's too horrible. " His father sat in silence, thinking. " Well, it can't hurt to let it shrink a little bit at least. " The same thought had occurred to Christopher. It must have happened, while he wasn't there. Which meant that it must have stopped, eventually. No balloons had ever opened up before, not after being made. Christopher wondered what might have come out. He wondered how big his balloon might have been, if it hadn't started leaking. " I suppose it can't hurt to give it a try then, " his father said, and the two of them moved far away, to where no one would notice them, and they sat peacefully, for only a short amount of time, waiting for the next leak. Despite their intent, it was every bit as startling as the others when it appeared. A loud, jarring hiss, of folding probabilities and diverging fates. So offensive was it, that Christopher automatically went right back to work, trying to find out why. " No, stop! Let it go! " his father said. Christopher did. He let it go, and go, and go. It went for a long time. And under the cacophony, through all the roaring chaos, they suddenly noticed. The balloon wasn't shrinking at all. It was growing. Eventually it stopped, every bit as quickly and violently as it had began. The balloon wasn't noticeably larger. But it HAD grown. Of that they were both quite sure. Father and son looked at each other, staring quietly. Finally, his father said; " I think we're in trouble. "

Many of today's machine learning (ML) systems are built by reusing an array of, often pre-trained, primitive models, each fulfilling distinct functionality (e.g., feature extraction). The increasing use of primitive models significantly simplifies and expedites the development cycles of ML systems. Yet, because most of such models are contributed and maintained by untrusted sources, their lack of standardization or regulation entails profound security implications, about which little is known thus far. In this paper, we demonstrate that malicious primitive models pose immense threats to the security of ML systems. We present a broad class of model-reuse attacks wherein maliciously crafted models trigger host ML systems to misbehave on targeted inputs in a highly predictable manner. By empirically studying four deep learning systems (including both individual and ensemble systems) used in skin cancer screening, speech recognition, face verification, and autonomous steering, we show that such attacks are (i) effective - the host systems misbehave on the targeted inputs as desired by the adversary with high probability, (ii) evasive - the malicious models function indistinguishably from their benign counterparts on non-targeted inputs, (iii) elastic - the malicious models remain effective regardless of various system design choices and tuning strategies, and (iv) easy - the adversary needs little prior knowledge about the data used for system tuning or inference. We provide analytical justification for the effectiveness of model-reuse attacks, which points to the unprecedented complexity of today's primitive models. This issue thus seems fundamental to many ML systems. We further discuss potential countermeasures and their challenges, which lead to several promising research directions.

The Command Module (CM) was the conical crew cabin, designed to carry three astronauts from launch to lunar orbit and back to an Earth ocean landing. It was the only component of the Apollo spacecraft to survive without major configuration changes as the program evolved from the early Apollo study designs. Its exterior was covered with an ablative heat shield, and had its own reaction control system (RCS) engines to control its attitude and steer its atmospheric entry path. Parachutes were carried to slow its descent to splashdown. The module was 11.42 feet (3.48 m) tall, 12.83 feet (3.91 m) in diameter, and weighed approximately 12,250 pounds (5,560 kg).

Calculating the masses of stars is actually fairly straightforward under certain circumstances, mainly that we can observe something orbiting around those stars. We know from our understanding of gravity and motion how orbits works, and we can predict very well the orbits of things in our solar system, so it's a very solid theory. So if we have something like a planet (or even a 2nd star) orbiting a star, we can make a few straightforward measurements that let us determine the mass of the star fairly accurately. The first measurement is the timing: how long does it take for the planet to make one complete orbit. The second measurement is the orbital speed: how fast the planet is moving (or, equivalently and easier to measure, the star will wobble slightly because of the planet's gravity, so how fast is it wobbling?). This can be measured straightforwardly through Doppler shift measurements on the light coming from the star. So with these two measurements, we can use the equations that describe the orbit, and turn them around. We know the timing and the speed, so we can determine the size of the orbit and how heavy the central star must be. As long as our measurements are accurate (and they can be done very accurately these days), our estimate of the star's mass can be quite accurate as well, within a few percent in many cases. Edit: A lot of people like the say that we can't really know, or that it's'just theory'. But all it is, in many cases, is simple applications of basic laws of physics that we have tested very very thoroughly on Earth. The laws of orbital mechanics are very well understood; we use them every time we launch a satellite.,If you know what its made out of and how much of what its made out of weighs AND you know how big it is then you know the weight!

You can spend several hours being jostled by French camera crews, squashed by Italian snappers, or shoved unceremoniously out of the way by any one of 27 other countries' journalists as the leaders of the European Union arrive one by one, and we frantically try to grab a word with them as they rush past. There'll be sharp elbows in the press pen, craning of necks and stretching of microphones, as David Cameron arrives at this summit, which could define not just his leadership, but the future of his party and his country's place in the world. But how on earth did the man who once accused the Conservatives of being out of touch for "banging on about Europe," get himself into a position where he has already been "banging on about Europe" for months and months, and will spend the next four months still doing precisely that? Since he made that claim in his first season as party leader in 2006, appearing in front of a huge video screen tastefully projected with a giant tree, there have been three big changes, linked, that have got him to this juncture, which of course ultimately is a product of his own political calculation. Most simply, as the years have passed, his party has changed. Since the Maastricht rebels failed to get a public vote in 1993 on the treaty that created the modern version of the European Union, there has been a rump of Conservatives deeply passionate about the cause, significantly concerned that the EU's laws, not Britain's own, are more important - the question of sovereignty that's a big part of the current talks. But their concerns, while shared by many Conservative Party members, were not considered mainstream in the parliamentary party - balanced, if not squeezed out, by heavyweight Europhile voices. But as the EU expanded, and generations of MPs came and went, a soft scepticism towards the European project, neither full-throated support, nor hardcore opposition, became more common, and sympathy for the idea of a referendum spread from the margins. The eurozone financial crisis, and the EU's stumbling approach to sorting it out, gave a fresh energy to eurosceptic MPs who wanted to campaign to leave. In part that apathy, if not downright dislike, towards the EU spread because of the enormous rise in the numbers of people from around the Union who came to live and work in the UK. Numbers that took the political establishment completely by surprise began to arrive from the moment new countries like Poland joined the EU in 2004. There is a complicated, and emotional debate about the impact of the numbers, but few can dispute that the effect has been very significant in some parts of the country, with figures this week showing the numbers still rising, standing at more than two million now. For many people, that very visible impact of our membership of the EU has given them pause for thought. And it was that steep rise in EU immigration that gave David Cameron his most pressing political reason for - in the end - promising a referendum. UKIP's appeal grew alongside the rise in immigration. By 2012, they were greedily nibbling at the Conservative vote with a record performance in the local elections and a leader who in some moments seemed to appeal to swathes of the public for his plain speaking, in a style that also alienated many others. A drive to address the threat from UKIP and satisfy growing internal demands for the promise of a referendum led eventually to Mr Cameron's commitment in the 2013 speech to give the public a vote on whether to stay or go. It's worth remembering that, perhaps strangely, the 2013 speech in which he made his promise to hold a vote made no mention of immigration. But add a general election and increasing public concern to the mix and three years later, his hopes of limiting benefits for migrants are the centrepiece of his renegotiation. The prime minister is not a politician who is known for getting hung up on the past, his seemingly bomb-proof - if maybe sometimes misplaced - confidence in his own abilities tends to lead him to look forward. He is not a prisoner of his record. But as he arrives in Brussels on Thursday, and gets out of the shiny black limousine to sweep past the journalists clamouring to ask a question, will he consider even, for a moment, the irony that he may be risking it all for something he once more or less dismissed as a fringe concern?

Scientists have grown plants in lunar soil using samples collected during the Apollo missions to the moon. The scientists grew thale cress, a small flowering plant that is attractive to fungi and mammals such as rabbits and squirrels The study was published on Thursday in Science Advances. 'It's exciting because it shows we can grow crops on another world,' said lead author Jason Spindler of Ohio State University. 'We just need to find out how well they will do.' Researchers used two different methods for growing plants inside these artificial soils: one method called microgravity-induced root growth (MIGR), which involves a liquid medium containing nutrients, and the other known as cryopreservation - freezing at subzero temperatures so that seeds don't die when planted outside. First the researchers plopped about 20 grams or less of seed into each of three separate plastic containers. Then they placed them in an incubator where the temperature reached around minus 300 degrees Fahrenheit. After a few weeks, all four containers were frozen. These are then taken back up to Earth to be rehydrated before being tested again with seeds from a variety of plants including lettuce, spinach, mustard greens, broccoli, melons, onions, potatoes, tomatoes, cucumbers, beans, carrots, peas and strawberries In this image made available by the Planetary Society, Jason Spindler holds seeds he helped cultivate in Lunar Lab Zero Two in December 2020 When night time came, tens of thousands of microbes started grazing in the soil - helping to break down the nutrients already present within the container. Finally, after a month, the team ran tests to see if any of the seeds had germinated. That way they could tell whether the plants actually survived after landing on Mars in the hopes of finding a permanent home there someday. All but seven of the 100 sent in for testing sprouted. But only 19 percent of those discovered viable pieces of thale cress, even though it supposedly grows well on the Red Planet. Only 10 potted plants did not survive after planting. There may also still be some issues ironing out how best to feed Martian plants once astronauts arrive on the planet, the authors noted. Mars has no atmosphere like the ones found on our own planet, meaning carbon dioxide for photosynthesis cannot reach the surface. So scientists might use different types of food, perhaps produced on board the spacecraft itself rather than brought in from earth.

On March 17, 1752, the Governor-General of New France, Marquis de la Jonquiere, died and was temporarily replaced by Charles le Moyne de Longueuil. The new administration would experience little or no support from Montreal until after his death on April 20, 1755. By that time, two important events had occurred: an attempt at Count Frontenac's succession and a political crisis within the colony itself. When Jean Talon became administrator for Louis XV (1715-23) he did not believe that Quebec City should be used as headquarters. He wanted all government personnel sent there instead. In fact, it took him almost five years before he went himself. As early as June 23, 1714, Jean Talon made elaborate plans with the intendant, Francois Dollier de Cassagnolles, for sending most administrative staff to Canada. These included both officials who held civil posts directly under provincial governors, such as Claude Le Normand Destouches and Nicolas Duguay Legare, and those given ordinary "governor" rank, like Gilles Hocquart Dufresny and Denis Gendre. They also included every other kind of clerk necessary for running the office. For example, Enemond Masseau, son of one of Talon's aides de camp, was appointed commissaire generale du service des affaires courantes et extraordinaires; while Pierre Babineau was named secretary cabantier [acting chief engineer]. All this meant far more than simply moving some offices out into the field people were being detached and sent away permanently. Even individuals whose position was only temporary could now find themselves uprooted to distant locations. Note that none of these persons ever returned to replace their predecessors once they left. It is safe to assume that the exodus deprived the Crown of its best officers as well as the colony of much needed help. There are many reasons why colonial administrators might become disgruntled, but the very nature of the job seems especially difficult when compared to present day conditions. Most administrative services can easily come back home if possible, but these men were professional employees they knew what they were doing! And then even a simple request for a promotion or appointment may have been refused outright. Thus, it must have seemed impossible to move them: their families lived somewhere else; perhaps they had already found jobs elsewhere... After leaving office they remained officially unemployed. To make matters worse, the loss of business to competitors abroad increased competition among colonial traders. This was particularly true in naval stores trading where several French colonies competed with each other. If a ship let us say British ran aground off Newfoundland or Nova Scotia, her cargo would go straight through the hands of Canadian merchants who paid duty when passing through French ports. On returning to port, if her cargo contained goods which could not be sold in a landlocked area, she too lost money. Ships bound for markets further east carried supplies intended chiefly for foreign consumption sugar, tobacco, rum, etc., rather than local needs. The current system worked reasonably well in wartime situations, when military supply ships brought large quantities of foodstuffs or equipment essential to the war effort. During peacetime, however, the same vessels transported goods grown in local agriculture suitable mainly for domestic purposes. Finally, the weight of taxes levied in France forced prices up so high that market forces ceased to operate effectively. A good deal of commerce came to depend upon royal licences to export particular products, or on governmental monopolies established specifically for industry. While commercial interests naturally attempted to secure favourable regulations, they often clashed with agricultural interests because few farmers produced enough profitably to justify large enterprises. By contrast, maritime trade required a steady supply of cheap labour and capital investment. Since much of the available work force consisted of women, husbands, sons and fathers seldom joined merchant fleets unless their own occupation was seasonal or malarial in character. Trade thus depended heavily upon the goodwill of successive governments. However, the purchase of raw materials, tools, building material and machinery often required considerable credit extended against future sales. Here again the Crown played an active role. At times, the nature of the purchases gave rise to serious disputes between British authorities and Canadians. One striking instance was the case of trees cut down along Saint Lawrence River banks during construction of docks and fishing smacks. Petitioners claimed damages totalling millions of livres owed unanimously to landowners who opposed cutting the timber without permission. The courts awarded compensation of about 2,000 per tree in addition to standard customs duties but eventually decided in favour of opponents. When each part of a federation has identical authority, it is referred to as 'symmetric federalism.' On the other hand, 'asymmetric federalism' arises when certain areas hold varying degrees of power or autonomy compared to others, typically acknowledging unique regional cultures. In Spain, the Basques, Catalans, and Galicians led a significant effort to acknowledge their national distinctions through "historical communities" like Navarre, Galicia, Catalonia, and the Basque Country. These regions enjoy more privileges than those included in the broader framework for other Spanish territories, known as the "autonomous communities" or the "one size fits all" approach. This accommodates their distinct identities and addresses peripheral nationalist sentiments while honoring historical entitlements. Nevertheless, despite these differences, Spain does not conform to true federalism; rather, it operates under a decentralized government system.
