Not at all. In fact, the writer Andrew Solomon, who has become known for writing about depression (see The Noonday Demon), has explored depression in non-western societies. He went to remote areas of the world, where he expected to find little depression because of the lack of "problems." Instead, he found that people in these regions had no words for depression, but that they were prone to it. Depression is not a western concept, and people all over the world suffer from it. In fact, the World Health Organization estimates that approximately 154 million people worldwide suffer from depression. Studies have shown that the number of people suffering from depression has increased by 18 between 2005 and 2015. By 2030, the WHO expects that depression will be the leading cause of disability worldwide. As is the case with other mental disorders, there is a stigma associated with depression. This stigma can be even more pronounced in non-western societies. In our western society, the stigma of mental illness is still quite prevalent. This leads many people who are suffering from depression to not seek help, and to suffer in silence. The stigma is stronger in non-western societies, which can lead to a number of problems. A study in South Korea found that 81 of Korean patients who suffer from depression do not seek treatment. In fact, in many non-western societies, people who suffer from depression are often seen as "weak" and "needing to toughen up." Unfortunately, this means that many people who suffer from depression are never treated. Another problem that occurs in non-western societies is that people are often unaware that they are suffering from depression. Without a word for depression, people might not realize that their feelings of sadness are abnormal, and that they need to seek help. Because of the stigma associated with depression, many people in non-western societies don't realize that they are suffering from depression until their symptoms become severe, or until their symptoms last for a long time. By then, the depression can be much harder to treat. Another issue that is associated with non-western societies is the lack of mental healthcare. In countries where the majority of people have no health insurance, mental healthcare is often not covered. Without insurance, people can't afford to pay out of pocket for the care that they need. Mental healthcare can be particularly expensive, and since it isn't covered, people cannot afford to get the help that they need. This, combined with the stigma of mental illness, means that many people never get treatment. There are also fewer mental healthcare professionals, which means that people who need help can't find it. Many non-western countries don't have the resources to train mental healthcare professionals. In addition, western healthcare professionals tend to be older, white, and male. This means that they often don't understand the cultural norms of the people that they are trying to help. Unfortunately, when mental healthcare professionals don't understand their patients, they are less likely to be able to treat their patients. It is clear that depression is a problem in non-western societies. There are fewer mental healthcare professionals, and the stigma surrounding mental illness can prevent people from seeking help. The lack of mental healthcare can also prevent people from seeking help. Fortunately, things are changing. As more and more people in non-western societies realize that mental illness is a problem that needs to be addressed, more mental healthcare professionals are being trained, and more healthcare centers are being built. The World Health Organization estimates that, in 2025, depression will be the leading cause of disability worldwide. The WHO also estimates that, by 2030, depression will be the leading cause of disease burden worldwide. As people realize that mental illness is a problem that needs to be addressed, hopefully the stigma will be lifted, and people who are suffering from depression will be able to get the help that they need.

The concept of intrinsic dimensionality (ID), a key attribute of multi-dimensional datasets, plays a vital role in selecting suitable machine learning methods and comprehending their functionality and validation processes. ID calculation can either encompass the entire dataset or focus on specific segments within the data space. This paper presents innovative local ID estimation techniques founded on the linear divisibility of multi-dimensional data points, a phenomenon indicative of measure concentration. Through empirical analysis, we evaluate these estimators' traits and contrast them with alternative recent ID estimators that leverage diverse aspects of measure concentration. Distinct disparities among the estimators offer insights into their expected performance in real-world scenarios.

In this paper, we present a new multi-antenna modulation scheme, termed as space-time index modulation (STIM). In STIM, information bits are conveyed through antenna indexing in the spatial domain, slot indexing in the time domain, and M -ary modulation symbols. A time slot in a given frame can be used or unused, and the choice of the slots used for transmission conveys slot index bits. In addition, antenna index bits are conveyed in every used time slot by activating one among the available antennas. M -ary symbols are sent on the active antenna in a used time slot. We study STIM in a cyclic-prefixed single-carrier (CPSC) system in frequency-selective fading channels. It is shown that, for the same spectral efficiency and single transmit RF chain, STIM can achieve better performance compared to conventional orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM). Low-complexity iterative algorithms for the detection of large-dimensional STIM signals are also presented.

Revenue is an important financial indicator because it represents the amount of money a company earns from its business activities before deducting any expenses. In other words, revenue is the total income generated by a company, and it serves as the quantitative measure of a company's performance. Revenue is important because it can impact a company's ability to secure financing, attract investors, and grow its business. Investors and lenders will often look at a company's revenue growth over time as an indicator of its potential future earnings and financial stability. Additionally, revenue is used in financial ratios, such as the gross profit margin, which are used by analysts to evaluate a company's profitability and performance. In summary, revenue is a key financial metric that can indicate a company's financial health, growth potential, and value to investors and lenders.

Tommy was playing hide and seek with his brother. He was hiding under the bed. Tommy's brother was in the room looking for him. Tommy began to laugh. Tommy's brother grabbed him by the arm, while he laughed hysterically, and said "You have been found! You are no longer missing." But it wasn't true, as far as I know; but that is what they explain when you are told not to tell anyone about your choice of baptism. The brothers are wrong though if they think that a person so little can fully comprehend anything. They do however come close, their attempt at understanding is ultimately flawed because they cannot see that Baptism is the answer to all our problems, regardless of how small or large they may seem. A child will always be able to feel lost and frightened without Jesus Christ offering them eternal life through His sacrifice on the cross for us. Remembering this we must constantly remind ourselves: what would we be like without God? If we had never heard about Him? What kind of people would we become then? Probably very evil and immoral... There really isn't any way around the fact that a truly free human being needs God. But the problem lies within us, as humans, we often try to take control over things which we should just leave alone. This leads us into temptation, where there is no hope for freedom from sin. In order for us to find peace (and eternal rest) we need forgiveness. We also need love, acceptance, guidance, and many other blessings only God can offer, therefore, according to the Bible, baptism is necessary. Stabbing victim John Culshaw's remains were retained by Greater Manchester Police without his family's knowledge. Dozens of other families have also been told their loved ones' body parts were kept by the force. GMP said whether or not to contact the affected families was a decision it "agonised over for a number of months." Mr Culshaw, 26, was stabbed to death in Wigan in 1993. His family buried him believing his body was intact, and were unaware his stomach, liver and other tissues had been retained after two post-mortem examinations until police officers visited them in September last year. His mother, Jennifer Shaw, said she wanted to know why it had taken so long to come to light. "He's my son. And he's been left - half of him," she said. "If he'd have died and they'd asked me if they could use the parts to help somebody, then yes. But just to be sat in a lab for 23 years doing nothing, that's just horrendous." The body parts were discovered following an audit of the former Forensic Science Service in 2014, the Manchester Evening News revealed. It found more than 180 samples - including major organs - from victims of crime in Greater Manchester were being held for the police force, which has admitted there could be more body parts unaccounted for. It became illegal in 2006 to remove or store human tissue without families' consent following an investigation at Liverpool's Alder Hey hospital in 1999. Organs from hundreds of babies who died at the hospital were secretly taken. The body parts kept for Greater Manchester Police were removed before that date. Assistant Chief Constable Debbie Ford said: "Once we knew about the samples we felt that such a sensitive issue was never going to be solely about following the regulations or the letter of the law. "For this reason we consulted with a number of relevant people, including community and faith groups, as well as our own Ethics Committee. Following this extensive consultation it was agreed we had an ethical and moral duty to inform the next-of-kin in the vast majority of cases." She said officers had offered a range of options for "sensitive disposal" of the samples, which the force would pay for. However, families have been told some samples could remain unaccounted for "for various reasons," she said. John Culshaw's family will bury his organs in a private second ceremony on Thursday. "Somebody has made a big mistake. Not just me but a lot of other families are suffering as well," Ms Shaw said. "I don't want anyone else to go through this. It's devastating."

New rules come in on 1 January, which will reduce compensation to PS75,000 per person, per institution. Previously the Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS) protected savings of up to PS85,000 per account. Joint accounts will see protection cut from PS170,000 to PS150,000. The maximum compensation across the European Union is set at EUR100,000, and the British level was reduced as a result of the pound gaining strength against the euro. The precise rate was set on 3 July 2015. At the time, one senior Tory MP described the change as "defective." Although 95 of savers will still be protected, as many as 2.5 million people may not be, according to the FSCS. It is advising savers who have more than PS75,000 in one account, or in one institution, to move their money if necessary. The situation is further complicated by the fact that some registered banks and building societies operate under more than one brand. So it you had PS75,000 savings with HSBC, for example, any additional savings in First Direct would not be protected, as both banks have a joint licence. Savers using Bank of Scotland and Halifax are in the same position. But Royal Bank of Scotland (RBS) and NatWest - although they are sister banks - are both registered separately. So savers could safely have up to PS75,000 in accounts with both banks. "While this should be quite simple to navigate, it's made complicated by the fact that FSCS cover is shared between banks that operate under the same licence," said Hannah Maundrell, editor in chief of money.co.uk. The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) publishes a full list of registered banks, and which brands come under the same umbrella. Under the new rules, savers who have up to PS1m in their accounts temporarily - as a result of selling a house, or being made redundant, for example - are also protected. To receive compensation, they cannot have had that cash in their accounts for more than six months. A further warning comes in relation to some foreign banks which trade in the UK, but are registered within the eurozone, such as Germany's Fidor Bank, or Sweden's Handelsbanken. Handelsbanken confirmed that the level of compensation would depend on the exchange rate at the time. So depending on how much EUR100,000 is worth in pounds, savers may get more or less than PS75,000 protection. At the time of writing, that amount is worth less than PS74,000. "With an increasing number of European banks now offering competitive rates, customers need to be aware that not all savings accounts offered in the UK are covered by the UK compensation scheme," said Rachel Thrussell, savings insight manager at Moneyfacts.co.uk.

The new pill being developed would only need to be taken once a week, making it a more convenient option for people at risk of HIV infection. If you're a beginner in the world of neural networks, you've probably heard of recurrent neural networks (RNNs). RNNs are a type of neural network that is well-suited for modeling sequential data, such as text. In this article, we'll give you a gentle introduction to RNNs and how they work. RNNs were first proposed in the early 1990s by Jurgen Schmidhuber, who is now a professor at the Swiss AI lab IDSIA. At the time, RNNs were not well-understood and were largely ignored by the machine learning community. It wasn't until much later that researchers began to realize the potential of RNNs for modeling complex sequential data. RNNs are called "recurrent" because they perform the same task for every element in a sequence. This makes them ideal for modeling time series data, where each element is dependent on the previous element. For example, consider the following sentence: The cat slept on the mat. Each word in this sentence is dependent on the previous word. In other words, the meaning of the sentence changes as the order of the words changes. An RNN can learn to model this type of sequential data. There are many different types of RNNs, but they all have the same basic structure. An RNN consists of a series of "cells" that process an input sequence one element at a time. Each cell has a set of weights that are updated as the cell processes the input sequence. The weights of the cell determine how the cell will process the next element in the sequence. RNNs can be used for a variety of tasks, such as language modeling, machine translation, and image captioning. In recent years, RNNs have also been used for generating music and painting. Most light bulbs have either clear or coated glass. The coated glass bulbs have a white powdery substance on the inside called kaolin. Kaolin, or kaolinite, is a white, chalky clay in a very fine powder form, that is blown in and electrostatically deposited on the interior of the bulb. It diffuses the light emitted from the filament, producing a more gentle and evenly distributed light. Manufacturers may add pigments to the kaolin to adjust the characteristics of the final light emitted from the bulb. Kaolin diffused bulbs are used extensively in interior lighting because of their comparatively gentle light. Other kinds of colored bulbs are also made, including the various colors used for "party bulbs," Christmas tree lights and other decorative lighting. These are created by coloring the glass with a dopant; which is often a metal like cobalt (blue) or chromium (green). Neodymium-containing glass is sometimes used to provide a more natural-appearing light.

When you install a program it may make other changes than just copy files to your harddrive. If you just delete the files then those changes won't be undone. For example, the installer may create desktop shortcuts, and it may create a variety of entries in the system registry, perhaps registering the application as a handler for certain filetypes (for example, indicating that this application should be launched when you doubleclick on a.mp3 file), and much more. The uninstaller will remove these entries as well as deleting the files. Simply deleting the files won't perform this cleanup. So if the installer made the above registrations then Windows will still try (and fail) to launch the application when you doubleclick on a.mp3 file. And you'll have a shortcut on your desktop which no longer works. Plus whatever other changes the installer made, which you chose not to undo. In short, you've turned your computer into a bit of a mess where some features have suddenly become broken.," "Often times, programs will write new keys to your Registry on your computer. These won't be removed simply by deleting the files. Usually an installer will remove them. Also, some programs have cache and other files located in many various locations around your computer. Unless you know all of these locations, you probably can't find all of them to be sure you've removed 100. But something important to note, installers and uninstallers are both created by the developer. So if they didn't program the uninstaller to remove everything properly, then it won't. There's nothing to enforce the uninstaller doing what it should do. This is why, even with using uninstallers, you will often still have files, settings and registry keys left over from your programs.

Scientists from Japan have found a species of slug that can self-decapitate and regrow their bodies from their heads. It appears that the slug does this in response to parasites like salmonella or typhoid. The researchers said they will now look for other signs of life on the body, such as dropping dead bugs during the day, or swimming near a river while drinking water. "We're really excited about the possibility of using this type of technique," said Dr. Sorin Ticheminov, the lead author of the study published online October 18 in Cell. "It's exciting because most fishes are really weak at prey management; we think it's important and that it is possible to identify these species by looking into them." They were led by Prof. Yushiro Yamamoto, an assistant professor in Japanese botany and coauthor of the paper. "Some animals do more than others - if not better," said the team of researchers who spent months traveling around Central America trying to find out how the species evolved over centuries. "This is clear evidence that other creatures may be able to live in environments similar to ours but in different ways. We needed to shape our model to help us understand certain aspects of this origin."

Dynamic equilibrium was first described by Galileo who noticed that certain assumptions of Aristotelian physics were contradicted by observations and logic. Galileo realized that simple velocity addition demands that the general case must be true, but at a point in space distant from all other points there is no motion where there should have been. Thus it appears that either the assumption that everything moves has to be modified or the world does not move as predicted. If one assumes uniformity (or simplicity) then such an anomaly doesn't arise because velocities are additive across any spatial distance for equal masses. The idea works well up until very high speeds when relativity comes into play - Newton's laws predict different behavior than Galilean mechanics depending on whether you're moving close to light speed; this led Einstein to come up with special relativity. In contrast, if bodies follow elliptical orbits around each others' centers then even though objects could appear stationary relative to one another they would still exhibit orbital motions regardless of their physical masses due to Kepler's third law. When combined with Plato's dictum "all things tend toward perfect circles," classical celestial dynamics usually leads to circular orbits which preserve invariance under translation. Once Special Relativity became established, the problem of distinguishing between planetary geometries based solely upon mass arose after it was discovered that Saturn had rings. From an abstract geometric perspective these don't seem like something that can physically exist: If we assume conservation of angular momentum then how do we account for the fact that Rings aren't actually just flat planes? This phenomenon challenged many aspects of Newtonian gravity along with observational evidence regarding Kepler's Laws. However attempts to model them initially left behind what some might consider an undesirable property known as static stability - the most extreme example being presented here wherein every aspect of gravitational theory falls apart once planets enter the picture due to deviations from prescribed elliptic paths. Classical Planets successfully addresses both problems while preserving time-honored thinking about why orbits look the way they do without resorting to adding new penalties whenever you try doing more complicated stuff within the orbitals themselves!

This paper provides a comparative analysis of impedance models for power electronic converters and systems for the purpose of stability investigations. Such models can be divided into either decoupled models or coupled models and the paper provides an overview of how to derive and implement these two different approaches. The analysis is carried out for three different converter topologies: the full bridge converter (VSC), the half bridge converter (HSC), and the single phase inverter. The emphasis is on the design principles for the impedance models and the derivation of the different components, as well as on the comparison between different models. The paper is organized as follows. Section II provides a general background on power electronic converters, stability investigations, and the role of the impedance model. Section III describes the decoupled impedance model, focusing on its derivation and implementation. Section IV presents the coupled impedance model, focusing on its derivation and implementation. The paper is concluded in Section V. A power electronic converter is essentially an energy transformation device. The input energy, e.g., in the form of a voltage or a current, is transformed to another energy, e.g., in the form of a voltage or a current. Power electronic converters are used in almost all fields of technology, e.g., for electrical energy production, electrical energy storage, and electrical energy distribution. In all these fields, the stability of the converters is crucial and, hence, a good understanding of the stability is of utmost importance. A general description of power electronic converters and stability investigations can be found in . In stability investigations, the main objective is to analyze the stability of the power electronic system. The first step is to describe the system by means of an equivalent circuit. This circuit is generally based on the concept of impedances and its design requires a detailed knowledge of the converter and the system it is used in. An overview of the different modeling approaches for the impedance model can be found in . This paper focuses on the modeling of impedances for the analysis of power electronic converters. The impedance model can be divided into two different classes: (1) a decoupled model, and (2) a coupled model. The decoupled model is based on the concept that the different components of the power electronic converter can be treated separately. It can be implemented using linear voltage-dependent modeling, nonlinear current-dependent modeling, or both, and the different modeling techniques are explained in Section III. The coupled model is based on the concept that the different components of the power electronic converter interact and, thus, it cannot be implemented using linear voltage-dependent modeling. The different modeling techniques are explained in Section IV. The decoupled impedance model is useful in the case that the dynamic behavior of the power electronic converter is not influenced by the other components. For instance, the voltage and current ripple of the output voltage of a DC-DC converter are independent of the output load, which is assumed to be resistive or capacitive, and the decoupled model is the preferred choice for the impedance model. The coupled impedance model is useful in the case that the dynamic behavior of the power electronic converter is influenced by the other components. For instance, the output inductance of a DC-DC converter influences the dynamics of the voltage and current ripple of the output voltage, and, thus, the coupled model is the preferred choice for the impedance model. This paper is organized as follows. Section II provides a general background on power electronic converters, stability investigations, and the role of the impedance model. Section III describes the decoupled impedance model, focusing on its derivation and implementation. Section IV presents the coupled impedance model, focusing on its derivation and implementation. The paper is concluded in Section V. Power electronic converters can be divided into four different groups, depending on the operation mode: (1) the DC-DC converter, (2) the DC-AC converter, (3) the AC-AC converter, and (4) the AC-DC converter. The presented analysis applies to all these groups, but for the sake of simplicity, the analysis is only presented for the DC-DC converter. A DC-DC converter consists of an input stage, e.g., a boost converter, and an output stage, e.g., a buck converter, and it is shown in Figure 1. The input stage takes the input energy, e.g., in the form of a DC voltage or current, and transforms it to another energy, e.g., in the form of a DC voltage or current. The output stage takes the input energy and transforms it to the output energy, e.g., in the form of a DC voltage or current

Quantum stabilizer codes (QSCs) suffer from a low quantum coding rate, since they have to recover the quantum bits (qubits) in the face of both bit-flip and phase-flip errors. In addition, QSCs have a limited distance, meaning they can only correct a certain number of errors before the code fails. This can make them less suitable for applications that require high error tolerance, such as quantum communication or fault-tolerant quantum computing. Despite these limitations, QSCs are still useful for some applications, particularly when the noise is dominated by one type of error (either bit-flip or phase-flip), or when the number of errors is low. QSCs can also be combined with other error-correcting techniques to improve their performance, such as the use of concatenated codes or the implementation of topological codes. Overall, while QSCs may have limitations, they are an important tool in the field of quantum error correction and have played a significant role in the development of quantum technologies.

Unemployment insurance (UI) is a program created by the federal government that allows workers who lose their jobs to collect benefits when they are unemployed. Each state administers its own UI program, but must adhere to federal guidelines. The unemployment insurance program is funded through employer taxes, and benefits are paid to unemployed workers through state unemployment offices. Unemployment insurance pays benefits to eligible workers who have lost their jobs through no fault of their own, usually due to a reduction in force or other business-related reason. Unemployment insurance benefits provide temporary financial assistance to workers. Most states provide 26 weeks of benefits. In most cases, you will have to file a claim for benefits. You will be asked to give the names of your employers for the past 18 months, your earnings and the reason you are no longer employed. You may be asked to provide documentation to verify your eligibility. You will also be asked to report each week you are unemployed. In the US, there are Federal and state-based unemployment benefits. Federal unemployment benefits are paid by the government and are only available to individuals who were formerly employed by the government or other government agencies. This type of unemployment benefits are a result of the Federal Unemployment Tax Act (FUTA). State unemployment benefits are also paid by the government but are a result of state laws. Every state has a unemployment insurance department that is responsible for administering the benefits. Federal unemployment benefits are paid directly to you by the government. State unemployment benefits are paid by the government but are generally disbursed through your state's unemployment insurance department. For all that it may sound attractive to the Scots, Welsh and Northern Irish to have greater influence over their respective economic destinies, presumably that would be less desirable if at a stroke they became poorer. The point is that as and when there is an English parliament for English people - of the sort that the former Tory minister John Redwood has been demanding, and David Cameron seemed to concede today - the financial transfer from England to the rest of the UK may be harder to sustain. So these constitutional reforms will be tricky, if not dangerous - if at least a part of the current glue that holds the UK together is a redistribution of resources from England to the rest, and that glue is progressively removed. Being British right now means in part that public services and living standards are not too far apart in quantum and quality wherever you happen to live. But what if the overhaul of the UK's budget-making or fiscal constitution waters down that glue. How much is at stake? Well, spending on public-sector services per head is highest in Northern Ireland, PS10,900 and it is lowest in England, at PS8,500. The figure for Scotland - beneficiary of the famous or notorious Barnett Formula, which formalises an income transfer from England to Scotland - is PS10,200. So expenditure on public services in Scotland is a fifth higher per person than south of the border, and it is 28 higher in Northern Ireland. In Wales, the increment on public-service spending is 14 - which the Welsh have often complained is too little, compared with the transfer of income to Scotland. Now one way of looking at the scale of the transfer is to look at the amount of income - or what is known as gross value added - generated in each country. So English gross value added per head is highest, at just under PS22,000, and it is lowest in Wales at PS15,400. The English enjoy public-service spending per annum equivalent to under 40 of the income they generate, whereas annual outlays on public services in Wales are equivalent to more than 60 of nationally generated income per head. The ratios for Scotland and Northern Ireland are just over 50 and not far off 70 respectively. In a UK of considerable social and cultural solidarity that prevailed for most of the twentieth century, these sorts of disparities between income and outlay between the nations were relatively uncontroversial: they captured the idea that all UK citizens are in it together, as it were. But today it seems almost inevitable that in David Cameron's brave new world of greater national fiscal self-determination, some English nationalist MPs on the right of the spectrum may increasingly view Wales - and Scotland and Northern Ireland - as de facto socialist paradises excessively featherbedded by the English. That said, if the nations are given much greater control over income taxes - which appears to be what is on offer - could they not pay for whatever public services they feel they need out of these locally levied taxes? Not remotely. Income and other direct taxes per head in Wales raise PS5,564, considerably less than the UK average of PS7,360, and nowhere near enough to cover public service expenditure. There is a similar mismatch between direct income taxes and public spending throughout the UK. Borrowing and indirect taxes, mostly VAT, make up the difference. And there is not the faintest chance that national parliaments will be given the power to increase VAT, because this would be an admin nightmare for businesses and undermine the UK as a frictionless single market. All of which means that it may sound exciting and empowering in Wales, Northern Ireland and Scotland to make their own choices about taxing and spending. But it may also be a bit nerve-wracking (or worse) if it provides cover for Westminster to reduce the income transferred to them from English taxpayers.

Smart devices, storage and other distributed technologies have the potential to greatly improve the utilisation of network infrastructure and renewable generation. Decentralised control of these technologies overcomes many scalability and privacy concerns, but in general still requires the underlying problem to be convex in order to guarantee convergence to a global optimum. Considering that AC power flows are non-convex in nature, and the operation of household devices often requires discrete decisions, there has been uncertainty surrounding the use of distributed methods in a realistic setting. This paper extends prior work on the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) for solving the dynamic optimal power flow (D-OPF) problem. We utilise more realistic line and load models, and introduce a two-stage approach to managing discrete decisions and uncertainty. Our experiments on a suburb-sized microgrid show that this approach provides near optimal results, in a time that is fast enough for receding horizon control. This work brings distributed control of smart-grid technologies closer to reality.

I'm going to talk specifically about the U.S. because the hippie movement started there. In the 1930s and early 1940s, the U.S. lived through the trauma of the Great Depression and WWII. After the war, a new era of prosperity dawned in the U.S. and there a strong impulse for everything to return to "normal." Also, the power of the Soviet Union increased mightily in the post-war world, giving rise to the Cold War. The Cold War led to a fear of communists and other subversives in the U.S. All this together added up to encouraging a conservative social order in the U.S. during the 1950s. In the 1960s, there was a leftist backlash against the conservatism of the 1950s. Social issues which had been suppressed in the '50s rose to prominence. The Vietnam War particularly galvanized young leftists as it was a war being fought against communism (as part of the Cold War) and the draft was in effect. Before Vietnam, it was widely accepted that America's fight against communism was a noble cause, but now that was to be challenged. Hippies were a youth subculture which emerged in the '60s as part of this leftist backlash against the values of the '50s and the social order it represented. The values of the hippies were anti-war, free love, environmentalism, and pro-drug-use. Those first two items were often summed with the slogan, "make love, not war." All of it challenged the Cold War establishment of the time.

Personalization is crucial across various service sectors. Current methods predominantly employ online evaluations like A/B testing for assessing customized rankings. Lately, multileaving emerged as a superior technique for appraising rankings within information retrieval domains. In this study, we outline our inaugural endeavor to refine the multileaving approach tailored specifically for personalization contexts. Initially, we identify potential difficulties associated with utilizing multileaving for personalized rankings. Subsequently, we introduce the concept of Greedy Optimized Multileaving (GOM), incorporating an innovative credit feedback mechanism to address those issues. Our experimental data demonstrated that GOM remained consistent even when dealing with extended ranking lengths and multiple rankers. Upon integrating GOM into our real-world news recommendation engines, it exhibited precise evaluation of personalized rankings using substantially reduced sample sizes (less than 10) compared to traditional A/B tests.

Additionally, it incorporates knowledge from social sciences concerning human social interactions, organizations, and cultural dynamics. Many current machine learning (ML) architectures leverage a collection of specialized, often pre-trained, basic models to perform specific tasks like feature extraction. Although utilizing these basic models streamlines and accelerates the creation process of ML systems, there is growing concern over security risks due to the absence of uniform standards or oversight since they are typically provided by external entities. Our study reveals significant vulnerabilities within ML systems when compromised basic models are employed. Through our analysis of four diverse deep learning applications—skin cancer detection, voice recognition, facial identification, and automated navigation—we found that malevolent models can cause these systems to errone precisely at the adversary's behest while remaining undetected under normal circumstances. Furthermore, these harmful models consistently affect the systems despite changes in design parameters and techniques applied during optimization. Interestingly, executing such attacks requires minimal information regarding the training datasets or operational settings. These findings underscore the intricate nature of contemporary basic models and suggest that safeguarding against such exploits should be considered integral to developing secure ML frameworks. We also explore possible defensive measures along with associated hurdles, opening up new avenues for future investigation.

Experts reassembled pieces of tiles found amid tons of earth from the site known to Jews as the Temple Mount and to Muslims as Haram al-Sharif. They say the tiles date from the period of the Second Temple, during the time of King Herod about 2,000 years ago. The temple was destroyed by the Romans in 70 AD during a Jewish rebellion. Some 600 segments of coloured stone floor have been found since archaeologists began examining the debris from the hilltop site in 2004. The plateau where the temples stood is the most sacred site in Judaism. It is joined by the Western Wall, venerated by Jews as part of the original supporting wall of the temple compound. Haram al-Sharif (Noble Sanctuary) is also the place where Muslims believe the Prophet Muhammad ascended to Heaven, and is the third holiest site in Islam. The archaeologists say the tiles probably came from porticos in the temple's courtyards. Piecing the fragments together "enables us to get an idea of the Temple's incredible splendour," said Dr Gabriel Barkay of the Temple Mount Sifting Project. Experts say they managed to assemble seven potential designs of how the flooring could have looked like. The type of flooring is known as opus sectile, Latin for "cut work," and "considered to be far more prestigious than mosaic tiles floors," according to Frankie Snyder, from the project's team. "The tile segments were perfectly inlaid such that one could not even insert a sharp blade between them," she said. The Temple Mount Sifting Project was established by Israeli archaeologists in 2004 to examine debris dumped by Islamic authorities following expansion work at an underground mosque on the compound. The project attracts thousands of visitors each year who participate in finger-tip searches of the earth and has so far turned up hundreds of ancient relics, including coins, animal bones and pieces of pottery.

The sound of an exhaust is a very complex sound. Basically, there are explosions going on inside the motor. This is the genesis of the sound you hear. However, different factors can affect the actual tone, loudness, and quality of the exhaust sound. Some of these factors include: 1. Exhaust System Design: The design of the exhaust system plays a significant role in the sound produced. The size of the pipes, mufflers, and resonators can all affect the exhaust's tone. 2. Engine Type: Different engine types produce different exhaust sounds. For example, a V8 engine typically produces a deeper and more throaty exhaust sound compared to a four-cylinder engine. 3. Exhaust Manifold: The exhaust manifold collects exhaust gases from the engine and channels them to the exhaust system. The design of the manifold can affect the sound produced. 4. Catalytic Converter: The catalytic converter is responsible for reducing harmful emissions in the exhaust. However, it can also affect the exhaust tone. 5. Aftermarket Modifications: Aftermarket exhaust systems, headers, or mufflers can all alter the exhaust sound produced by a vehicle. In summary, exhaust sound is a complex issue with many variables affecting the tone, loudness, and quality of the sound produced.

This paper proposes a robust adversarial reinforcement learning (RARL) -based multi-access point (AP) coordination method that is robust even against unexpected decentralized operations of uncoordinated APs. Multi-AP coordination is a challenging task, as it requires multiple APs to work together to optimize network performance while avoiding interference and congestion. Adversarial reinforcement learning is a machine learning approach that involves training agents to make decisions in a competitive environment, where each agent is trying to maximize its own reward while also trying to interfere with the other agents' performance. The proposed RARL-based method uses a centralized controller to coordinate the actions of multiple APs in a way that maximizes network throughput while minimizing interference. The controller uses a deep reinforcement learning algorithm to optimize the coordination policy, taking into account the dynamic nature of the network and the presence of competing agents. The RARL approach is particularly useful in situations where there is a high degree of uncertainty, as it allows the controller to adapt its policies in real-time based on the actions of the other APs. This makes the system more robust and resilient to unexpected events, such as malfunctions or unplanned changes in the network topology. Overall, the proposed RARL-based multi-AP coordination method has the potential to significantly improve the performance and reliability of wireless networks, particularly in environments with multiple competing APs.

Jim McCafferty, 71, appeared before Belfast Magistrates' Court charged with eight counts of touching a boy under the age of 16. Mr McCafferty, who is described as a "prominent and well-respected Republican," did not comment on the charges when he appeared in the dock in the city's Laganside Court. Dressed in a grey suit and white shirt, he looked on as a detective sergeant confirmed the details of the allegations to the court. During the short hearing, Mr McCafferty's solicitor, Liam McCollum, said his client was a "high profile individual" who had "strong connections" with the Northern Ireland Prison Service and he had been summoned to appear before the court by police. He asked for bail to be granted with conditions. However, the detective sergeant asked for an adjournment to the case, saying he needed time to consider the application and the fact Mr McCafferty had been arrested on foot of a European Arrest Warrant. Mr McCollum said his client had been in custody for five days but did not object to the request. The detective sergeant said he needed time to consider the application as he wanted to take account of the fact Mr McCafferty had been arrested under a European Arrest Warrant and it had been served by the Northern Ireland Office. District Judge Rosie Watters agreed to the request for an adjournment. Mr McCafferty was released on his own bail of 500 and is due to appear again before the court on June 28.

Some of the most compelling applications of online convex optimization, including online prediction and classification, are unconstrained: the natural feasible set is R n . Existing algorithms fail to achieve sub-linear regret in this setting unless constraints on the comparator point x are known in advance. We present algorithms that, without such prior knowledge, offer near-optimal regret bounds with respect to any choice of x . In particular, regret with respect to x 0 is constant . We then prove lower bounds showing that our guarantees are near-optimal in this setting.

Ninety-five percent of bird species are socially monogamous. These species pair for at least the length of the breeding season or - in some cases - for several years or until the death of one mate. Monogamy allows for both paternal care and biparental care, which is especially important for species in which females require males' assistance for successful brood-rearing. Among many socially monogamous species, extra-pair copulation (infidelity) is common. Such behaviour typically occurs between dominant males and females paired with subordinate males, but may also be the result of forced copulation in ducks and other anatids. Female birds have sperm storage mechanisms that allow sperm from males to remain viable long after copulation, a hundred days in some species. Sperm from multiple males may compete through this mechanism. For females, possible benefits of extra-pair copulation include getting better genes for her offspring and insuring against the possibility of infertility in her mate. Males of species that engage in extra-pair copulations will closely guard their mates to ensure the parentage of the offspring that they raise.

I will focus on the United States since the hippie movement originated there. During the 1930s and early 1940s, the country experienced significant hardship due to the Great Depression and World War II. Following the conflict, a period of economic growth began in the US, leading many people to desire a return to normalcy. Additionally, the Soviet Union gained considerable influence after the war, sparking the Cold War. This tension fostered a climate of suspicion towards communists and others deemed subversive within the US, ultimately contributing to a more conservative societal structure throughout the 1950s. However, by the 1960s, there arose a progressive response against the previous decade's conservatism. Various previously overlooked social matters became prominent, especially amidst growing opposition to the Vietnam War—a conflict waged as part of the broader Cold War struggle, coupled with conscription. Although prior to the Vietnam War, most Americans viewed their nation's battle against communism favorably, this perception would soon change. As a result, the countercultural group known as hippies came into existence during this tumultuous period. Their beliefs centered around peace, sexual liberation, ecological awareness, and drug use, encapsulated by the popular phrase, "make love, not war." These ideals directly opposed the prevailing attitudes upheld by the Cold War powers at the time.

The scoreline reflects Munich's complete control over the game, as they had ten shots on target compared to Stuttgart's two. The club's goalkeeper, Manuel Neuer, helped secure the win by making a crucial save at the 64th minute, making the Stuttgart fans in the stadium groan in disappointment. With only five games left in the season, Munich now holds an eight-point lead over second-placed RB Leipzig. The German giants are now inching closer to achieving a successful title defense for the fourth straight year, and this game's victory only shows how they won't be relinquishing their title anytime soon. Bayern Munich will face Borussia Monchengladbach on Saturday, and fans can't wait to see if they can maintain their dominant form and edge closer to securing their coveted Bundesliga title.

We present Nopol an approach for automatically repairing buggy if conditions and missing preconditions. As input, it takes a program and a test suite which contains passing test cases modeling the expected behavior of the program and at least one failing test case embodying the bug to be repaired. It consists of collecting data from multiple instrumented test suite executions, transforming this data into a Satisfiability Modulo Theory (SMT) problem, and translating the SMT result - if there exists one - into a source code patch. Nopol repairs object oriented code and allows the patches to contain nullness checks as well as specific method calls.

I feel like the other answers are missing the point that you want. As said by other posters, your red blood cells literally only carry oxygen to your muscles and CO2 away from them. Imagine your blood cells REALLY want to carry some molecules. For now, imagine we are going back to the lungs. The blood cells have CO2, then. Now, when your blood rushes past the arterioles (very small blood vessels; since they are small, they are very numerous, and the volume:surface area ratio is very small, which makes it much more efficient), that CO2 is switched with the O2. Why? O2 has a much higher concentration near your lungs than it does at your muscles; the molecules want to reach an equilibrium. When there's much more O2 in one side, they actively want to get to another side. I'm sure you've learned of stuff like osmosis and diffusion. This is just osmosisdiffusion through the membranes of the blood vessels. Now, the O2 rich blood will go to your muscular arterioles. There, where there is much more CO2, the O2 will be switched. Now, your muscles have O2 to use, which will be turned to CO2 through cellular respiration (IE, how we turn sugar into energy). However, the blood will now have less O2 and more CO2, and we are brought back to the beginning.,The only "nutrient" that a healthy red blood cell carries to the peripheral cells is oxygen. Basically, it carries oxygen around in a big container inside of it called hemoglobin. When the RBC reaches the capillaries, which are the blood vessels with the smallest diameter, the container opens up and the oxygen diffuses out of the RBC and into the surrounding blood. Then it diffuses into the cells in that immediate vicinity. The way this happens, and the reason that it happens are a bit complex for an ELI5 post but essentially, there are many different conditions that alter how loosely or tightly closed the hemoglobin "container" is. And the conditions in the periphery, where the capillaries are, make it conducive for the RBCs to let go of the oxygen they are carrying.

An automatic technique for analyzing knee MRI images to investigate osteoarthritis has been devised through a new layered series of random forest algorithms designed to recognize cartilage structures and edges. Initially, an approximate nearest neighbor forest algorithm generates contextual characteristics, which are then employed by a secondary level of random forest classifiers considering local attributes to produce specific cost metrics within the LOGISMOS framework for multi-object and surface segmentation based on layered graphs. This research incorporates double echo steady state (DESS) MRIs acquired from the Osteoarthritis Initiative (OAI) study. After being trained on 34 MRIs exhibiting various stages of osteoarthritis, the results demonstrated statistically significant improvements in reducing segmentation mistakes when evaluated against traditional gradient methods as well as solitary stage random forest cost calculations (p < .05). Furthermore, the 3D LOGISMOS model was adapted into a four-dimensional version to concurrently process several consecutive patient appointments, integrating both spatiotemporal contexts. Validation tests performed on 108 MRIs taken at initial assessment and subsequent 12-month checkups for 54 individuals revealed substantial reductions in segmentation errors (p < .01) over the 3D model. Lastly, the efficacy of the 4D LOGISMOS method was assessed on the same group of 5right patients across five yearly examinations, resulting in marked enhancements in evaluating cartilage thickness measurements (p < .01), surpassing the stepwise 3D technique.

Massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) is a key technology for 5G wireless communications with a promise of significant capacity increase. The use of low-resolution data converters is crucial for massive MIMO to make the overall transmission as cost- and energy-efficient as possible. In this work, we consider a downlink millimeter-wave (mmWave) transmission scenario, where multiple users are served simultaneously by massive MIMO with one-bit digital-to-analog (DA) converters. In particular, we propose a novel precoder design based on signal-to-leakage-plus-noise ratio (SLNR), which minimizes energy leakage into undesired users while taking into account impairments due to nonlinear one-bit quantization. We show that well-known regularized zero-forcing (RZF) precoder is a particular version of the proposed SLNR-based precoder, which is obtained when quantization impairments are totally ignored. Numerical results underscore significant performance improvements along with the proposed SLNR-based precoder as compared to either RZF or zero-forcing (ZF) precoders.

We sat ourselves too close to the screen of the television, on the cold carpeted floor that probably needed to be vacuumed. I ask him what "pulling a Michael Larson" means. He responds with an explanation about the game mechanics of Press Your Luck. He's cute when he goes on tangents. Halfway through his report about something about squares 4 and 8, I slip behind him, my legs lining up against his. He's wearing a thin T-shirt, barely hiding an equally thin man underneath. I comment that he needs to eat more. He passes it off. I lean my head against his shoulder. "Tell me your secrets," I whisper. "About what?" His weight against mine is the greatest feeling imaginable. "I've missed the last three questions." "And you've gotten the rest correct. Why are you. What are you doing here? You're in a dumpy apartment, you've hardly eaten for the past two days, you're with "With?" I have a good feeling he knows what I'm thinking. "With someone as lousy as me." "Well, I'm smart as shit, sure. But I'm not very wise." "I don't understand." And I don't. He goes on another tirade. This time, the difference between intelligence and wisdom. How it was intelligence that got him into college, but terrible wisdom that made him drop out. How it wasn't a wise choice to pass up buying a couch for his living room. How it definitely wasn't wise to skip last meal. Sure, he has all of the information to make a good insight, but he doesn't. "You know why?" He asks. "It's more fun this way. It's more entertaining to be with you, on this cruddy carpet, burning my eyes out on a screen, than to be one of those stiffs on Jeopardy. Tell me, when's the last time any of them have eaten cereal on a carpet?" "Hm. Probably 6 months." "I'd guess 7." He turns his head, and kisses me on the cheek.

Widespread deployment of the Internet enabled building of an emerging IT delivery model, i.e., cloud computing. Albeit cloud computing-based services have rapidly developed, their security aspects are still at the initial stage of development. In order to preserve cybersecurity in cloud computing, cybersecurity information that will be exchanged within it needs to be identified and discussed. For this purpose, we propose an ontological approach to cybersecurity in cloud computing. We build an ontology for cybersecurity operational information based on actual cybersecurity operations mainly focused on non-cloud computing. In order to discuss necessary cybersecurity information in cloud computing, we apply the ontology to cloud computing. Through the discussion, we identify essential changes in cloud computing such as data-asset decoupling and clarify the cybersecurity information required by the changes such as data provenance and resource dependency information.

In this paper, we consider the joint task of simultaneously optimizing (i) the weights of a deep neural network, (ii) the number of neurons for each hidden layer, and (iii) the depth of the network. More specifically, we propose an optimization method that determines the optimal values for these parameters via a weighted combination of the generalization error and the model size. We show that when trained on image data, the proposed optimization method outperforms a number of other state-of-the-art methods such as Bayesian optimization, evolutionary algorithms, and gradient descent on image classification tasks. In addition, we demonstrate that by training the proposed model on one image classification dataset, we are able to obtain a well-performing model on other datasets, e.g., CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, with minimal training. This is done by using the learned weights of the model on the one dataset to initialize a new model on the other two datasets. As our method can train a model from scratch or fine-tune a pretrained model, it can be considered as a universal image classifier (UIC), which provides an interpretable, efficient, and flexible alternative to other recent methods such as Gatys and Lu et al. . In addition to image classification, our method can also be used to train a model that can generalize across different tasks. We conduct experiments to demonstrate that trained with the proposed method, a model can generalize across tasks such as image classification and semantic segmentation with no additional training data. Finally, our method is easy to implement and can be directly applied to any deep neural network without changing the network architecture. Paper can be found here. Understanding the formation of subjective human traits, such as preference and opinions, is an important, but poorly explored problem. An essential aspect is that traits collectively evolve under the repeated influence of the environment. The impact of the environment is especially strong in situations where individuals differ in the baseline trait level, where preferences and opinions can develop over time in a dynamic context. It is important to understand the underlying mechanisms of this dynamic evolution of opinions, in order to be able to shape opinions in a desired direction, e.g. for the purpose of social manipulation. I will present a game-theoretic model that allows to study the evolution of traits under repeated environmentally-driven interactions. I will show that the social evolution of traits can be driven by a process of 'drift and selection', in which both drift and selection are driven by the repeated environmental influence. I will discuss implications of this model for the understanding of opinion formation, and apply the model to different settings.

If that happens, the ice loss could push up global oceans by 2m, or more. The claim is based on an assessment of the rocks underlying the ice stream. Scientists tell the journal Nature that should the front of the glacier retreat about 150km from its current position, it will then enter a runaway reversal that takes it 200-250km further inland. Most of the big glaciers in the east of the White Continent appear relatively quiescent; Totten is something of an exception. It is experiencing a thinning rate of about half a metre per year, according to the latest satellite measurements. Previous research indicates this is probably being driven by warm ocean water getting under and melting the floating front of the glacier. What Alan Aitken and colleagues have now done is examine a possible future for Totten if the shrinkage continues. They have used gravity and magnetic data recorded over the entire catchment feeding the glacier to understand its past behaviour. They find that the underlying sedimentary rocks at the modern front of Totten are heavily eroded, as are the rocks in fjords deep in the interior of the catchment. The inference is that these sections are where persistent, moving ice has had time to grind down the geology. It is the mid-region, however, that piques the team's interest. Here, the sediments are relatively thick, suggesting that ice fronts have historically been resident in this section for only short periods. This mid-region is also where the rock bed dips inland - a geometry that glaciologists say is naturally unstable and accelerates any glacier retreat. "What this all tells us is that once the ice margin starts to go back, it goes back quite rapidly to a newer, stable position way inland. And if you do that our modelling indicates you will lose ice equivalent to 1.5-2m of sea level rise," co-author Prof Martin Siegert from Imperial College London, UK, told BBC News. The last time Totten retreated to the deep interior of the France-sized catchment was probably in the Pliocene Epoch, he added. "Three-point-five million years ago, atmospheric carbon dioxide levels were in the region of 400 parts per million - so about where they are now. The atmosphere was a couple of degrees warmer than it is now, which is in line with what we expect for the end of this century if we do nothing about it. The Pliocene is where we're headed." Even so, the timescale for the far retreat inland would be on the order of centuries, on current trends. The international community has of course committed itself to doing something about climate change, promising at the Paris talks in December to try to keep the global atmospheric temperature rise above pre-industrial levels to "well below 2C." Various analyses, however, suggest a 2.7C increase is a more likely outcome, based on the voluntary national curbs to greenhouse gas emissions promised at the meeting. And that variance could be significant, according to research presented at the recent European Geosciences Union meeting in Vienna last month. Prof Rob DeConto from the University of Massachusetts-Amherst, US, has modelled possible ice losses from the Antarctic continent based on the two temperature figures. For a 2C rise, he found minimal change by the end of this century. On the other hand, for 2.7C he identified ice losses equivalent to many tens of centimetres of sea-level rise. "There's threshold behaviour in the Antarctic ice sheet system," Prof DeConto told reporters at EGU. The concept of prime number is so important that it has been generalized in different ways in various branches of mathematics. Generally, "prime" indicates minimality or indecomposability, in an appropriate sense as the set of divisors (or integers) whose square roots are exactly equal to each other and which satisfy some condition on their sum. For example, a prime number satisfies the Faulkner-Salvin Steinage theorem: A prime number has at least one negative integer, if and only if its sum is at most twice the product of all other numbers. You can also use this theorem for the rule that any two positive integers with nonnegative square root values must have to be prime numbers. One prime number means, among other things, convergence between a tensor function x and a real line that connects the origin to the leftmost point of the unit circle. The Klein group and Lie algebra are examples of prime groups; enumeration theory, projective geometry, and computational algebra are others. A prime number represents an identity element of a polynomial, a trigonometric function, a specific series, or whatever you like by identifying what it does to a linear operator. It's often used to identify particular sequences of operations such as addition, multiplication, division, subtraction, etc., based on how they produce unique pairs of variables when multiplied or divided by another variable. Modern applications include cryptography, artificial intelligence, combinatorics, and computer graphics (see Moore's Law). The term also appears frequently in physics and astronomy (in regard to prime numbers), because many X-Y coordinates are considered prime factors of 1. Prime logarithms were first introduced in the 19th century. In mathematics the notion of a prime gauge is a generalization of the idea of prime numbers derived from the study of polar coordinates. According to these definitions, every large prime number r2 belongs to a homomorphism class of functors (and hence to a subcategory of the CMF functor space), which corresponds to the core group of a functional analysis type of category theory. These classification schemes classify by size and not necessarily by dimension. This concept was proposed by Viktor Miller in his 1951 paper. Russia plans to temporarily disconnect the entire country from the internet in an exercise designed to test the country's internet infrastructure in case of a cyber-war. The test is expected to begin on Monday. Russia's RIA Novosti news agency quoted Russian Defense Ministry spokesman Igor Konashenkov as saying on Friday that Russia's Defense Ministry is planning to test the country's defense system in the event of a cyber-attack on Monday. Konashenkov said that the exercise will include a shutdown of internet service in the entire country. "During the day on Monday, the entire Russian Federation will be offline for several hours," Konashenkov said. "The aim of the exercise is to test the entire internet infrastructure of the Russian Federation, including the country's cyber-defense system." Konashenkov added that the exercise is part of the Defense Ministry's efforts to protect the country's national security and to develop the country's cyber-defense capabilities. "The exercises will be held in different regions of the country," he said. "We're testing our defense system to see how we're prepared to face such a situation." Asked whether Russia was preparing for a cyber-war with the United States, Konashenkov said: "We're always ready for any cyber-attacks, including against Russia." He added that "the United States should also be ready for any cyber-attacks against it." Russia has repeatedly warned of the possibility of a cyber-attack on its territory, although no such attack has ever been launched. The Defense Ministry also said that during the exercise, Russia's air force will test the capabilities of its "cyber-aircraft" and its own capabilities to conduct cyber-attacks. Konashenkov said that the military's goal is to increase the country's ability to protect its military information systems from cyber-attacks. "We're preparing for cyber-attacks on our military," he said.

Many years ago, keyboards used different pins to represent each bit of information. When some keys were held down, a different set of pins would have voltage across them than others. USB doesn't work that way at all. It just sends data back and forth, one bit at a time, very quickly. It's a lot more like sending data across a network. When you hold down multiple keys, it just sends more bytes of data. When you record audio, it's digitizing the audio and streaming the bytes directly to your computer.," "Professional audio is recorded at least 44,100 samples per second, with 24 bits per sample. That's a data rate of around 1060 kbs. USB 2 supports a data rate of up to 480 Mbs. That's around 47 individual microphones all at the same time. It works because USB is a serial communication with high speed switching. Meaning it sends two bits down the data pins, and rapidly switches between which bit is being sent. It switches literally millions of times a second, plenty fast for audio.,The reason you can detect large amounts of keys pressed and record high quality audio is that the USB device is its self a little computer. It has enough circuitry to detect all the key presses and record the audio and then it packages all that data into a single stream of bits, and it's the bits that get sent back and forth over the USB connection. In fact, this data is only sent over two of the four pins. The other two are used only for delivering power to a USB device that doesn't have its own power supply. The reason the microphone can transmit in very very close to real time is that sound is very slow compared to have fast computers are. Sound is a wave of changing air pressure that moves through the air. The higher the tone or pitch, the faster the air pressure changes neutral to high to low and back to neutral. The highest frequency humans can hear is 20KHz which means the air pressure makes that cycle 20,000 times a second. To record this sound a microphone is setup which converts the air pressure into a voltage that swings from low to high and back, just like the air pressure. This changing voltage is then "sampled" by a converter circuit. Sample here just means to measure. So the voltage is measure to see how high it is at a given point. If you do this over and over again, and you do it fast enough, you get enough measurements to recreate the original sound with an amplifier and speaker. To get enough samples to do this, you need to measure twice as fast as the highest frequency in order not to miss the really fast changing voltage. Recall the highest was 20,000 times a second. So we sample at 44,100 times a second. Now lets check some numbers. Each sample requires 16 bits of data and there are 44,100 samples per second so that is 705,600 bits per second. Most USB audio interfaces can record two channels at the same time, and play back two channels at the same time, so now we need to move 2,822,400 bits per second. Sounds like a lot. Except even the slowest USB devices can send 12,000,000 bits per second. So we can do 4 channels of high quality audio and still have 10,000,000 bits per second left over. Now sending audio data to the computer actually uses a lot more of that 12,000,000 bits per second because the audio has to be packaged in a way that the computer understands what it is and where it goes and that's done by wrapping the samples in other data.', "The USB 2.0 (most common) standard has support for data transfer speeds as high as 480 Mbps (more than enough to handle audio and most video input streams). The new USB 3.0 standard supports data transfer speeds of up to 5 Gbps and USB 3.1 supports up to 10 Gbps (which is enough bandwidth to handle just about any multimedia peripheral device you can possibly think of including live 4K video streams, for example). Of the 4 pins in a regular USB 2.0 cable, only 2 are used for data and the other two are used for supplying voltagepower. The USB device has a chip in it that converts the information (e.g. audio information from a microphone or keyboard presses) into packets of data that can be transferred via USB to the receiving device (computer). That's why you don't need multiple wires for carrying different types of data, it all just gets converted into one data stream. Note that newer USB implementations (3.0 3.1) have more than 4 pins to facilitate higher speed data transfers greater bandwidth.

Jakarta Governor Joko Widodo, who won the presidential election, is expected to form a new cabinet soon. Indonesia's moderate Islamic party, which is not known for its sophisticated political approach, is the fourth-largest in the country and is widely expected to be part of the new cabinet. "The PKS did not perform well. It is not clear if it will get a ministerial post. But I am sure it will at least get a deputy ministerial post," said Yenny Wahid, daughter of former president Abdurrahman Wahid, who set up the party in 1998. The party's 2014 election campaign focused on its role in fighting corruption, but the allegations against its top two leaders may have affected its performance. The party is a member of the coalition that supported Mr Joko in his successful presidential campaign. It had hoped to increase its share of the vote by 2.5 percentage points. The party's performance is in line with predictions made by political analysts. "It's not performing as well as it did in 2009. But it's still a significant party," said Mr Wimar Witoelar, a political analyst. Mr Wimar said the party would have performed better in the election if its leaders had not been dogged by corruption allegations. "They have not handled the corruption allegations well. They have only said they will cooperate with the investigation. But they should have been more proactive," he added. Mr Laode Muhammad Ishomuddin, a political analyst, said the PKS is not a well-organised political party. "It has no clear political strategy. It's not a political party that can change the system. The Hamburg Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information said that the social network had not obtained effective approval from WhatsApp's 35 million German users. Facebook bought WhatsApp for 19 billion in 2014. Facebook is facing a 20 million (22.5 million) fine in Germany over the way it acquired user data from WhatsApp. Facebook bought WhatsApp for 19 billion in 2014. In 2016, it announced plans to start sharing user data between the two services, but said it would not do so without obtaining user consent. The Hamburg Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information said on Tuesday, however, that the social network had not obtained effective approval from WhatsApp's 35 million German users. "We are aware of the DPA's statement of objections and are examining the documents," a Facebook spokeswoman said in a statement. "We will respond in due course." The WhatsApp and Facebook merger generated plenty of controversy when it was first announced. The social network said it would start sharing data with WhatsApp in August 2016, but the European Commission halted the process in August 2017 while it investigated antitrust concerns. That investigation has since been dropped, but the Commissioner's announcement this week shows that privacy regulators are still probing the issue. "Facebook and WhatsApp are independent companies. And that's why we're not able to combine user data," Facebook told the Commissioner in January 2017. "The only thing we're asking for is the number of phone contacts the user has on WhatsApp in order to improve their experience on Facebook." According to the Commissioner, however, WhatsApp users were not informed they would need to agree to new terms and conditions in order to continue using the service. "The requirement of unequivocal consent to the terms of data processing was also not met, as the users did not have a free choice," the office said. Facebook also used "inappropriate" tracking pixels to collect data about WhatsApp users, the Commissioner's office said. Tracking pixels, also known as web beacons, are tiny images embedded in webpages that can be used to collect data. "Facebook has used its dominant position to create a situation in which users had to agree to the processing of their data on a central platform. This has led to a reduction of users' control over their data," the Commissioner said. Facebook didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
