The woman actually smiled a bit, pushing the worst of the mud off her body armor. "That's easy. They said'the bad guys are coming for your world, we need help.' Went straight to a recruiting station and signed up. This world's my home, figure I owe it at least that much." Nodding, I turned toward the man, who shrugged and tried to look sheepish. "She says it better than me. I was military before, though, so I knew they needed bodies. Signed up that day, haven't been home since." "I see - so how did you end up with the legendary Red Vipers, a special forces regiment." Scratching his chin and ignoring the blood, he shrugged again. "Honestly, I don't know. I told them, I'm military, I want to be near the front lines, where can I do the most help? They looked up my records and said'we want you to help with the Vipers.' I won't complain about anything, just give me a shot. Next thing I know, I'm meeting this tall drink of water who tells me I better ask for help when I need it, and I better get it when I ask." Nodding, I flipped the camera to face me. "The Red Vipers have been at the front of many battles, despite being on the flanks and behind enemy lines. They were the first to respond to this new incursion just last month, even though they've been fighting for 7 years straight. Tell me, how do the Vipers you work with look?" "Scary," the woman offered calmly, "they see a target, they go for it, they make it dead, and they get everyone out. Sure, we get a few wounds, but we live." Inadvertently answering the question as to why he'd been embedded here. Of course, my thoughts get interrupted as a MAC90D set opens up full rate on an enemy something. Even in the trench, I can feel the wind from the launching shells and reloads. That's when it occurs to me; they said social interest. I turned toward one of the Bovi - looks like a Major. "Sir, can I ask you a few quick questions?" He grunted and nodded, using a soaked handkerchief to try and clear some of the mud from his muzzle. "You've had the volunteers here a few days now. How would you describe the relationship?" That actually made him pause, thinking about it, not necessarily in diplomatic terms. "A week ago, would've refused. Sat'em down as aides. But frankly, having seen them fight? Maybe they can't haul an AMR, maybe they can't carry a hundred kilos at a go, but damned if they don't have it where it counts." Rising to his hooves, he turned and actually saluted the two humans. "I'd take these two into hell with me - done themselves more than proud." Predictably, they both saluted back, clearly stunned. That setup always worked for the propaganda stuff. Besides, folks like that never shirked their duties. They'd fight twice as hard just to prove they were every bit as good as the other species. "Then can I ask you all.... how do you think the battle is going here?" Looks were quickly exchanged, and the Major took over again. "Official canned answer, we expect to rout the enemy any hour and completely destroy their assets. Unofficially, we've taking a pounding but they're getting it worse. Soon as we get some air support, it's mopping up time. We're in a good position, we have the best people, we'll be home for breakfast at least." "So we're winning?" "Yep. We're winning," he agreed, "just as soon as the air support gets here." There was a scream of engines approaching, and he looked up while also pointing. There was no mistaking that it was a Hog II ground attack aircraft. There was an unusual whirring as the main gun fired, the camera tracking as it moved off into the distance. And didn't turn around. "Well shit. Bingo ammo. So we wait a little longer." All I could do was turn toward the humans, who looked elated and dejected at the same time. "So what are you thinking?" The woman shrugged helplessly, but the man shook his head confidently. "Bad call, should have sent fresh planes. Gotten some of ours out of mothballs faster, maybe. Let's begin by understanding the fundamentals of American utility firms specializing in televised media. The realm of television can be divided into distinct segments such as Broadcast Networks and Cable Television Networks. It is important to note that these categories differ significantly from Antenna versus Cable Television options available to consumers.

Broadcast Networks refer to major American broadcast channels including ABC, CBS, FOX, and NBC. They serve as primary sources for network television and are commonly linked with local news coverage. By law, these four (and sometimes more) networks must provide freely accessible signals using antenna-based transmission methods. Although no subscriptions are necessary to receive this content, these networks depend heavily on advertising revenue, viewer ratings, and various sales initiatives to sustain themselves. Over time, they have amassed significant financial resources due to their success.

On the other hand, Cable Networks emerged from the concept of Community Access Television (CATV). Initially, localized CATV systems produced unique content specific to individual communities. With an abundance of unused capacity independent of traditional radio wave technology, community groups created original programming. This content then became distributed among different regions, leading to further growth and development. Popular cable channels such as CNN, FXX, USA, TNT, and TBS originated as smaller, locally-focused establishments before expanding beyond the scope of federal regulations governing Broadcast Networks. Unlike its predecessors, Cable TV evolved into a paid service, offering exclusive content while facilitating communication between various production centers. Eventually, prominent cable operators like Alert Cable, Adelphia, and Carolina Cable merged with larger corporations.

As you go deeper into the Earth, both pressure and temperature increase greatly. They increase so much, that it makes it incredibly difficult to get too far past the crust into hotter depths. The reason why this is true in general, but also especially for hot magma from deep within the earths interior (which can reach temperatures of several thousand degrees C when erupted), comes down to two different things: 1) The more energy dissipation there is along a system's lengthline, 2) the higher heat capacity of materials closer to their melting point. To oversimplify things, as we drill through rock deeper into the Earth, it gets harder each time because at some depth, all of the energy can be absorbed and not redistributed or converted back into something else. This means that after a certain depth, extracting energy is like hitting brick walls with your hands instead of removing them via kinetic action. It's important to note here that while we're talking about the existence of 'hot rocks' on the surface of our planet, these are actually cold by comparison - they don't have enough thermal mass to maintain very high internal heats without being eroded away fairly quickly. If I had an analogy relating to my favorite sport, swimming, imagine trying to swim laps underwater without goggles...it'd be nearly impossible! But if one was wearing large sunglasses over said goggles, then yes; the ability would dramatically improve! So what happens? Some of that hard-hitting heat transfers up to the surface of the oceans, where it melts icecaps and snowpack for example.

Humans' large brains may be due to a single "typo" in their genetic code, according to new research. In a study recently published in the journal Nature Ecology and Evolution, researchers from the University of Edinburgh analyzed the DNA of humans and Neanderthals. They found that humans have a unique variation in a gene called NOTCH2NL, which is known to affect brain size. The researchers believe that this variation may have occurred as a result of a random error in the genetic code when our ancestors first split from Neanderthals, around 600,000 years ago. This "typo" then became part of the human genetic code, contributing to the larger brains we see today. This study adds to the evidence that small changes in our genetics can have a huge impact on our evolution. It also provides further insight into why humans have such large brains compared to our closest evolutionary relatives. Lead researcher Dr. Gunchin Zhang said: "Our findings suggest that a single letter change in the genetic code was enough to give rise to an important difference between humans and Neanderthals. We don't know yet what precise role this gene plays in brain development, but our research opens up new avenues for future studies." The team now plans to investigate further how this variation affects the development of the human brain, and how it has impacted our evolution.

In the world of international football, there is much debate over which team can claim to be the greatest of all time. Many nations have had teams that have achieved unprecedented success on the biggest stages and have gone down in history as some of the most iconic sides ever seen. The Brazil national side of is often hailed as one of the best international teams of all time. Led by the likes of Pele, Jairzinho and Garrincha, Brazil won three World Cups during this period and were the first nation to win consecutive titles. They also boasted an impressive record in friendly matches, winning 79 out of 103 games, with 39 wins coming in a row. Another team considered to be among the greatest is the Hungarian side of the 1950s. Their run at the 1954 World Cup was particularly remarkable, where they beat West Germany 3-2 in the final. Hungary went unbeaten in 31 games leading up to the tournament, which remains a record unbeaten streak for any international team. In terms of individual honours, the Spanish national team of 2008-2012 is arguably the greatest ever. Under the guidance of Vicente Del Bosque, Spain won two European Championships and their first ever World Cup. During this period, they also reached the top of the FIFA rankings, becoming the first country to hold the distinction of being number one in the world for two consecutive years. The German national team of 2014-2018 is also deserving of recognition. They won the 2014 World Cup, becoming the first European team to win the title in South America. They then successfully defended their crown four years later in Russia, becoming the first nation to win back-to-back World Cups since Brazil in 1962. So who can claim to be the greatest international side of all time? It is difficult to definitively answer such a subjective question. However, the four aforementioned teams are certainly worthy contenders for the title.

For the first several decades of disc record manufacturing, sound was recorded directly on to the "master disc" at the recording studio. From about 1950 on (earlier for some large record companies, later for some small ones) it became usual to have the performance first recorded on audio tape, which could then be processed andor edited, and then dubbed on to the master disc. A record cutter would engrave the grooves into the master disc. Early versions of these master discs were soft wax, and later a harder lacquer was used. The mastering process was originally something of an art as the operator had to manually allow for the changes in sound which affected how wide the space for the groove needed to be on each rotation.

I'm sure you have heard that once you have something in your brain it doesn't leave. False. Your memory has certain connections that you use more than others. When the neurons that contain certain information die, that's it. Dead. So by remembering and thinking about certain things, you make more neurons of that information and they make more connections to surrounding neurons. Saying that though, your memory on'cats' for example isn't confined to 1 neuron. You have around 70 Billion neurons, each one connected to others in a certain way. So let's say that you learned german in second grade and don't use it for 10 years. Now let's say you and a stranger who has never learned any german both try and learn german. The primary reason for writing direction being left-to-right is due to the majority of individuals being right-handed. In early written languages like Hebrew, inscriptions began by carving symbols onto stones. Given that the majority were right-handed, it was more convenient to grasp the tool with the left hand while striking it with the right. Considering the ease of this method when moving from right to left, reversing the direction seemed awkward unless one held the instrument with their left hand. As time progressed and these scripts transitioned to using parchment, the habit of left-to-right writing remained. With the advent of Indo-European languages such as Ancient Greek and Latin, where papyrus and ink became prevalent, the issue of ink smearing for right-handers arose when writing left-to-right. Consequently, adopting a left-to-right orientation resolved this inconvenience.

The girl looked at her, and Mariposa could tell that she was trying to decide if this was true. "I'm not going to hurt you," Mariposa said again. "I promise." The girl nodded, and Mariposa knew that she was finally going to say yes. She'd finally decided to let Mariposa help her. "Okay," she said. "I guess I can trust you." Mariposa felt a sudden surge of happiness. "Thank you," she said. "Thank you so much." "I'm not doing it for you," the girl said. "I'm doing it for me." "I know," Mariposa said. Where every component state of a federation possesses the same powers, we are said to find 'symmetric federalism'. Asymmetric federalism exists where states are granted different powers, or some possess greater autonomy than others do. This is often done in recognition of the existence of a distinct culture in a particular region or regions. In Spain, the Basques and Catalans, as well as the Galicians, spearheaded a historic movement to have their national specificity recognized, crystallizing in the "historical communities" such as Navarre, Galicia, Catalonia, and the Basque Country. They have more powers than the later expanded arrangement for other Spanish regions, or the Spain of the autonomous communities (called also the "coffee for everyone" arrangement), partly to deal with their separate identity and to appease peripheral nationalist leanings, partly out of respect to specific rights they had held earlier in history. However, strictly speaking Spain is not a federalism, but a decentralized administrative organization of the state.

Immigrants arrived from all over the world to search for gold, especially from Ireland and China. Many Chinese miners worked in Victoria, and their legacy is particularly strong in Bendigo today where there are many restaurants with a distinctly Asian flavour thanks to them. However, most people came here looking for work - Australian agriculture was booming around this time due to increasing demand by European countries such as Britain and France following World War I, so jobs were plentiful at first. This made life much easier for those coming across the seas into Australia; they could find employment almost immediately without having to pay recruitment agents or travel huge distances to reach these destinations (about 40 of immigrants travelled on ships that would take between 6-8 weeks). A lot of Irish emigrated during this period because of famine conditions back home, it's often said that more than 100,000 left after 1847 alone! There had been a gradual decline in job opportunities though throughout the 1880s which eventually saw large numbers of unemployed men who couldn't get off the boats. The solution? Ship out thousands of women instead. It took longer before any white man found himself compelled to leave his family behind simply because he lacked money. Most times they became labourers themselves rather than become homeless wanderers roaming through western Europe. Virtually all staple foods come either directly from primary production by plants, or indirectly from animals that eat them. This is what ecologists call the first trophic level. The modern forms of the major staple foods, such as maize, rice, wheat and other cereal grasses, pulses, bananas and plantains, as well as flax and cotton grown for their fibres, are the outcome of prehistoric selection over thousands of years from among wild ancestral plants with the most desirable characteristics. Botanists study how plants produce food and how to increase yields, for example through plant breeding, making their work important to mankind's ability to feed the world and provide food security for future generations. Botanists also study weeds, which are a considerable problem in agriculture, and the biology and control of plant pathogens in agriculture and natural ecosystems. Ethnobotany is the study of the relationships between plants and people. When applied to the investigation of historical plant-people relationships ethnobotany may be referred to as archaeobotany or palaeoethnobotany.

For example, a monitor running at 60Hz can display 60 unique images per second. If you force it to display 120 images per second, each image will be shown twice - it won't be displayed twice as fast. It'll be shown twice, and then the next image will be shown twice. It's not a big deal, but the video will look weird, because now every frame will be displayed twice. The idea is simple: it changes the refresh rate of your monitor dynamically. To understand how it works, let's take a look at a normal monitor. Your monitor, when it runs at 60Hz, displays 60 unique images per second. It refreshes the whole screen 60 times per second. And it refreshes the screen at the same rate, no matter what. So if your video card generates 60 frames per second, the monitor will display each frame once. If it generates 120 frames per second, it will display each frame twice. Now, let's see what happens if we turn on G-SYNC. You can see that now, your monitor is refreshing at different rates. In fact, the rate at which it refreshes the screen is completely determined by the video card, and is dynamic - the refresh rate changes as the video card generates new frames. If your video card generates 120 frames per second, the monitor will refresh at 120Hz, and each frame will be displayed once. The adoption of resilient control algorithms leveraging graph theoretical attributes related to r- and (r, s)-resilience has grown. Such algorithms ensure consensus among standard functioning agents even when there is a limited number of unpredictably malfunctioning agents, provided that r and s are chosen appropriately high. Nonetheless, assessing a graph's resilience poses a significant challenge. In this study, we propose a new technique for calculating the r- and (r, s)-resilience of directed graphs through mixed integer linear programming. To our knowledge, this marks the initial application of mixed integer programming techniques in addressing the resilience calculation issue. Our strategy relies solely on understanding the graph Laplacian matrix and incorporates binary integer variables. We utilize mixed integer programming procedures like branch-and-bound to progressively refine the estimated range for r and s. We also present simulations contrasting the effectiveness of our method against existing approaches for computing robustness.

Members of the genus Dinophysis have a phycobilin-containing chloroplast taken from a cryptophyte. However, the cryptophyte is not an endosymbiont - only the chloroplast seems to have been taken, and the endosymbiont's nucleus has been lost. Dinophysis also contain a protein complex (a phycobilisome) that is composed of phycobiliproteins, but they lack the typical phycobilin pigments. Thus, it is believed that they were once free-living, photosynthetic organisms, but acquired a phycobilisome via endosymbiosis. Other species of the genus have lost the phycobilisome and now contain a single membrane-bound chlorophyll-containing plastid. Like most cyanobacteria, dinophysids are rod-shaped, but their plastids are flattened and form a small disk. This structure, called a prostoclum, is located at the distal end of the cell, near the base of the rod. They are usually transparent, but they sometimes stain green or blue. The two-celled dinoflagellates have been studied in a variety of detail because of their importance as model organisms for the study of cell biology and biochemistry. They are known to be able to accumulate large amounts of copper in their cytoplasm, which is then stored in the mitochondria. The copper is then taken up by bacteria in the surrounding water, and they use it to fix carbon dioxide. Some species of dinoflagellates can also oxidize manganese. One of the most common species of dinoflagellate is Karenia brevis. The genome of this organism was sequenced in 2012. Dinoflagellates are unusual in that they contain more than one nucleus, located at different sites in the cell. The nucleus located in the prostoclum has been shown to have the ability to proliferate in vitro. The mitochondrial nucleus is a vestigial remnant of the endosymbiotic event, and is found at the base of the cell near the end of the rod-shaped body. The mitochondrial genome is also double-stranded, but the nuclear genome is single-stranded.

A species can be listed in two ways. A "species" under the act can be a true taxonomic species, a subspecies, or in the case of vertebrates, a "distinct population segment." The procedures are the same for both types except with the personorganization petition, there is a 90-day screening period.

Missile Defense Systems, contrary to what their title suggests, aren't intended solely for defensive measures. Their primary function is to prevent a counterattack by intercepting and neutralizing incoming missiles, based on the assumption that a preemptive attack would eliminate most of an adversary's nuclear arsenal, thereby ensuring the defensive systems can handle any subsequent retaliation without becoming overloaded. Whether used against countries like Iran or Russia, every nation has the legitimate right to implement whatever defense mechanisms they choose. However, these systems challenge the principle of Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD), which hinges upon both parties having equal destructive capabilities, making warfare a lose-lose situation with devastating consequences for both sides. A stronger defense could tilt the scales, granting one side the upper hand and potentially allowing them to decimate their opponent while sustaining minimal losses themselves. This imbalance raises concerns about triggering an escalating cycle of military enhancement between rival states, each striving to match or surpass the other’s capabilities. Such a dynamic transforms conflicts into contests that might seem winnable, leading to greater instability in international relations.

Autism is a neurodevelopmental disorder typically diagnosed in early childhood that affects communication and interpersonairelationships, including challenges with language and abstract thinking. Asperger syndrome is another neurodevelopmental condition involving notable struggles with social interactions, nonverbal cues, and exhibiting consistent behaviors and interests. ADHD, or Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, is a lifelong issue featuring constant distraction, restlessness, and occasionally impulsive actions. Are these explanations clear now?

To rephrase further, autism represents a range of conditions centered around social skill difficulties. Symptoms differ significantly among individuals and might encompass problems recognizing body language, feeling timid, or misunderstanding humor. Many people unknowingly interact with those on the autism spectrum, perceiving them as socially awkward due to varying degrees of severity within the spectrum. Asperger's syndrome falls under the umbrella term 'autism.' On the other hand, ADHD/ADD predominantly involves issues with sustaining attention, lacking drive, and struggling to concentrate. Its root cause lies in decreased neural activity levels, prompting the individual's brain to continuously seek fresh stimuli to compensate. Consequently, this leads to frequent episodes of boredom. Treatment options, such as stimulant medications like Adderall, help increase baseline brain activity, thus improving focus. It is worth mentioning that many individuals with autism or ADHD demonstrate exceptional skills in certain domains; some even possess remarkable talents dubbed as 'savant' abilities.

We often refer to physicians as 'Doctor,' even though most aren't Doctors of Medicine. Historically, this term signified someone with extensive knowledge and teaching abilities across various subjects, such as medicine, law, or philosophy. Although academic standards for earning the title 'Doctor' differ today, requiring completion of a doctoral program and thesis post-master's degree, surgeons are traditionally addressed as 'Mr.' or 'Mrs.' Surgeons lacked formal university training compared to physicians historically. Interestingly, at universities like Cambridge and Oxford, they confer distinct titles: Ph.D. and D.Phil., respectively. Both stemming from the Latin root meaning "to teach," indicating that individuals possessing these qualifications should utilize their expertise to educate others. While medical practitioners follow similar educational paths, obtaining a specific designation known as a Doctor of Medicine, other professions like lawyers ('Juris Doctor') and pharmacists ('Doctor of Pharmacy') also boast unique doctorate-level degrees. Addressing conventions may differ based on regional practices; for instance, some regions reserve the title 'Doctor' exclusively for medical professionals, whereas surgeages might just receive basic courtesies like 'Sir' or 'Madam.'

For the next three hundred years, Scotland was directly governed by the Parliament of Great Britain and the subsequent Parliament of the United Kingdom, both seated at Westminster, and the lack of a Parliament of Scotland remained an important element in Scottish national identity. Suggestions for a'devolved' Parliament were made before 1914, but were shelved due to the outbreak of the First World War. A sharp rise in nationalism in Scotland during the late 1960s fuelled demands for some form of home rule or complete independence, and in 1969 prompted the incumbent Labour government of Harold Wilson to set up the Kilbrandon Commission to consider the British constitution. One of the principal objectives of the commission was to examine ways of enabling more self-government for Scotland, within the unitary state of the United Kingdom. Kilbrandon published his report in 1973 recommending the establishment of a directly elected Scottish Assembly to legislate for the majority of domestic Scottish affairs.

Software development typically involves integrating existing components rather than building everything from scratch, which means potential security flaws could originate from third-party sources or open-source elements. Consequently, ensuring comprehensive cybersecurity for a product necessitates collaboration across different entities. Our research investigates how companies within a software ecosystem approach the exchange of data concerning identified weaknesses. Additionally, we evaluate these approaches against current best practices in cybersecurity. To gather insights, we conducted a qualitative analysis using a structured questionnaire consisting of sections addressing both suppliers and consumers. Findings indicate that firms are generally amenable to exchanging vulnerability data without viewing it as detrimental to their own digital security or commercial interests, although most recognize the sensitivity of this type of information. Nevertheless, while they support information sharing, they tend not to actively initiate it. Suppliers also reported limited customer demand for such details. Overall, the corporate stance on sharing vulnerability intelligence appears receptive yet largely passive, differing from recommended practices advocating active engagement and transparent communication among all parties involved.

Instead of fees rising to PS9,250 per year in the autumn, Jeremy Corbyn is proposing a complete handbrake turn in saying that university tuition should not cost students anything. It's one thing for a Labour leader to ignore or even misunderstand the issue - but it does no good at all when such an approach against student loans has been taken every time they've won power since 1997. The only reason I can think why he might take this line now would be because there are so many universities around who charge comparatively little compared with others. But what about when you're trying to get on the housing ladder? Do we still go against market logic and offer free museums or parks? No, it just doesn't work like that. We must face up to the fact that some things have price tags attached to them and they're valid ways of financing these activities. Universities do lots of decent work which needs funding too: the OU alone offers over 1,000 courses each year; my own institution (the Open University) provides distance learning as well as online content development services. The government already funds much of our teaching costs so we really don't need any more money from Parliament; instead we need greater flexibility in how we use resources. Of course, there are other types of spending where "free" could arguably apply, such as healthcare - but that's another story altogether!

The growth of electric cars and hybrids in recent years has been helped by the development of fast chargers, which can quickly charge a car's batteries. US electric car sales were up 28 percent in the first seven months of this year compared with the same period last year. The Obama administration said the plan was a part of a broader push to reduce emissions and improve fuel efficiency. But the administration also announced that it would be delaying the implementation of fuel-efficiency standards for trucks and buses. The new standards would have required heavy-duty vehicles to increase fuel efficiency by 20 percent by 2018. The administration said the delay would give it more time to study the issue.

We study the problem of joint information and energy transfer in a two-hop channel with a Radio frequency (RF) energy harvesting relay. We consider a finite battery size at the relay and aim to maximize the system throughput subject to the energy causality constraint and the battery capacity constraint. The channel includes a source node, an energy harvesting relay, and a destination node. The source node has information to transmit to the destination node, and the relay harvests energy from the RF signal transmitted by the source and then uses it to forward the information to the destination node. The energy harvested by the relay is used to power both the relay's circuits and the retransmission of the source's signal. To solve this problem, we propose a joint power allocation and relay selection algorithm that maximizes the system throughput while satisfying the energy causality constraint and the battery capacity constraint. The algorithm considers the trade-off between maximizing the harvested energy and minimizing the transmit power at the source node. It also selects the best relay to forward the information to the destination node based on the channel state. Simulation results show the effectiveness of our proposed algorithm in maximizing the system throughput while ensuring energy efficiency.

Occasionally a bisyllabic word is written with two characters that contain the same radical, as in hudie "butterfly," where both characters have the insect radical . A notable example is pipa (a Chinese lute, also a fruit, the loquat, of similar shape) - originally written as with the hand radical, referring to the down and up strokes when playing this instrument, which was then changed to (tree radical), which is still used for the fruit, while the character was changed to when referring to the instrument. In other cases a compound word may coincidentally share a radical without this being meaningful.

Rents in economic terms means a return on some input that exceeds its opportunity cost. The classic example is land in the city vs land far from a city, whatever it costs to build and maintain an apartment building. So what about the benefits of land use? It's less expensive than housing investment, as well as people who live here are more likely to invest in themselves while others don't have access to overpriced apartments or share with their families property values due to the lack of affordable housing options surrounding them (at least those directly affected by the city). Also, real estate can be valuable for personal wealth creation versus property value because that helps create jobs; businesses could also benefit if they're able to provide affordable housing where otherwise private developers might not want to compete against each other again financially because there aren't any vacancies outside of the city limits. That said, real estate isn't necessarily cheap either compared to apartments built near downtown Minneapolis, as neighboring communities such as North Minneapolis would need to pay much higher taxes and fees alone worth hundreds of thousands of dollars per month just to keep up with the competition. The impact this has had upon the economy has been considerable: The city spent 200 million replacing aging streetscape improvements on the east side last year - a project that could easily fund itself through a new tax credit program funded entirely locally controlled by the city. It should come as no surprise that land prices at the center of Minneapolis have fallen dramatically since the city launched the City Council's Land Use Zoning Review Commission two years ago despite the city being one of only five cities nationally without land transactions tax incentives, according to a recent report released Wednesday morning by the real estate experts National Farm Bureau Federation. Land transaction approvals under Minnesota Revised Statutes require bids submitted within 90 days prior to sales price estimation beginning Oct 1st. Land deals deliver payments between 20 and 50, depending on how close to your hometown you reside. A construction contract requires approval from the city council before the company can install structures above 20 feet tall onto the parcel owned by the owner. Land transactions occur when construction contracts expire, causing land owners to relinquish ownership rights later in the process after the purchase agreement expires. But all real estate transfers must pass through a commission established by the commission's members which pays out grants based solely on factors including buyer satisfaction associated with a deal approved and customer satisfaction. Land transactions go beyond that threshold amount into consideration as long as a developer agrees to pay the full compensation cost, including permitting costs and paving costs. These calculations include land acquisition costs like capital improvement projects, purchasing permits required for street repairs executed overseas and relocation expenses incurred during operations inside the city limits. Minnesota's Land Transaction Tax Credit Program annually receives statewide funding totaling 63 billion across the state but it doesn't cover all development purchases, such as roads, sidewalks and parks. Land deals fall outside this definition so reporting requirements vary greatly among municipalities nationwide, especially considering Minnesota does not pay for public transportation services currently. The city still needs federal assistance to finance an influx of new affordable housing units slated to arrive soon via the Minnesota Housing Fund. The city already received 29 million invested back homebuyers last year and has committed additional money toward affordable rentals needed for residents displaced by the COVID-19 pandemic. The city will also receive 22 million to help pay down existing debts stemming from the pandemic recession caused by the pandemic. However, the grants won't translate instantly enough once the apartments open next spring unless representatives from other jurisdictions agree to waive passage fees, which is currently set to expire June 30th 2021. Once those loans start paying off and income begins flowing, Minneapolis can expect to add another 180 rental units along with new homes purchased in the coming months thanks to the city's 5 million Housing Trust Fund.

If I force quit the program then we'd have another disaster like last time - where we had to start again from scratch thanks to corrupted code. The process of compiling took a few minutes. I was quite eager, to be honest. I hadn't tested the program since I'd updated the core files a few weeks back, and I wanted to see how they fared with the old structure. The screen pinged on to my right. I assembled the cameras, which would be its eyes, and then a microphone and a few speakers. It was essentially a human, but a better one. "Why?" it said. "Good morning, how was your afternoon, goodnight?" it slowly uttered. Uh oh, I'd done something wrong. I looked in the code. Wait a minute...... I enabled the "Reasoning" section again. "That's better" it muttered. I looked at the camera and responded. "It certainly is. If you saw the hours I'd put into you then you'd be grateful" "You love me, don't you?" it said, catching me off guard. It saw the visible shock in my eyes. "Why do you say that?" This paper derives a closed-form method for computing hybrid force-velocity control. The key idea is to maximize the kinematic conditioning of the mechanical system, which includes a robot, free objects, a rigid environment and contact constraints. The method is complete, in that it always produces an optimalnear optimal solution when a solution exists. It is efficient, since it is in closed form, avoiding the iterative search of previous work . We test the method on 78,000 randomly generated test cases. The method outperforms our previous search-based technique by being from 7 to 40 times faster, while consistently producing better solutions in the sense of robustness to kinematic singularity. We also test the method in several representative manipulation experiments.

James had been searching for his brother since the shadows fell upon them when the Believing members of the Believers began to fearlessly proceed over to the ruined house where he believed he belonged before he vanished along with the gunpowder barrel. But the Believers did not find James, and they could hear the sounds of rain pounding on the roof of the ruined house across the street. James' body lay buried beneath his father's grave beside his father's coffin awaiting burial by the Stone Temple Church Cemetery while the Believers prayed to God to restore their brother to his family. This story became a legacy if you're a believer, an enduring testimony of the faith that came alive in the aftermath of James' death even through the centuriesfrom the very first day the Believers showed up at the church to the last seconds they left James behind to bury James alive under the rubble below. But that tradition faded almost instantly once James died too soon so there are no sacred cows anymore about Jim's grave. Jim's remains will always remain hidden somewhere near the stone monument where he lived his final days, waiting for those who lived past him to finally see him burial alongside his mother and brother. "Jim" is a name that has become synonymous with the Believers, their faith founded still stronger than ever following James' death because the brothers were once among the most holy men of Christendom. It was Jim who laid the foundation for the Believers' new faith that took over Christianity forever, according to the Believers themselves, but was it not Jim himself who started the tradition? What happened to Jim in the last days of his life doesn't seem like much more than a coincidence any way you look at it. Instead, it seems like Jim was trying to prove that his faith existed beyond the gates of the Stone Temple Church, even as his siblings tried desperately to keep it alive despite the deadly darkness surrounding them. So could Jim have done something wrong? No one knows, save the Believers themselves. We don't really know how long the Believers have known each other, whether it was long ago or today. Only Jim survived his childhood and his adulthood, yet each step of that journey reveals itself anew every time we visit the church that once stood atop the crumbling ruins of James' home. There may be no such thing as a perfect church, but the Believers believe it must hold a place of honor to all believers worldwide thanks to Jim's dedication. That dedication lies within the Believers themselves, the brotherswho worship at the Stone Temple Church now called Mt. Olivet Church. It stands rememberable due to its simplicity, its simple architecture carved into the walls of a church filled with stained glass windows reflecting Jesus's eternal lifeblood. Jim's brother James' heart wounds seem etched into the stone walls as his sister Mary and her children seek to heal this broken heart and rebuild the faith that inspired their faith. James' funeral service rests inside Mt. Olivet Church, where James' ashes lie scattered amongst his classmates from grade school onward. There's a grand piano playing music outside the church, but the mournful silence surrounds someone dying alone amid the wreckage of his former home. This memorial serves as a reminder of who Jim was, why he fought this battle against the odds, and what he wanted most during his lifetime. Jim's death shouldn't be blamed solely for his own demise. It should also serve as a warning to others seeking salvation through the faith, allowing them to receive instead from the Lord through the Savior who has died for everyone else's sins. Now that Jim's life has been restored for everyone to gather together again, it makes sense that Jim should be remembered closely as the man who helped bring the Faith to life in his home town.

Tesla was 6 feet 2 inches (1.88 m) tall and weighed 142 pounds (64 kg), with almost no weight variance from 1888 to about 1926.:292 He was an elegant, stylish figure who loved good clothes and enjoyed buying clothes for himself as well as his friends.:262, 264 At the Astor House he was often seen in formal evening wear.:143 At times Tesla was a vegetarian, but at times he was not: he often dined on chicken and other white meats.:294 Tesla walked eight to ten miles each day, and he averaged 175 miles per month.:268 Tesla never smoked tobacco or used alcohol,:281, 282 although he once admitted to experimenting with opium in his youth. Tesla was an ardent fan of swimming, and said he thought he was the first American to swim a mile.:282 Tesla had a lifelong passion for pigeons, which he used in his experiments on mechanical flight and considered an ideal vehicle for carrying messages. Tesla claimed he once took care of a wounded bird that, after he nursed it back to health, followed him around the laboratory for the rest of its life.:282 Tesla was also a fan of pigeon racing, a sport that was at its height in the 1890s. Tesla wrote many articles for magazines and journals. Among his achievements, Tesla discovered the resonant frequency of the Earth and claimed to have developed a means to project electrical power long distance, with little to no loss across the intervening distance. He never put this last claim into practice, however, and eventually abandoned the idea. His patents included the Tesla coil and alternating current motor. He developed the first wireless-controlled robotic boat, and designed the world's first hydroelectric power plant. He also invented fluorescent lights, the bladeless turbine, and the wireless radio. Tesla is honored in the "Inventor's Hall of Fame" and a unit of magnetic induction is named after him.

A team of engineers in Korea has designed a new Virtual Reality glove that can create the sensation of touch when manipulating digital objects. VR gloves are not new, but they have been limited to creating animated images on screens using haptic feedback rather than the interaction with real objects. The glove could allow for more realistic interactions between digital items and could be used at home or in the workplace. The team's work is described in "Virtual Reality Gloves without Haptic Feedback," an article recently published in IEEE Transactions on Interactive Technology (IT). They use two metal plates and glue them together to form a base for their device which then contains four motors within it. These move the fingers and wrist within the glove so you feel what is happening as you manipulate your object through the touchscreen controls on your computer monitor. The team also found a way around a limitation - if you don't want fingers moving as quickly, you can turn off the motors. This approach allows the glove to maintain its tactile qualities while being able to function like any other virtual reality glove. It should be possible to design future devices based upon this technology and integrate similar functions into existing controllers, making it much easier for users to manipulate physical objects interactively through VR. A potential application would be the development of virtual assistants such as Siri who could appear in user interfaces by allowing us to link up our electronic gadgets via wi-fi.

Distinction among nearby poses and among symmetries of an object is challenging. In this paper, we propose a unified, group-theoretic approach to tackle both. Different from existing works which directly exploit the symmetry structure of individual objects or their properties, our formulation generalizes the concept of similarity between objects while preserving invariant geometric structures and interacting covariantly with the context in which they are embedded. We first define topological average distance as a function that measures how far each point on a manifold remembers its neighbors. Then we establish the notion of spherical regression metric for surfaces endowed with such averages (i.e., all points). Finally, we prove that sphere regression metrics can be naturally approximated by spherical harmonic functions. Remarkably, the convergence rate of these algorithms depends only on parameter values that characterize the object itself and not on those of its environment. To demonstrate their relevance, we give two examples: relocalization problem for two-dimensional graphs and clustering tasks based on boreal feature vectors extracted at various scales.

Mencap president Lord Rix urged the speaker of the House of Lords to push through legislation allowing those in his situation to be assisted to die. He had previously opposed euthanasia, but in a telephone interview with BBC Radio 4's Today programme said his decision was due to a deterioration in his health which he said was preventing him from dying a peaceful death. He said he had been suffering from Alzheimer's for some time and that he would be happy if he had just two years left to live. His comments were part of a wider debate about assisted suicide and euthanasia in the wake of the death of his friend, the 66-year-old former Conservative MP, Brian Sedgemore, in his home in Oxford. Sedgemore, who had had multiple sclerosis since he was in his 20s, was supported by a physician. Lord Rix said he was hopeful that the House of Lords would give quick consideration to legislation passed by the Commons on assisted dying. He urged the government to respect the wishes of Sedgemore, who had said he would have wished to die in the same way. Lord Rix said: "I have no wish to be a martyr. But I would like to get my message out, which is that I can see there is a pressing need for legislation to allow assisted dying, and that I hope it will be implemented as soon as possible. "I would hate for people to think I was in the same category as Brian Sedgemore. I would never have given him an injection myself, but I can see how it might have come about. The idea of a dose of morphine, possibly with a little bit of codeine, to ease the pain is not totally out of this world. The government should not stand in the way." His comments follow those by Sedgemore's partner of 21 years, Jennifer Green, who said she was shocked by the government's suggestion that the MP's death was "premeditated." "It was a horrible thing to say, really. I would have thought the government would have known Brian and would have known his family. I am shocked they could have come out with a statement like that," Green told the Guardian. Sedgemore, a former parliamentary aide, was a member of the hardline leftwing Social Democratic party before joining the Labour party in 1981. He was MP for Hackney North and Stoke Newington from 1987 to 1997, when he lost to the Lib Dem Lynne Featherstone. In the mid-1990s, Sedgemore campaigned for an assisted-dying bill, which was rejected by the House of Lords. He also campaigned against war in Iraq and had been a key ally of Tony Benn. He had a long-running campaign to promote disabled people's rights, including setting up a network of libraries for the blind, and was vice-president of the disability rights organisation UNITE, which he helped to set up in 1997. In 2009, Sedgemore admitted that he had been diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in the early 1980s and that his condition had worsened in recent years. According to his family, he died on 11 April and they have decided not to seek a postmortem. This article was amended on 17 April 2011. Debate portals and similar web platforms constitute one of the main text sources in computational argumentation research and its applications. While the corpora built upon these sources are rich of argumentatively relevant content and structure, they also include text that is irrelevant, or even detrimental, to their purpose. In this paper, we present a precision-oriented approach to detecting such irrelevant text in a semi-supervised way. Given a few seed examples, the approach automatically learns basic lexical patterns of relevance and irrelevance and then incrementally bootstraps new patterns from sentences matching the patterns. In the existing args.me corpus with 400k argumentative texts, our approach detects almost 87k irrelevant sentences, at a precision of 0.97 according to manual evaluation. With low effort, the approach can be adapted to other web argument corpora, providing a generic way to improve corpus quality.

Title IV of the 1978 Spanish constitution invests the Consentimiento Real (Royal Assent) and promulgation (publication) of laws with the monarch of Spain, while Title III, The Cortes Generales, Chapter 2, Drafting of Bills, outlines the method by which bills are passed. According to Article 91, within fifteen days of passage of a bill by the Cortes Generales, the sovereign shall give his or her assent and publish the new law. Article 92 invests the monarch with the right to call for a referendum, on the advice of the president of the government (commonly referred to in English as the prime minister) and the authorisation of the cortes.

Conventional methods for constructing backhaul networks involve radio-frequency backhauls (RF) or optical fibers (OF). Although RF is more budget-friendly than OF, it has limitations in supporting higher data rate needs. Free-space optics (FSO), on the other hand, provides a balance between high data rate capabilities and reasonable costs, making it a viable alternative. Nevertheless, FSO is vulnerable to environmental factors such as rainfall and fog. In this study, we propose a combined approach using both RF and FSO, introducing a novel hybrid RFFSO backhaul methodology. Our objective is to reduce the expense of the backhaul network by selecting either OF or hybrid RFFSO connections between base stations (BS) while meeting criteria related to data rate, connectivity, and dependability. We demonstrate that when certain realistic assumptions are made regarding the costs of OF and hybrid RFFSO links, the issue simplifies into a maximum weight clique challenge, solvable with manageable computational effort. Preliminary simulation outcomes suggest our suggested strategy performs nearly optimally, particularly when considering practical pricing for hybrid RFFSO connections.

Tycho's ball flew over the schoolyard fence. He quickly climbed over the fence and threw the ball back over. On his way back over the fence, Tycho's coat got stuck. There was a big hole where his sleeve used to be! "Oh no!" Tycho cried. "I have to go home and change." The bell rang. "Hurry up, Tycho," called his friend, Olive. "We don't want to be late for class." Tycho climbed back over the fence. He was in a hurry now. He ran to the classroom and slipped inside just as Mrs. Brisbane closed the door. "You're late, Tycho," Mrs. Brisbane said. "I'm sorry, Mrs. Brisbane," he replied. "I had to go home and change. I tore my coat." Olive giggled. "Tycho tore it," she said. Tycho frowned. "I didn't mean to." "Never mind," Mrs. Brisbane said. "Go hang up your coat and sit down." "I don't have a coat," Tycho said. "Of course you do," Mrs. Brisbane said. "I see it right there." "That's not mine," Tycho said. "I mean, it is, but it's the new coat my parents gave me to replace the one I tore." "Oh," Mrs. Brisbane said. Tycho hung his coat on his hook. He took his seat and opened his notebook. "Would you like to tell the class what happened?" Mrs. Brisbane asked. Tycho nodded. He explained how he'd thrown the ball over the fence and how his coat got stuck. "What happened next?" Mrs. Brisbane asked. "I pulled my coat loose, but the fence ripped the sleeve right off," Tycho said. "I'm sorry to hear that, Tycho," Mrs. Brisbane said. "You might want to tell your parents they can bring your new coat to school. We don't want you to miss any more time." Tycho nodded. He understood. "In class, we're going to make paper plate pumpkins for our pumpkin patch," Mrs. Brisbane said. "We'll also make up a story about the pumpkin patch." "Can I tell the class about how Humphrey and I tried to help Mr. Sweeney's pumpkins grow?" Olive asked. "I know all about that," Rosie said. "That would be nice, Olive," Mrs. Brisbane said. "I wish we could go out to the garden and see the real pumpkins," Olive said. Mrs. Brisbane looked out the window. "It's drizzling out there," she said. "I think we'll stay inside today." A 1-carat gem weighs approximately 200 milligrams; thus, a 9-carat stone would be three times heavier than a 3-carat one. The high cost of a 9-carat diamond isn't due to its scarcity but rather because there are fewer quality ones available compared to those with just 3 carats. It's worth mentioning that while diamonds themselves aren't exceedingly uncommon, their perceived rarity has been influenced by companies like De Beers, who limit the supply to maintain higher prices. However, what I refer to here is specifically the infrequency of well-cut 9 versus 3-carat diamonds being released into the market.

With the shortage of physicians and surgeons and increase in demand worldwide due to situations such as the COVID-19 pandemic, there is a growing interest in finding solutions to help meet this challenge. One potential solution could be using robots for some surgical procedures. The use of robotic systems has been proven over the past few years and considered safe compared with traditional laparoscopy or open surgery for certain types of surgeries when performed by experienced surgeons (see "Robots: A tool that can significantly change medicine. However, robot-assisted colonoscopes are still experimental devices because they involve more technical complexity than other endoscopic procedures. In order to facilitate the development of these new technologies, the European Commission recently published a communication on the future challenges facing healthcare, which included how technology might address them during the next five years. It stressed that technological developments will have an impact not only on patient care but also on clinical practice and education. As part of its strategy, it introduced Horizon 2020, one of its key programmes, dedicated specifically to developing health-related technologies and innovations. One particular project under consideration regards colonoscopy, focusing on different issues including improving image quality, eliminating any contact between human hands and the instrument, optimizing safety features and ensuring better results. In addition, developers announced plans to conduct pilot tests to assess their feasibility before implementing commercialization strategies. According to a study from Yale University Medical School released last year about colorectal cancer screening trends, colonoscopies had remained unchanged since 2013 despite the existence of newer techniques that were expected to make diagnosis easier and decrease the number of people who would need further examinations based on symptoms alone. The researchers believe their findings support efforts made around Europe in reducing unnecessary diagnostic testing through increased awareness among patients of the risks associated with getting screened too often - even if much remains unknown regarding what precisely should happen at each level of screening. A recent survey conducted by Gallup showed that while many Americans do feel comfortable undergoing medical treatment without talking directly with doctors, less than half say they like having reminders sent to their mobile phone regarding upcoming appointments. In order to reach out to patients who want personalized notifications instead of generic messages containing lists of preventive services offered by hospitals and practices, companies have developed user-friendly apps that allow individuals to keep track of all scheduled appointments related to his or her own wellness management program online. To date, most platforms offer reporting tools allowing users to monitor their weight, blood sugar levels, cholesterol readings, physical activity levels and medication intake. Some websites even include calculators tailored according to individual needs so that visitors can evaluate whether existing medical conditions may affect certain aspects of well-being.

Kenya's services sector, which contributes 61 of GDP, is dominated by tourism. The tourism sector has exhibited steady growth in most years since independence and by the late 1980s had become one of Kenya's three largest sources of foreign exchange earnings. Tourism grew rapidly during as a result of the purchase of nearly 400,000 new tourist accommodation units (hotelsmotels), at an average cost per unit [about US28 million]. This activity was largely financed through government loans from abroad, mostly from East European countries; interest on these loans became a burden for the national budget. In 1994 the Kenyan Government introduced legislation to regulate the development and operation of hotels; this led directly to a decline in hotel construction that lasted until 1996. Nevertheless, the number of tourists visiting increased steadily over because Kenya's major civil wars prevented international travel. As such troubled times receded, tourism began increasing once more around 1998. Official statistics indicate that between 2000 and 2005, annual visitor numbers averaged 1.5million in 2004 alone. By contrast, total revenue jumped 30 annually to 1.7 billion in 2006 and 3-year rates average 10. Tourism contributed about 15 percent of exports in 2011. Of particular importance are roughly 2.2 million domestic tourists who visit every year, travelling both within the country and internationally.[8] A further 0.959 million Kenyans visited other African nations in 2010,[1011] with trips to South Africa being the top choice among them.[12] National parks and sanctuaries are also popular destinations. Wildlife viewing ranks second only to safaris in attracting visitors to their natural environments. National Parks contribute significantly to employment opportunities and income generation for local communities. Nearly 60 of all jobs in Nairobi come directly or indirectly related to wildlife protection activities. From 2001 to 2009, Tanzania and Zambia were identified by the World Travel Organization as among the world leaders in providing high value-added safari experiences.[13] These two countries have long been known for offering excellent game viewing but have not traditionally played well with western tourists due to political instability and wariness regarding disease transmission. However there has recently been significant investment in improving facilities and working closely together with aid agencies to develop best practice health protocols while enhancing security measures needed to ensure safety of travellers.[14] Nearly 90 per cent of travellers to Kenya spend less than six days here. The lion population is estimated to be 700 - 1000 individuals with approximately 100 lions roaming areas outside national park boundaries. There are around 200 elephants in Amboseli Park where they can often be seen grazing along roadsides throughout Nairobi. Elephants like ambling slowly and will sometimes stand still in open spaces if you walk close enough. It is safest to stay under cover when observing them. The giraffe population is large, ranging in age from newborn calves up to old matriarchs. They tend to move across savannah lands searching out fresh grasses and green leaves. If approached too quickly it may appear as though they intend to charge so stick your hand out and wave before stepping aside! Policy changes enacted in 2007 restricted elephant hunting. With the establishment of coalition rangers including private volunteers, poaching levels decreased.[15] Despite these efforts, some experts argue that illegal ivory trade continues,[16] particularly between Somalia[17] and neighbouring states. Illegal wildlife trafficking severely threatens conservation in east Africa; it undermines long term ecotourism goals.[18] Examples include rhinos whose horns are used to produce cocaine.

As technology continues to advance, there is no doubt that the human touch will remain an essential aspect of customer service.

This study introduces T-Net, an advanced architecture incorporating a compact encoder-decoder within an existing EDiED framework. Unlike U-Net's singular concatenate layer connecting the encoder and decoder, T-Net innovatively organizes pooling and upsampling during both encoding and decoding stages, enabling it to produce multi-scale feature maps within one unit. Consequently, this allows comprehensive utilization of features ranging from low to high levels originated from the encoder, facilitating the generation of highly accurate segmentations via the decoder. Our assessment involved comparing U-Net with two versions of T-Net—one standard and another fine-tuned specifically for primary vessel segmentation in coronary angiography imagery. Notably, our results showed that T-Net achieved a superior Dice Similarity Coefficient score (DSC) by 0.095 and 0.170 when compared to U-Net, respectively. Furthermore, analysis of convolutional layer activations revealed that T-Net commenced mask prediction at earlier decoder stages relative to U-Net. Based on these findptaions, we anticipate that T-Net holds promise as a potent tool for addressing analogous challenges encountered in the realm of medical image segmentation.

Charon gently paddled the long oar across the dark waters, silence his only companion in the foggy waters of Styx. He craned his bony neck as he stared off into the mist and rain, listening for any sound that would indicate the presence of a soul. He knew it would not be easy. The grief-stricken, the weeping, the tortured, the angry and confused all came to the river, but none were always ready to step off the bank into the boat and on to the next life. No one knew this better than Charon, who had been ferrying the dead to the underworld for countless centuries. Some souls were stubborn, preferring to cling to the belief that there was something else waiting for them when they reached the end of the journey. There was no explanation for their disbelief, no reason for their fear. Charon did not judge them, simply did his duty, waiting patiently, determined to carry out the task until the last breath had been exhaled. For a thousand years, he had been waiting. He had ferried souls from every corner of the Earth, from the great cities of Rome and Paris, from the vast expanses of the plains of Russia and the steaming jungles of the Far East, from the icy tundras of the Arctic to the steamy jungles of the Amazon. He had ferried souls from the battlefields of the American Civil War and the trenches of World War I. From the beaches of Normandy, the shores of Guadalcanal, the fields of Vietnam and the deserts of the Gulf War. He had ferried souls from the World Trade Center on 911. He had seen many wars, many natural disasters, and the death of millions of souls. It was hard for him to believe he was still waiting. The long oar dipped into the water with a barely perceptible splash. Charon's ears twitched, and he stared through the misty fog. He heard it again, a little louder this time. There was nothing he could do but wait. He had a boat full of souls, and while he would not force them to leave the comfort of the world they knew, he would have to wait for the boat to empty before he could go in search of the one who called to him. He waited, listening to the gentle lapping of the waters against the sides of the boat. He had been waiting for more than a thousand years. He waited for what seemed like an eternity. He looked up at the dark clouds hanging low over the waters. Rain began to fall, and Charon cowered slightly in the bottom of the boat, letting the water run down his face and neck. He closed his eyes, and felt the dampness seeping into his bones. When he opened them again, the darkness was gone. The clouds had cleared and the fog had lifted, and the waters of Styx were clear and bright in the morning sun. Charon looked down into the bottom of the boat. They were all gone. He looked over at the bank, and saw a lone figure standing there. He could barely make him out, but he recognized him. He had waited so long for this moment. Charon stood up and began to walk toward the bank. He reached the edge of the boat and extended a bony hand to help the soul step out of the boat. It had been such a long time since he had carried a soul. He would not make that mistake again. The man looked back at Charon and gave him a small smile, then began to walk up the bank. Charon nodded and smiled. He had waited so long. He had finally ferried a soul. The utilization of attention mechanisms bridging encoders and decoders has gained widespread adoption across various applications such as object recognition, image captioning, visual question response, and neural machine translation, leading to notable enhancements in their respective performances. This study introduces a novel approach called bottom-up gated hierarchical attention (GHA) specifically designed for image captioning tasks. Unlike conventional methods, our architecture integrates a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) as the decoder capable of discerning diverse concepts within distinct layers; each concept corresponds uniquely to specific regions within an image. To capitalize on these insights, we implement the GHA system wherein lower-level concepts are synthesized into higher-order ones while concurrently directing lower-level focused features towards upper levels for accurate prediction generation. Implementing this method results in substantial improvements over single-layered attention models—demonstrated by our model's increase in the CIDEr metric from 0.923 to 0.999, rivaling cutting-edge techniques that leverage attribute amplification and Reinforcement Learning (RL). Further comprehensive evaluations were conducted to examine both the CNN decoder and the newly introduced GHA technique. Results indicate that deeper decoder networks do not necessarily yield superior outcomes, with excessively deep convolutional decoders prone to training instability or 'collapsing'. Additionally, the source code used throughout this research can be accessed through provided links.

A recent study by the National Institute of Dairy and Frozen Treats (NIDFT) has uncovered the key to keeping ice cream creamy, not crunchy. To break free from Earth's gravitational pull, one must attain escape velocity, which decreases as distance increases. This means that a slower-moving rocket could eventually achieve escape velocity once it descends far enough. However, carrying excessive fuel adds weight, making it harder to reach greater heights without additional propulsion. Thus, rockets typically consume most fuel during initial acceleration, then continue moving swiftly towards a low Earth orbit.

In terms of physics, there is no restriction on leaving Earth gradually. Escape velocity varies according to altitude, allowing an object to break free with diminishing speeds as it ascends. Imagine throwing a ball straight upwards from the Moon while disregarding air resistance – as it rises, both the force of gravity weakens and its velocity decreases. Throwing the ball with sufficient force results in gravity reducing at a slower rate compared to its deceleration, ensuring it won't return to the surface. Regardless of the direction of launch, as long as it's not directed downward, achieving a speed above escape velocity guarantees departure from the celestial body. For example, launching from a tall structure necessitates a lower escape velocity due to the shorter distance traveled. It's important to note that these concepts apply specifically to escape velocity, whereas reaching the edge of space involves different considerations.

It was a necessary chore, attending these sessions. Without a minimal functional certification of mental health, he would lose access to the colony's automated systems, the only thing now keeping him alive. It was just one of the hoops he had to jump through, and by far his least favourite. "Hello again..... Technician Chang." The waxy mannequin face of the therapeutic droid jerked creepily into life as its tinny voice ran through the same pre-recorded lines. "How are you feeling today?" "Just fine, doc." His reply came through a strained smile, carefully ticking all the boxes in the droid's mental health and wellbeing checklist. "A little lonely, but I keep active." "Why do you think you are..... lonely?" "Oh I don't know, doc. I think it's something to do with that meteor shower killing everyone else in the colony, you remember?" The droid's head tilted slightly in a mimicry of thoughtfulness. "You have spoken of this before..... The system shows no record of such an event." "Well no, not after the mainframe was smashed to pieces by all that space rock. It's a miracle anything survived." "Do you consider yourself..... divine..... Technician Chang?" "No," he sighed. "Just unlucky. It's not that kind of miracle." He rubbed his face, already fatigued by the talk. "Can we just skip to the part where you diagnose me with colonist isolational delusional disorder and give me my partial systems access for the month?" The droid's head tilted to the side again erratically. "There is no need for hostility..... Technician Chang." He threw up his hands, suddenly afraid. "No hostility, doc, no hostility." He beamed, manically, in an attempt at friendliness. "Everybody's calm here. Please continue. I'm cooperating." The remainder of the session continued as normal, he answered the droid's questions about his habits succinctly, his voice draining of life with every question. When it was done, he snapped up his systems access and quick marched out of the wellness assessment room toward the mess and his monthly ration of alcohol, fuming and miserable, as he always did. The droid waited a moment, until a section of wall behind it slid to one side and turned to greet the men in white coats much more smoothly than it had moved before Chang. Its voice was more sophisticated and less mechanical now, very nearly human, with that undertone of silicon that was mandated for almost all humanoid constructs. "The subject is showing more strain with every session, doctors, as I'm sure you've seen." "Yes," said the foremost of the scientists as he distractedly scribbled on a notepad. "Yes, it is fascinating. The machine is utterly convinced that it's human, with all the human frailties." He turned to his colleagues. "Soon we'll see if an AI can go insane."

I love her like she's my daughter and it's been so good to watch her grow up, but sometimes I feel like I have two children and I feel like one of them is missing," she said. The story of how the syndrome came to light has become something of a myth. One story is that the eye was discovered when the owner of a boat was floating in the water and the eye came into view. "I'm not sure how that story got started," said Dr. Joan Werth, an ophthalmologist at the University of Minnesota Medical Center who is also the PIO. "I do know that I remember having a patient with this, and I think it's very rare," she said. According to Dr. Werth, about 10 to 20 cases of sclerocornea have been documented in the medical literature. It is estimated that about 1 in 10,000 people have it. "The number of people who are affected by this is really very small," she said. The most common symptoms are distorted vision, double vision and decreased vision. If the disease progresses, there may be pain and problems with seeing near objects. Dr. Werth says that because of the condition, the person who has sclerocornea will have trouble seeing well in bright light and poor contrast vision. It is not a disease that affects the entire eye. "It affects one eye and the person has a slightly different appearance. They have a cataract in the other eye," she said. "There's no one way to describe it. It's hard to see if it's really one eye or two eyes. It's not the same person." In her case, she was first diagnosed with sclerocornea in 1976. Her ophthalmologist found that the eye was attached to the cornea but that the iris was missing. She had been living with the eye for 10 years before it was found. Dr. Werth said that it was the right thing to do to remove the eye. "I was concerned that if I didn't remove it that she would continue to have pain and problems and not be able to see. I did not want to keep her eye in. I thought it was a good decision," she said. The condition was discovered when she was 10 years old. She went to the University of Minnesota Medical Center because she had been experiencing blurred vision and was concerned about her vision. "The reason that I went to the University of Minnesota was because my ophthalmologist was from there. He had worked with them before. He recommended that I go to the University of Minnesota," she said. The eye was removed at the University of Minnesota Medical Center and the sclerocornea was repaired. "I was the first case in the world that was removed and repaired," she said. She was in her early 20s when she had the surgery. The eye is in her head and will never be replaced. "It's kind of a quirk in my life," she said. "I can't see very well and I have to wear glasses. I'm not happy about that, but I can see. I don't know what I'd do without my glasses." Now, the eye is part of her history. "I have it on my shelf. I look at it every day," she said.

Progress in Web technologies allows for personalization agents that help users meet their intricate requirements for tracking and compiling information by consistently interrogating various unstable data repositories. These agents, however, encounter challenges related to scaling up while striving to serve numerous clients without compromising on meeting each client's specific demands. This study introduces a method based on complex execution intervals (CEIs), which are derived from basic execution intervals (EIs) to represent user preferences, and applies pre-existing offline approximation techniques as a reference point for enhancing the thoroughness of CEIs capture. We propose three heuristic methods aimed at tackling the live issue of arranging queries to fulfill complicated user profiles. The initial approach focusages solely on attributes of singular EIs, whereas the subsequent pair incorporates insights from every EI within the CEI. Through comprehensive tests using actual logs and simulated datasets, our findings reveal that strategies employing knowledge of CEIs outperform others under diverse conditions.

Fast Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is highly in demand for many clinical applications in order to reduce the scanning cost and improve the patient experience. This can also potentially increase patient throughput and reduce the need for repeat scans. In the context of this project, the problem of accelerating MRI is treated as an image reconstruction problem, i.e., the main goal is to reconstruct a high-quality image from under-sampled k-space data. This project is a joint collaboration between Dr. Hanjoong Jo and Dr. Haris Vikalo. Dr. Hanjoong Jo is a professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the University of Illinois at Chicago (UIC), and the leader of the Medical Imaging Research Laboratory (MIR Lab). Dr. Haris Vikalo is an assistant professor at the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering (ECE) at the University of Iowa (UI). This collaboration brings together the complementary expertise of the two groups in order to address the problem of accelerating MRI. In this project, we propose a novel image reconstruction algorithm for MRI based on the following premise: in order to accelerate MRI, we should capture the sparsity of the image in the spatial domain, and the sparsity of the image in the Fourier domain. Our algorithm is a regularized image reconstruction algorithm. We use the 1-norm of the image to capture the spatial sparsity, and the 1-norm of the Fourier transform of the image to capture the Fourier sparsity. This idea of enforcing sparsity of the Fourier transform of an image is novel. To the best of our knowledge, it has never been employed for the purpose of accelerating MRI. The algorithm is computationally efficient, because it does not require the computation of the Fourier transform of the image. This project is currently funded by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) through the National Institute of Biomedical Imaging and Bioengineering (NIBIB).
